Episode One: Welcome to Danim City

The Book Edition

Novelised from the final script. The script remains canonical on any conflict.

1. Two Kinds of Problems

Welcome to Danim City.

You will find it hidden away in the roots of England, if you know where to stop looking at maps and start looking at people. Home to some of the wonders of the world, or so the brochures insist: the Danim Bridge, stretching its iron arches across the river like a man showing off an old scar. Danim View, where tourists photograph a skyline that has stopped photographing back. The Pendulum, the great clock at the centre of everything, ticking forward for a city that mostly looks backward.

It was mid-morning the day this story begins, high summer, the sun well up and the light flat and honest, the kind that leaves nothing anywhere to hide. Red double-decker buses crawled through traffic. The underground rumbled beneath the streets like an old man's stomach. Long has the world forgotten this once popular city, which continues to suffer beautifully, bringing in tourism as the years go by.

Look closer, though. Below the bright rooftops there were homeless men sleeping against the roadside. Boarded-up shops. Reconstruction barriers on roads that had been half closed for years. Sirens, always, somewhere.

While the economy struggled, new leaders brought new laws. New laws brought new problems.

And new problems, as the city was about to be reminded, bring new leaders.

That morning, a figure in a dark cloak sprinted past a group of pedestrians so fast that none of them could honestly say what they had seen. A gust of wind. A blur. Gone. One of them looked over her shoulder, frowning at the empty street, and decided she had imagined it.

She had not.

2. The Fight

The cloaked figure moved through the streets with silent precision, weaving between people, ducking scaffolding, cutting through alleys. His breathing was controlled. Measured. He was running, but not the way frightened men run. He ran the way a man walks when he happens to be in a hurry.

Then, without warning: BOOM.

A figure clad in black and gold dropped out of the sky and landed directly in his path, hard enough to crack the pavement. The attacker rose slowly, rolling his neck, taking his time about it, the way people do when they believe the ending is already written.

It was a quiet stretch of urban Danim, overhead passes and train-line signage, thin rather than empty at that hour. It was also wide open and it was bright, and every person on that street could see exactly what was about to happen. Which was the problem. Whatever else this was, it was not hidden.

The air went still. Neither man moved. The cloaked figure's hood shadowed his face. The attacker's eyes burned behind his mask.

Then they both moved at once.

The fight exploded. Hands, elbows, knees. Every strike fast, sharp, precise. The city noise seemed to drop away out of respect, until all that remained was impact, scraping feet, and breath. The cloaked figure blocked a straight punch and answered with a low sweep. The attacker anticipated it, sprang back, launched a combination: two hooks and a spinning back fist. The cloaked figure took the first hook on his forearm, slipped the second, and let the back fist clip him.

He recovered. He did not touch the place where he had been hit.

The attacker pressed. Every strike a step ahead, every combination designed to be the last one. The cloaked figure gave ground, absorbing pressure, and to anyone watching it looked like he was losing. But things kept happening that saved him. A block arriving at the exact right moment. A lean that took him out of range by millimetres. A pivot that turned a direct hit into a graze. It was far too consistent to be luck.

Then came the smirk. Small. Almost invisible under the hood.

The attacker saw it, and his rhythm broke for a fraction of a second, and the fraction told him everything. He became enraged. Precision gave way to fury. His strikes started landing on the world instead of his opponent: a parked car's window shattered, a street sign bent, a wall cracked. He was no longer fighting the cloaked figure. He was swinging at everything.

And the cloaked figure kept positioning himself, again and again, between the attacker and the bystanders, as if he had known all along where the violence would spill.

The attacker noticed. Something clicked behind his mask, and a realisation crossed what could be seen of his face. He fired a zipline cable from his wrist, anchored it to a building, and zipped upward, scaling the wall in seconds. From high above he looked down.

"Cuz... you're a joke."

He pointed his weapon at the cloaked figure. Then his eyes drifted, deliberately, to a woman clutching her child, trying to flee the wreckage.

"I don't think you understand what man is all about."

A crimson aura began to ooze from him, subtle as heat distortion, and the air around him shimmered with menace.

3. Don't Move

The cloaked figure did not hesitate. He was already moving toward the pedestrians, scanning for anyone still in danger, vaulting a crushed car bonnet without breaking stride.

This isn't a fight, he thought, with the calm of a man reading a newspaper. It's a temper tantrum.

The attacker launched from the building. Ahead of his flight path a line of bladed rope waited; he spun to avoid it, and mid-spin he hurled his blade, not at his opponent, but at the woman and child, before ziplining away to another wall.

The cloaked figure, still sprinting, pulled a knife and threw it without looking like he had thrown it. The two blades met in the air and fell together, harmless, ringing on the pavement.

He reached the woman and her child and pushed them gently but firmly back against the wall.

"Don't move."

His voice was calm. Completely calm. Not a trace of urgency in it.

The woman, clutching her child, looked up into the hood. Even in that much daylight the shadow inside it held. She did not get a face. She got pieces of one: the line of a jaw, the shape of a cheekbone, the mouth. Enough to build something out of, and nowhere near enough to describe to anybody afterwards.

What she got clearly was the demeanour. He was completely relaxed. Nothing in him was braced. His eyes were serene, as if this were routine, as if she were the most important thing in the world right now and all the rest of it was noise happening somewhere else.

She felt safe. She did not understand why. She simply did.

He was already gone, cutting across the street, shoving a man clear of a doorway, redirecting a teenager frozen in panic, while above them the attacker hunted new targets.

This is what happens, the cloaked figure thought, when you give power to those who haven't earned it.

The attacker, gliding toward a second group of pedestrians, spotted a sticky bomb clinging to the wall along his path, counting down. He smirked, changed course with a thread of cable, and clung to the face of another building, satisfied with himself.

The cloaked figure pressed a button on his glove. The bomb stopped counting. Deactivated, like a toy with its batteries out.

Then he looked up at the attacker on the wall, and at the landmines blinking quietly around the man's position, which the man had not yet noticed. He crouched. And he launched himself upward.

He hurtled toward the attacker with his cloak trailing behind him like the tail of something falling the wrong way, and everything slowed, and his thoughts stayed level. Life seemed easier back then, he mused, closing the distance. Things like this were left to the military... maybe.

The attacker saw him coming, and what unsettled him was not the speed. It was the face inside the hood. Calm, mid-flight. Completely and utterly unbothered.

The attacker scrambled to reposition. His eyes found the landmines. They went wide.

What does it matter, the cloaked figure thought. All the same.

Too late.

BOOM.

The collision triggered every planted device at once. The explosion ripped through the upper floor of the building, cascading glass and rubble into the street, close enough to the scattering bystanders to part their hair, and not one centimetre closer. Almost as if the falling building itself had been aimed.

Inside, the attacker crashed through an office, rolled, skidded, caught himself on his cables, and came up on one knee, breathing hard. He looked left. Nothing. He looked right.

The cloaked figure was standing at the window. Calm. Finished. One hand resting on the window frame as he considered the street below, the way a man stands at his own kitchen window.

"Please," he said. "Just leave."

The rage drained out of the attacker's face and something else replaced it, because in that moment, with the figure's hand resting on the frame, he saw it. A mark on the wrist. Small. Raised. A burn, old and healed and deliberate. Not a tattoo. Something done by hand, a long time ago.

His face changed completely.

"What... the... fuck?"

The cloaked figure dropped from the window and was gone into the daylight, which ought to be harder than vanishing into the dark, and somehow was not.

The attacker stayed on one knee, listening to the sirens grow. "Who are..." he said, to nobody, and did not finish.

High above the flashing lights, on a rooftop, the cloaked figure crouched and watched the ambulances arrive, the bystanders shepherded to safety, the yellow tape going up.

"What a waste," he said, and stood, and walked away.

4. Sharon

Below, police cars screeched in, officers spilling out with their orders. "Check the building!"

One more car pulled up. The door opened on a heeled boot and black trousers, and Sharon Young stood up out of the driver's seat and looked, immediately, exactly where nobody else was looking: up. The attacker was crouched at the lip of the ruined wall, surveying the commotion.

For half a second, across all that distance, they made eye contact.

"Sharon! I need you to call in a 4.02, now!"

She glanced at the officer shouting at her, one second, no more, and looked back up.

"But sir, there is a man over..."

The wall was empty.

"...there."

"Sharon! Wake up!"

"Sir!" she snapped, alert again, professional again. But her mind stayed on the empty ledge.

The camera of the night pulled upward along the broken building, past the wound in its side, and just before the scene ended something moved in a far alley. A dark figure, swinging away between buildings, gone before anyone else could have seen it.

Somewhere below a voice said, "We need to take some of these people in for questioning," and faded.

The crime scene, seen properly, was worse than the first glance suggested. The building's upper floor had been ripped open, a gaping hole exposing mangled office furniture and dangling cables. Police tape cut sharp yellow lines across the street. Three ambulances sat with their doors open, paramedics wrapping civilians in thermal blankets. A fire crew stood staring up at the damage like men trying to argue with physics. Reporters had arrived. Neighbours leaned out of windows. A kid filmed on his phone.

We leave her there.

5. The Sock

A television bled the day's chaos into a small living room in North Danim.

"Breaking news... A mysterious incident has been reported in Central Danim. Witnesses claim to have seen figures fighting near the scene, and a massive hole was left in the side of a building. Authorities are still investigating..."

Nobody was watching it. Upstairs, a thirteen-year-old boy was on his knees on his bedroom floor, arm buried under a pile of clothes, hunting a sock.

"Where are you..." the boy muttered.

His room was a landscape of dropped things: clothes over chairs, school books stacked at angles that disproved geometry, a game controller hanging off the bed by its cable. He found the sock. Held it up. Sniffed it. His whole face folded in on itself. He considered his options. There were no options.

"...it'll do."

He pulled it on and went to war with his shoe, one hand hauling the tongue, the other jamming his heel, sitting on the edge of the bed while the shoe rejected the terms.

Then he heard it. Outside. Muffled through the window: raised voices. Not shouting exactly, but that particular tone that carries through glass, the sound of kids deciding something is about to happen.

He looked up, shoe half on. He hopped to the window.

Down the road, near the end of the block, a boy in a black hoodie stood surrounded by four other kids. White letters across the chest of the hoodie read LIT. The four were in his face, circling, one pushing his shoulder, another pointing, getting closer. He could not hear the words. He did not need to.

The boy in the LIT hoodie did not back up. His posture did not change. He was smaller than all four of them, and he stood like he was alone in a field.

One of the bigger kids shoved him hard. The boy stumbled back a step.

His hand went to the window latch.

The boy in the LIT hoodie moved.

It was fast. Not regular-kid fast. Something else. He sidestepped the next shove, took the kid's wrist, pivoted underneath, and threw him into the pavement. Before the second one had processed it, the boy drove a short palm strike into his chest that nearly lifted him out of his shoes. The third swung a wide, panicking haymaker; the boy ducked it like it had been posted to him a week in advance, swept the legs, and the kid folded. The fourth swung faster, smarter. The boy slipped it, caught the wrist, and put an elbow into his ribs. He went down wheezing.

The fifth kid did not swing at all. He stood with his fists half raised, subscribed to no particular plan, while the boy in the hoodie stared at him. Dead still. The fifth kid backed away, turned, and walked very fast in the opposite direction.

Four kids on the ground. One walking away. Seconds.

The boy stood among them, eyes moving from body to body, checking that nobody was getting up. Calm. Hands at his sides. In no rush whatsoever.

His mouth hung open. His hands were still on the latch. He did not blink. Then he snapped, wrestled the shoe onto his foot with two hops and a grunt, and bolted.

Down the hallway, past the family photos he never looked at: himself as a toddler; Sharon in a graduation gown; a faded photo of a boy who looked like him but older. Down the stairs, into the kitchen.

"Have you finished cleaning your room?" his mum said.

"Be right back, mum."

"Where are you going?!"

The front door answered her.

Outside, he ran.

He went past the end wall of the block without slowing and without looking. There was old spray-paint on it, faded so far back into the brick that it read as texture more than lettering: a shape that might have been wings, letters that had lost their edges years ago, and underneath, a bunch of flowers cable-tied to the drainpipe, long dead, the cellophane gone milky. He did not look at it. He had never looked at it.

He carried on down the street to the battlefield. The four kids were peeling themselves off the pavement, one holding his ribs, one on all fours spitting blood, one testing his jaw against a wall. The fourth had already gone.

The boy in the LIT hoodie was nowhere.

He turned a full circle. Left. Right. Down the side road. Rooftops. Nothing. Gone, like he had never been there at all.

"Where did that boy go?"

The kid spitting blood looked up at him, wiped his mouth, and spat again, pink.

"I don't know but he's fucked when I see him."

He barely heard it. He was still scanning: alleys, walls, the park at the end of the road. Searching for something he had already lost.

"KEVIN!!" His mum, from the front door, at a volume that moved birds three streets away.

"I'm coming, mum!"

One more look down the side road. Nothing. He turned back toward the house, and something in his face had changed on the way. The wide-eyed wonder had settled into something quieter and more focused. He had a question now. A burning one.

And he knew exactly who to ask.

In the kitchen his mum was waiting with her arms crossed and a spatula that had been promoted to a weapon.

"Where. Did. You. Go."

"I just... thought I saw someone I knew."

"You THOUGHT you saw someone? So you just run out my house without eating, without your coat, without telling me where you're going?"

"Mum, I..."

"Sit down. Eat. Now."

He sat. She pushed a plate of toast at him and watched him take a bite, and the anger softened at its edges the way it always did, and then, because she was who she was, she picked up a fork and pretended to help herself to his plate.

"Mum!"

"What? It looked lonely."

He dragged the plate closer, hiding a smile. She grinned, quick and warm, and went back to packing her work bag.

At the table, Grandad sat with his tea and his newspaper, having witnessed all of it and moved not one muscle.

"You know in my day we wake up before di sun."

"Grandad, the sun's already up."

"Exactly."

Kevin went back to his toast. His mother turned to the counter and began packing her bag for work, still talking, something about the bins, something about his shoes.

On the shelf above the radiator there was a small photograph in a wooden frame: a boy of about eighteen in school uniform, caught mid-laugh at whoever had been holding the camera. He had Kevin's face in him somewhere. Tucked into the corner of the frame was a memorial card, soft at the edges from being handled.

IN LOVING MEMORY. JADEN YOUNG. Two dates underneath, and seven years since the second one.

Beside the frame stood a glass candle, the inside of the glass black from the number of times it had been lit.

His mother crossed the kitchen and, without breaking her sentence and without turning her head, straightened the card with one finger as she passed, the way you straighten a picture in a hallway you have walked ten thousand times.

Nobody looked at it. Nobody mentioned it. It was furniture.

Grandad watched Kevin over the top of his newspaper. Kevin was scraping crumbs off the plate with his thumb.

"Him look more like Jaden every day," Grandad said. To Kevin's mum. Not to Kevin.

She did not turn round, and she did not stop packing, and her hand paused on the zip of her bag for perhaps half a second.

"Mm."

Grandad went back to the paper.

Kevin's eyes came up, just for a moment, and went straight back down to the plate.

Nobody said anything else about it.

Kevin finished the toast, grabbed his bag, made for the door, and was caught by the collar.

"Coat."

"Mum, it's not even..."

She raised the spatula. Not threateningly. Just enough.

He took the coat.

"Straight to the barbershop and straight back! And don't..."

The door closed on the rest.

She shook her head. Grandad turned a page.

"Him alright."

"Hmm."

6. The Woman at the Bus Stop

Kevin sat on the metal bench with his bag between his feet and the question burning quietly in his chest. How did that kid move like that? Where do you learn something like that? Who could teach him? He was assembling sentences and dismantling them again when the storm arrived.

She was late twenties, in tight leggings with STYLES written down the thigh, a leather jacket, and hoop earrings roughly the size of handcuffs. She had a phone against her ear, and she was not happy with it.

"Ahh, you men are all the same! Only stick around to get what you want!"

She dropped onto the bench beside him hard enough to bounce the slats. Kevin shifted half an inch toward the far armrest and studied the horizon.

"As soon as you bust your nut, you..."

She stopped. She had noticed him: a thirteen-year-old sitting rigid as a fence post, eyes forward, radiating a powerful wish to be elsewhere.

She looked at him. Looked at her own fist, still clenched mid-gesture like she was about to punch the sky.

She sighed. "...Shit."

She put the phone down, flexed her hand open, leaned back.

"Fuck it."

Silence. Kevin did not move. He was barely breathing.

Then, without any warning at all, she punched the bus stop window. CRACK. The safety glass spidered into a white web.

Kevin was up and standing several feet away before his brain had filed the paperwork, bag clutched to his chest.

She looked at the ruined glass. At her fist. At the boy holding his bag like a shield.

Then she closed her eyes and breathed out, long and slow, the way people do when they are counting down from something. She shook the hand loose at the wrist. Rolled her shoulders back. When she opened her eyes the storm had gone out of them, mostly, and she patted the bench beside her.

"Come sit. What are you afraid of?"

Kevin looked at her. At the glass. Back at her.

"It's fine. I'll... I'll stand."

"Suit yourself."

She crossed her arms and went back to her phone. Buses going the wrong direction hissed past. A pigeon inspected Kevin's shoes and found them wanting. A man strolled by eating a patty. Kevin's bus did not come.

Eventually, gravity and boredom won, and he sat back down. She glanced sideways at him, said nothing, and let a respectable interval pass before she studied him properly: the furrowed brow, the jaw, the eyes fixed on the pavement, a boy thinking hard enough to sprain something.

"You look like you're gonna meet your crush for the very first time."

"Huh?"

"What I mean is. You look like you want to crack the Da Vinci code."

He did not answer. She kept going anyway.

"Does she even know your name?" she said, rummaging in her bag.

"Who?" said Kevin, still looking straight ahead.

"Your crush." She pulled something out and extended her hand toward him.

"I'm not going to meet a..." He looked down, puzzled. Then his face changed. "...girl."

"Oh?"

She was holding condoms. Two of them, pinched between her fingers and offered as casually as a mint. The packaging said, in letters that felt personally accusatory: XXL.

Kevin's eyes came back up to her face, taking their time about it.

"Well," she said, reasonably, "why would you be heading to town at this time?"

She dropped them back in her bag and crossed her legs. Kevin found urgent business with the sky, then the pavement, then a lamp post, and finally, because something in him could not leave it alone, he answered the real question.

"I want someone to teach me something."

"Why?"

"I... I..."

He had no answer ready. How do you explain to a stranger that you watched a kid your own age put four people on the pavement in seconds, and that ever since, a door has been standing open in your chest?

The bus rounded the corner.

"Finally!" She stood with her whole body, waving it down like a rescue flare.

They got on. She tapped her card and immediately opened a second front against the driver.

"Do you know how long I've been waiting? The app said three minutes. THREE MINUTES. That was fifteen minutes ago. What were you doing back there? Playing with your fucking balls?"

Kevin tapped his Clam card, slid past the war zone, and climbed to the top deck, her voice pursuing him up the stairs.

"No, don't give me that fucking look. I pay for this service! I PAY! You think I'm standing out there in the cold so you can finish your wank break?!"

He took a window seat. From below, muffled and relentless, the campaign continued.

Kevin shook his head slightly.

Danim, he thought, and put his earphones in, and let the city start to slide past the glass.

7. The Bus and the Car

Two places, one stretch of time, and neither of them knew about the other.

Kevin's own reflection sat on the window, half there and half not, the streets running straight through his face. Growing up in this part of Danim had never been easy.

Across the city, Sharon sat half in and half out of her car, one leg on the tarmac, looking up at what was left of the fifth floor. She raised her phone and photographed it.

"What is going on in this city?" she said, to nobody but herself. "Am I just seeing things? Impossible things."

The eye contact flashed through her again and she blinked it away, and looked at the photograph on her screen.

Outside Kevin's window a parade of shops went by with half its shutters down, and a man asleep in a doorway with his coat spread over a dog. His dad had passed when he was young. And his older brother had been murdered, in cold blood.

Sharon was still looking at the photograph. Then, without deciding to, she came out of it, opened her contacts, and dialled.

It rang.

Worst of all, they never found his body.

In Kevin's coat pocket, against his leg, the phone began to buzz. Short pulse. Pause. Short pulse. He did not feel it, or he felt it and it did not register, because there was music in his ears and a window in front of him and he was thirteen.

They never found who did it, either. There were no witnesses. They never got close.

"Come on," Sharon said, under her breath, the phone at her ear. "Come on, pick up."

The buzzing in Kevin's pocket stopped. The reflection held. He had not looked down once.

His sister had left after that.

She was there as he thought it, phone at her ear, waiting. She had joined the police, and she had said she was going to get justice for him, and that had been the only thing she wanted. The bus stopped at a light. A woman crossed with a pram. The bus moved again. Years went by. The case went cold.

Sharon did not move. It was still ringing.

It was a long time ago, though, and they had all found their own way to cope.

The bus turned a corner and the light swung across his face.

His had been a barbershop.

8. Uncle Jon's

The bus crossed the invisible border where Central Danim gives way to South, and the streets grew quieter, the buildings smaller. Kevin got off at his stop and walked the side road that led to the narrower road that led to the old shopping street: a dry cleaner's, a faded newsagent, and tucked between them, a barbershop whose sign read UNCLE JON'S.

He stopped in front of it and looked up at the letters the way you check a thing is still where you left it. He had been coming here since before he could remember. His mum used to drop him off and go about her day. It was mad, he thought, how much time you could spend somewhere before you noticed how much it mattered.

The bell rang as he pushed the door.

We do not follow him in.

9. Nelson

Sharon sat half in and half out of her car. The phone came down from her ear. The screen was dark. It had rung out.

She looked at it.

"...Shit."

She dropped her head back against the door frame and shut her eyes.

The eye contact flashed through her again. She blinked it away.

"Sharon!!"

A policeman was approaching. Nelson. London cockney, and the kind of man who takes up more space than he has earned.

"Sir!" She stepped out of the car and stood to attention.

"What do we pay you for, aye?" He stopped in front of her. Close. Too close. "Why is it, you, I always have to cover for? Boateng's on my back about your disclosure again, and it ain't her I'm gonna hear it from, is it. If it were up to me you wud'a been out this force before the morning cock-a-doodles."

Sharon stared ahead. Jaw tight. Eyes forward. Taking it.

"What is it the Super sees in you?" He began to walk around her, slowly, like an inspection, and his eyes dropped where they had no business dropping. "...Or what is it he wants to put in you?"

Another officer drifted over. Nelson barely lowered his voice.

"Wouldn't mind mashing my gravy all over them bangers."

The other officer stifled a laugh. Sharon did not move. Her face was stone, and her hands, down at her sides, trembled very slightly, and not from fear.

She walked away, each step deliberate.

"Stupid Nelson," she said under her breath, threading between the ambulances. "Probably why you never got a promotion."

She was passing an officer interviewing a witness, a woman with a thermal blanket around her shoulders and a child on her lap, when she heard it.

"...and he just said 'don't move.' That's all he said. Just... 'don't move.' And the way he said it... I can't explain it. Like nothing was wrong. Like everything was going to be fine. I've never felt so..."

Sharon stopped walking.

Her breathing changed. Something shifted behind her eyes, like a door opening in a room she had forgotten her house contained.

What came was not a scene. It was pieces of one, and all of them were hers.

Sound before picture: running feet on pavement, a shout too far off to make out, and breathing that was fast and shallow and her own.

Daylight. A gap between two buildings. A small hand closing around her wrist and pulling, hard, and the world swinging.

Then brick against her back. She was small. Her bag was still on one shoulder and she could not make herself let go of the strap.

A boy. Younger than her, barely up to her shoulder. He put one hand flat on her chest and held her against the wall, not roughly, the way you steady something that might fall.

"Don't move," he said, quietly.

He was not looking at her. He was looking past the corner, leaning out just enough to see, his weight forward on one foot.

She was shaking. She could hear it in her own breath. She looked up at him and she wanted to ask, and half the question got out.

"What are yo..."

He lifted one finger without turning his head.

"Shhh."

Beyond the corner, something happened. She never saw it. She only ever had the sound of it, and she had it the way she had everything else from that afternoon, which was muffled and out of order.

The hand stayed on her chest. Steady. Not one tremor in it.

And then he began to turn back toward her, with the light behind him, his face starting to come round out of the shadow, and the memory was already going, thinning at its edges, the sound draining out of it.

She never saw that either.

Don't move, somewhere far off, echoing after her.

The memory ended and left her standing in the middle of a crime scene with one hand on her chest, breathing like a swimmer. She physically shook her head, crossed to the witness, and let the questions pour out of her, rapid-fire.

"Wait, what did you say? What did he look like? Did you see his face? How tall was he? What was he wearing? Did he say anything else?"

The witness recoiled. The interviewing officer raised a hand. "Sharon, relax. I've got the notes right here..."

She snatched the notepad out of his hand.

"Hey? You can't just..."

She was not listening. She was reading, lips moving. "Cloaked figure... don't move..." She looked up at the witness. "Can you tell me anything else? Anything at all?"

"Ahhh well... he hurled into the building." The woman pointed at the hole.

"Wait... what do you mean? He made that?"

"That's what I keep telling this gentleman."

"Ma'am, like I told you before," the officer said wearily, "sometimes when you are in these types of situations, the body goes through shock. We see things our mind is telling us. Now Sharon, can I have my..."

SNAP. She had her phone out and was photographing the notepad, both sides, close up, every word. She tossed it back without looking. He fumbled the catch against his chest, and he and the witness watched her walk away.

She went fast, through the tape, past the ambulances, her eyes fixed on the building ahead and the two men standing at its entrance, and the phone was already back at her ear. It connected on the third ring.

"Sharon?"

"Mum. Is Kevin with you?"

A pause on the line. Her mother had heard something in her voice already.

"No. He's gone to get a haircut. Why? What's happened?"

She kept walking. Her eyes went up the front of the building to the hole five floors up.

"I can't explain right now. It's police business. But when he gets in, I want him in. Tell him to stay in the house."

"Sharon, you're scaring me."

"Mum. Please."

Silence. Then, quietly: "...Alright. I'll tell him."

She closed her eyes, just for a second, still walking.

"Thanks, Mum."

She hung up. And she stopped, twenty feet short of the entrance, phone still in her hand, looking at the two men in black suits standing either side of the door. They had already clocked her. Neither of them moved.

10. The Circus

Inside was warm and unhurried. Three chairs, mirrors, a counter of products that had not been rearranged within living memory, a radio playing softly. The kind of place where time takes its coat off.

Jon looked up from the head he was working on.

"Kev."

"Uncle Jon."

Kevin dropped his bag and sat in the waiting area, and began, silently, the work of building his question. He had rehearsed it the whole bus ride. Uncle Jon, can you teach me how to fight? Or maybe: Do you know anything about fighting? Or just: How did that kid do that? He was organising the words, finding the nerve.

The bell rang.

Sleeze walked in like the shop owed him rent. Tattoos neck to wrists, gold chain, tracksuit, trainers so fresh they squeaked, and a grin aimed at nothing in particular. Two of his boys came in behind him, matching the energy, the tracksuits, and the swagger.

"Jon-Jon-Jon. My guy."

"Sleeze."

"You busy?"

Jon looked at the customer in his chair, then back at Sleeze.

"What does it look like?"

"Looks like you need some better customers, fam. Look at this man's head. Bro, your head is shaped like a Tic Tac."

The customer stiffened. Jon did not react. Kevin pressed his lips together and held.

"Sleeze, man, leave the guy alone," said the first boy.

"I'm being nice! I'm saying he needs Jon more than most. That's a compliment."

He dropped into the chair beside Kevin and spread his arms along the backs of the seats like a man on a throne. Then he noticed his neighbour.

"Yo, little man. You here again? You practically live here, fam."

"Just getting a trim."

"A trim? A TRIM? Bro, you come here every other week. What trim are you getting? You've barely got hair to trim. Jon, what are you even cutting on this yout's head?"

"More than I'd cut on yours if you're not paying," Jon said, without looking up.

"See, that's cold. That is cold, Jon. After everything I've done for this shop."

"What have you done for this shop?"

"I bring the vibes, bro. You can't put a price on vibes."

"He's got a point still," offered the second boy.

"I can put a price on a haircut though," Jon said. "Fifteen pounds."

Sleeze clutched his chest like he had taken a bullet.

"Fifteen?! Fifteen?! You hear this? Man's out here robbing people in broad daylight and he's meant to be one of the good ones."

Kevin was grinning now. There was no stopping it.

"See? Little man gets it. He knows the struggle."

"Yeah but little man doesn't pay either, does he?"

"That's different. Little man is family. He's like a nephew. You ever see Jon kicking a nephew out for a fiver short? No."

"You've never paid full price in your life though, Sleeze."

"And? I'm consistent. Loyalty is a price too, you know what I'm saying?"

Jon shook his head. The customer in the chair wished, visibly, for the release of death. Kevin laughed out loud, and whatever question he had carried in through that door, and it had been a burning one, dissolved into Sleeze's circus.

The customer paid, gave Sleeze the widest berth the room allowed, and escaped. Jon dusted the chair and nodded.

"Come."

Kevin climbed in. The cape settled over him. The clippers started, and Sleeze talked on, a story now about a girl who had blocked him on three different platforms, his boys laughing at the wrong parts on purpose, which only made him louder.

And Kevin, in the chair, watched the mirror. His eyes drifted. He noticed things. He always noticed things.

The door to the back room was closed, and it had a small deadbolt on it, which no other barbershop door in the world has ever needed. And as he watched, the front bell rang and a man came in, nodded at Jon, and walked straight through to the back without sitting down. Jon nodded back without breaking his sentence. The door closed behind the man.

Nobody reacted. As if it were normal.

Kevin filed it away.

"How's your mum?" Jon asked.

"Same. Stressing."

"And your grandad?"

"He's good. Told me in his day they woke up before the sun."

"Smart man."

"The sun was already up."

Jon smirked, barely, just the corner of his mouth.

Kevin's phone went in his pocket, under the cape, and he performed the whole awkward operation of reaching it without moving his head: elbow up, hand fishing, cape rustling. Jon lifted the clippers away and waited, patient, like a man who had done this a thousand times.

Kevin looked at the screen and answered.

"Mum."

A beat.

"Yeah. Yeah, I'm there now."

A beat, and an eye-roll at nothing.

"Will do."

A beat.

"Okay, mum."

He hung up, put the phone back under the cape, and Jon brought the clippers in again.

"Everything alright?"

"Yeah. Mum's just saying come back home."

Jon nodded and carried on cutting, and nothing in his face changed, and neither of them thought about it again.

Jon smirked. Barely. The corner of the mouth only.

Sleeze leaned forward.

"Yo, Jon, you hear about what happened in Central this morning? Some madness went down. Building got a hole in it the size of a bus. News saying gang activity, but bro... that weren't no gang. I'm telling you. Something's going on in this city."

The clippers paused.

A fraction of a second. Too brief for Sleeze, too brief for his boys. But Kevin was watching the mirror, and Kevin caught it: the hesitation, the slight tightening of Jon's grip.

Then the clippers carried on, smooth, as if nothing had happened.

"People talk too much," Jon said.

"I'm just saying..."

"And I'm just saying people talk too much."

Sleeze put his hands up, message received, and changed the subject to trainers and a debt. The moment passed.

But Kevin stored the pause in the same drawer as the deadbolt and the man who had walked through without a haircut, and the drawer was getting full.

Jon finished. Kevin tilted his head at the mirror, left, right. Fresh.

"Good?"

"Yeah. Safe, Uncle Jon."

He paid, grabbed his bag, checked his phone, and his stomach dropped. He had been in here well over an hour, and he had been told twice.

"I gotta go."

"Straight home."

"Yeah yeah."

The bell rang behind him.

11. Out of Your Jurisdiction

She did not move either. She stood there thumbing back through what she had: the notepad pages, both sides, the handwriting, the hole in the building, the notepad again. She stopped on one and read it, and her jaw set.

She looked up. The two men were still there. Still watching her.

"...Fuck it."

She pocketed the phone and walked straight at them, and two men in black suits stepped into her path. Not police. Military posture. Blank faces.

"Sorry ma'am. I can't let you through. This investigation is out of your jurisdiction."

"Where are you guys from?"

Sunglasses. Earpieces. Stone.

"What the hell is going on?"

Silence.

"You're not gonna tell me. Fine. I'll be back."

She turned to go, and behind her one agent murmured, "Don't waste your time," and the other chuckled, "Haha. Good one," and they pounded fists, deeply satisfied with themselves, which is why neither of them noticed the detective slipping into the alley at the side of the building.

She moved along the brickwork past dripping pipes, flinched at a bolting cat, and peeked around the back corner. One more agent guarded the rear door. "Shit," she whispered, scanning for an idea among the fire escape and the pallets and the wheelie bin, and finding none.

Then the back door opened, and a woman stepped out. Late forties. Sharp blazer, heels that clicked like punctuation, phone at her ear. She walked like the ground adjusted to her rather than the other way round.

"...No we don't have time... I need that report yesterday... That means you are running out of time..." She strode away from the door, the agent trailing her like a shadow. "...And make sure you keep reporters from this, otherwise it's my tits on the line..."

They rounded the corner. The door swung slowly on its hydraulic hinge.

Sharon moved. Fast and silent, catching the door with her fingertips just before the click, and she was inside: a dark corridor, sickly green emergency light, a stairwell sign. She climbed two at a time until her heels rang too loud on the metal, then carried them, bare feet on cold steel.

He hurled into the building, the witness had said.

Is that even possible? she thought. I'm having a hard time just imagining it.

At the fifth floor she pressed against the wall. Three agents blocked the corridor to the ruined office, deep in conversation.

"Then I told him, nah you ain't finished. You ain't washed behind your ear or..."

"Where are you?!" The chief's voice detonated down the corridor from somewhere unseen. "I said get here NOW!"

The three of them froze.

"Was that the chief?"

"Did you hear what I said?! I said get here NOW!"

"Yes ma'am!" they chorused, and scrambled around the corner, nearly trampling each other, their conversation abandoned mid-ear.

The corridor stood empty. Above where they had been, a ventilation grate swung open, and Sharon lowered herself out of the ceiling, arms shaking, blouse tearing slightly on the metal edge. She dropped the last foot, winced on the cold floor, and inspected the damage.

"Great," she whispered. "That was new."

The office, up close, stole her breath. The hole was far bigger than it had looked from the street. Half the floor was gone. Desks lay piled like matchsticks. Wind moved through the wound, carrying dust and siren-sound, and through it the whole skyline glowed: the river, the bridge, the city. Almost beautiful, if you could ignore what it was.

Voices. Coming fast.

She ducked behind a barricade of toppled desks and filing cabinets, pulled her knees in, and held her breath as the door slammed open.

"...And where's Adam?! He was supposed to be here before I showed up!"

The chief stormed in, heels crunching glass without a care, crossing the debris like it had personally offended her. The agent trailing her had learned not to speak. She palmed her forehead, massaged her temples in slow circles, exhaled.

"So... do you want me to take the footage to review?" the agent tried.

A long breath. The kind of breath that decides between firing everyone in the building or just the man in front of her.

"Yes."

"Copy." He set a mini USB hard drive on the one desk still standing and turned for the door. He got two steps.

"Wait."

He stopped.

"Put it down for now and come here."

What followed, Sharon watched through the gap between two desks with one eyebrow slowly rising. The chief took off her blazer and draped it on a chair. Unbuttoned her shirt. One button. Two. Unhurried, unembarrassed, administrative.

"One thing I love above all in this God-forsaken job is..." she said, reaching out and taking hold of the agent in a way that was neither professional nor resisted, "...I'll always have one of you clumsy idiots to take my anger out on."

"Yeah right, you horny bitch," Sharon mouthed, barely audible, and settled in to wait it out with detached contempt.

The contempt did not last. The sounds filled the ruined office and bounced off the broken ceiling, and Sharon, pressed flat behind the desks, found her breathing had changed, and then found, to her own genuine surprise, where her hands had got to. Images stacked behind her eyes, different people, different places, a club bathroom, a car park, a hotel that charged by the hour, faster, layering...

She snapped out of it.

She looked down at herself. Froze. Looked left. Looked right. Slowly and with great dignity she withdrew, wiped her hand on her already ruined blouse, observed the state of herself, closed her legs.

"...Whatever," she said, flatly, to nobody, and refocused.

The drive sat ten metres away. Between her and it: a minefield of glass and cable and two people conducting what could only be described as a hostile performance review. She crawled. Slowly. Under a dangling cable, over a shattered monitor, glass biting her palms and knees, sweat dropping off the end of her nose, while behind her the chief issued instructions to her subordinate in a voice that would strip paint. "Harder. HARDER. You think I'm made of glass? Move."

Sharon's fingers closed around the drive. She slid it off the desk and tucked it into her waistband.

"That's it. That's it right there. Don't you fucking stop."

She was already out the door.

She flew down the corridor, hit the stairwell, bare feet slapping metal, and then: voices, coming UP. Agents. One floor between them and her. She rushed to a window, shoved it open, looked down at a big square industrial bin and the air conditioning unit jutting out between her and it, heard the agents rounding the flight below, and climbed out onto the ledge and hung there by her fingers.

The agents passed a metre above her head.

"I tried proposing. He said no. But every time I..." The agent stopped himself mid-heartbreak. "...Are those fingers?"

Sharon let go.

Her hip caught the air conditioning unit on the way down. She yelped, spun, crashed onto the bin lid, buckled it, rolled off, and hit the wet concrete in a heap. For a second she lay on her back, remembering how breathing worked. Blouse torn. Knees bleeding. Feet black. Drive still tucked in her waistband, pressing cold against her skin.

"We have a perimeter breach!" from above.

She got up and ran, bare feet on wet concrete, between the bins, around the corner, into the side streets, and did not look back. When the agent burst out of the back door seconds later, the alley was empty.

Sharon Young was gone, and she had their footage.

12. The Queen Bee and the Report

In a different part of the city, on a rooftop, stood a structure that was not fancy: industrial, hidden, deliberately forgettable. The attacker from Central, Spike, pushed through its door with the posture of a man carrying a bad day.

A girl slid out of the shadows on rollerblades, backwards, matching his pace with her hands folded behind her, in a purple outfit with a belt of gadgets and a grin with history in it.

"What the fuck... was you thinking?" She chuckled.

Spike rolled his eyes and kept walking.

"Aw, talk to me, pumpkin," she sang, high-pitched and merciless, skating backwards alongside him. "You have blue balls? I mean, I can help you out with that."

"Shut up."

The corridor ended in a descending spiral staircase. She split her legs, set one skate on each railing, and ground down the whole flight with her back to the drop, looking at him over her shoulder.

"Well, darling, I just want you to know that whatever the case..." She bent lower, weight on her right, eyes glittering. "...A queen bee always gets the honey."

She landed at the bottom, rolled to the door, opened it, and presented the way in like a hotel concierge.

"Tss," said Spike, and walked through.

The den was an open space converted into a hideout: makeshift furniture, monitors, weapons resting on surfaces the way other homes keep fruit. Ninjas were scattered around it, cleaning blades, eating, talking in corners. The moment Spike entered, the room noticed.

"Spike?! What the fuck, fam?!"

"Broad daylight?"

Laughter, gathering bodies.

"Brooo!!"

"Shut up," someone tried.

"Tell your momma to shut up, brudda."

Spike stood in the middle of it, jaw tight, eyes down, while the room enjoyed him. The one who had tried to quiet them, his comrade, came over.

"Come with me."

The side room was a makeshift boardroom: one long table, mismatched chairs, shutters striping the daylight. "Sit," said the comrade. "I'll stand," said Spike, and leaned on the table with his arms crossed, which is a way of sitting that lets a man keep his pride.

The comrade walked the room slowly.

"A battle with an enemy should always be strategic and well thought through. A battle without a plan is suicide. I'm not gonna question why you are still alive because that goes without saying." He reached the window and looked through the shutters. "I always want to know the motives of my comrades, so before you got here I did a fair share of brainstorming. Even gone as far as thinking someone killed your family."

He turned.

"I want to see this town go down just as much as the next man, and I know you know everything the Hood stands for. So I'm still left with the same question..."

He faced him.

"Why?"

Spike kept his eyes shut a moment. Then:

"It wasn't supposed to turn out that way. The family was low in cash and rent was due. I just wanted to get some cash and that was it."

And he told it.

Summer, around eight in the evening, and the sun was still well up. Long gold light down a quiet parade of shops in a corner of Danim, shutters coming down, the street emptied out to the last few stragglers heading home. An electronics shop, still open. Through the window, a customer finishing up at the counter. Around the corner, Spike pulled a mask up over his nose and waited for the beep of the door.

Then he moved: over the counter in one motion while the cashier looked down at the register, a chokehold from behind, his signature blade pressed to the man's back.

"Stay still."

The cashier's hands shot up.

"Now walk away or die. Your choice."

He loosened the hold. The man looked at the exit and ran, his footsteps and panicked breathing swallowed by the night.

Spike turned to the register and began stuffing cash into his cloak, quick and focused, which is why it took him a moment to register the shadow that had fallen across the counter.

He looked up.

A cloaked figure stood in the entrance. Still. Calm. Holding a sandwich from the corner shop next door, one bite taken. Just standing there. Looking at him. Chewing.

"Jog on, bro. Nothing to look at." Spike pointed the blade at him.

The figure took another bite.

"What? You want some P too, brudda?"

Chewing. Swallowing. Nothing.

"Don't worry," Spike said, turning back to the register, "I got you."

He glanced down for one half-second to grab the last of the cash, and the world came apart.

A flash of light. Metal, spinning, coming at his face. Time went syrup-slow. His hand rose on pure instinct, years of training compressed into one reflex, and his palm caught the edge of the blade and deflected it upward, sent it spinning into the air above him.

He opened his eyes.

The cloaked figure was directly in front of him. Across the counter. No sound had announced him. Not a footstep, not a breath. He was holding Spike's wrist, the blade wrist, firmly and without strain, the way you hold a pen.

Spike looked into the shadow of the hood, and found the eyes, and the eyes had nothing in them. No anger. No excitement. Just calm, the calm of being so far above a situation that its outcome had never once been in question.

Spike's mouth opened.

The deflected knife came back down out of the air, and on its way down it sliced clean through his mask, diagonal, surgical. The two halves fell away from his face.

The cloaked figure released his wrist and caught the falling knife with the same hand, without looking up, and put it away.

"I have triggered the alarm," he said.

Spike glanced down. Under the register, a small red light, blinking. The panic button. When? How? The man had been across the room.

"...And your face is exposed."

And with that the cloaked figure turned and walked out of the shop, casual as a man who has just bought a newspaper.

Spike stood behind the counter with his mask on the floor and the alarm blinking and his face on record, dismantled, comprehensively, in under ten seconds, by a man eating a sandwich. He chuckled. Not because anything was funny. Because it was absurd.

He fired his cable through the shop front, hurled himself out through a confetti of glass, swung up to a rooftop, landed, turned, and looked down, and there was the cloaked figure below, watching him, still holding the sandwich.

Spike pointed down at him and opened his mouth to deliver something memorable.

Beeping.

He looked left. Nothing. Right. Nothing. Down, at the hem of his cloak.

A tiny device. Blinking. 4... 3...

"Shit!"

He ripped the cloak off, balled it, and launched it skyward on his cable, where it detonated in a bloom of orange against a bright blue sky, in full daylight, in full view of anyone in Danim who happened to look up, raining scraps of fabric like black confetti.

Below, the cloaked figure watched the debris drift down and took another bite.

"Now you've completely caused attention to yourself," he observed, to himself, and finished his dinner.

Back in the boardroom, the comrade stared at him.

"Wait... what? Your face was exposed?" He stepped forward. "Rule number one. Destroy all..."

"It's destroyed."

Somewhere in the city, an electronics shop's CCTV mainframe lay ripped open, wires sparking.

"Oight. Kool. Kool. Calm. Calm." The comrade paced it off.

"I'm still trying to work it out, though," Spike said, looking at his own fist, clenching it, opening it. "How did my man do it?"

"Do what?"

"Blood, have you heard a word I said?!" He pushed off the table. "You can take an L... but this brudda... I don't know. He left no openings, even when times were bad. Everything he did was necessary."

And as he talked it through, the fight replayed behind his eyes, angle by angle, and gave up its secrets one by one.

"The blade he chucked at the beginning to get me distracted..." The throw had never been aimed to kill. It was aimed to pull his hand upward, to expose the wrist, to create the grip. "I don't even know how he knew I would survive that." Because the man had calculated the speed, the angle, and the exact moment of Spike's reaction, and had known, with the certainty of arithmetic, that he was fast enough. "From my block, how did he get to me that quick?" Six metres of shop floor crossed in the time it takes a blade to be deflected, without one sound. "I don't know what's even more impressive, the fact that I didn't hear the sound for a customer coming into the store, or the fact that he knew exactly how his blade would end up revealing my face." The rotation of the deflected knife, calculated so that on its way down it would cut fabric and not skin. Not skill. Something else. "Not to mention he also pressed the trigger alert panic button." One hand holding Spike's wrist. The other, invisible, under the counter. Two actions at once, neither of them seen. "It was never my plan to leave the shop through the front, but in a way... I got excited." And there, in the blur of his own exit, the last move: a hand planting a tiny device on his cloak as he zipped past. One touch. Less than a second.

"When I zipped past him was the final icing on the cake to fully expose me."

He shook his head slowly.

"I can't keep thinking about..."

The door swung open. A ninja leaned in.

"He's here."

13. The Man They All Stand Up For

The energy in the den changed before anyone said a word. Conversations died mid-sentence. Blades stopped mid-polish. Phones went down. The room reorganised itself the way iron filings reorganise around a magnet.

A man walked in.

Nobody said his name. Nobody needed to. He did not rush and he did not announce himself, and he moved through the room the way gravity moves through a room, which is to say that everything in it adjusted to him without being asked. The ninjas parted. He sat in his chair, a worn leather armchair at the head of the room, the only piece of furniture in the building that looked chosen rather than found, and took a slow breath, and leaned back, and rested his chin on his hand. His eyes travelled the room. Every face. Every posture. Missing nothing.

They found Spike.

He closed his eyes.

"What happened?"

His voice was calm and quiet, and it was the kind of quiet that is louder than shouting. Every head in the room turned to Spike.

Spike glanced across the room and found the roller-skate girl leaning on another ninja, watching him, grinning. She made a gesture involving her hand and her mouth that clarified her position on the matter. His eyes dropped to the floor.

"Tsh. I got jumped."

"Jumped by who?"

"I couldn't see his face."

"Well, ain't he lucky. Why is that then?"

"He had a hood on."

"That doesn't seem much of a disguise. All this commotion and you couldn't give any sort of description?"

Silence. Spike's arms stayed crossed. His jaw worked.

"...He had a mark."

"Great. That narrows it down."

"On his wrist. Some sort of..."

The man's eyes, which had been half closed, began to open.

"...Burn mark. Like it was done on purpose. Old. Healed."

The room was silent. The man did not move. But something had shifted behind his eyes, and his other hand, the one resting on the arm of the chair, drifted across and brushed the inside of his own wrist, where his sleeve covered the skin. He did not notice himself doing it.

For one second, maybe two, something flickered across his face. Not recognition. Not memory. Something deeper and more broken than either: a word on the tip of the tongue, dissolving before it can be spoken.

Then it was gone. The hand returned to the armrest. The expression reset.

"What did you just say?"

His voice was different now. The calm was still there, but underneath it sat something that had not been in the room a minute ago.

Spike opened his eyes and looked at his leader, and saw something in his expression that he had never seen before, and the room held its breath.

14. Jewel Gems

At the bus stop the display said eight minutes. Kevin looked at it. Looked across the road at a corner shop, one of the little ones with a faded ice cream poster and a bell that had never quite rung properly.

Eight minutes.

"...I've got time."

Strip lighting. Narrow aisles. A shopkeeper watching a tiny television. Kevin went past the crisps and the drinks, straight to the sweets, and picked up a packet of Jewel Gems: small round hard sweets in colours not found in nature. He paid, pocketed them, and made the bus as it rounded the corner.

Top deck. Window seat. He tore the packet open, poured a few into his hand, popped one, and watched his city go by with the open packet resting on his lap.

At the next stop, hurried footsteps came up the stairs.

The man who appeared was Japanese, late forties, thin, in a jacket that had been worn for days and slept in for some of them. His hair was a mess. His eyes went everywhere: down the stairs, along the deck, out the window, back to the stairs.

The top deck was nearly full. The only empty seat was beside the boy with the open packet of sweets. The man hesitated, then sat.

Kevin glanced at him, popped another sweet, and went back to the window.

The bus pulled off, and the man's knee began to bounce. His fist clenched on his thigh. His head turned in a loop: stairs, window, stairs, window. Kevin's eyes slid sideways and took inventory: the twitching leg, the white knuckles, the sweat at the temple, the vein working in the neck. One eyebrow drifted up, an expression sitting somewhere between what's your problem and whatever, man, and he went back to his sweets.

The bus slowed. Doors below. The man's body went rigid, and he gulped loudly enough that Kevin heard the click of his throat.

Two men came up the stairs. Big, broad, dark-clothed, and nothing whatsoever like commuters. One said something short and clipped to the other. They took seats at the back.

The man beside Kevin stopped breathing. He looked at Kevin. At the stairs. Back at Kevin, and in his face was something between desperation and apology.

Then, commotion.

"WAIT! WAIT! This is our stop! Hold on, bus driver!"

Three or four passengers leapt up at once and stampeded down the aisle, bags swinging, elbows finding seat backs, and squeezed noisily past Kevin's row. And in those three seconds of shuffle and complaint, while every eye on the deck was on the stampede, the man's hand moved. Quick. Precise. Practised.

Something small dropped into Kevin's open packet of Jewel Gems.

Kevin saw none of it. He was pulling his knees in to let the passengers squeeze by, wearing the put-upon face of a boy whose personal space is public property.

The commotion settled. At the back, one of the big men scanned the deck; the other stared at nothing. The man beside Kevin sat rigid as furniture, staring forward, being invisible as hard as a person can be.

Stops passed. The man's stop came. He stood, stiff and mechanical, and walked to the stairs without one glance back, on legs that had forgotten how knees work. He went down. The doors hissed.

The moment his feet hit the pavement, he ran.

Kevin watched through the window: the man sprinting flat out down the street, arms pumping. Behind him, the two big men rose without hurry, moved down the stairs, stepped off the bus, walked fast in the same direction, and then, clear of the windows, broke into a dead sprint.

Three grown men, running down a street in Danim.

Kevin's face did not change. He shook his head slightly.

Danim, he thought.

He popped another sweet. His stop came. He stuffed the half-eaten packet into his coat pocket, grabbed his bag, and went home.

15. The Last Carrier

In East Danim, late, in an alley the streetlights only half claimed, the Japanese man from the bus was on his knees.

His jacket was torn worse than before. His lip was split, and blood ran from a cut above his eye. He had been there a while. The two men who had chased him stood over him, and up close they were what they had seemed on the bus: military posture, earpieces, the build of men who are paid to be dangerous. One crouched in front of him.

"Where is it?"

The man coughed. Spat blood onto the wet concrete. Wiped his mouth with a shaking hand.

"I don't... I don't know what you're talking about."

"Don't insult me."

"I'm telling you the truth. I don't know what you want."

The first man looked at the second. The second stepped forward and produced something from his coat, something that clicked, something that glowed at its tip, and pressed it to the kneeling man's shoulder. The man convulsed, teeth locked around a strangled sound, and when the device withdrew he sagged forward, steam rising from the point of contact.

"You were the last carrier," the first man said. "We've tracked every hand it passed through. Every single one. You are the end of the chain. So I'll ask again. Where. Is. It."

"You've made a mistake," the man gasped. "I'm... I'm just a tourist. Wrong place, wrong time."

"A tourist," said the second man.

"Yes. Visiting family."

"Your family is in Osaka. We checked."

"My cousin lives here. In Danim. I came to see him."

"What's his name?"

"Hiroshi."

"Last name."

A beat. The man's eyes flickered.

"Tanaka."

The device pressed into him again, longer. His whole body locked, and when it released him he hung forward gasping, drool and blood stringing from his lip.

"There is no Hiroshi Tanaka. We checked that too. You've been in this country for eleven days. You've made contact with seven individuals across four cities. We have all of them. Two of them are already dead. The other five gave us your name before they went. So I am not going to ask you a third time."

And the man laughed.

Quiet at first. Wet. Broken. He spat more blood.

"You're a long way from finding it. You know that, don't you?"

"Where. Is. It."

"Gone."

"Where."

"Somewhere you'll never look."

The second man hauled him up by the collar and slammed him back down. His head bounced off the concrete. He coughed, spat, and his breathing was ragged now, but his eyes had gone strangely clear, like a man who has made peace with his arithmetic.

Then the laugh came back, and it built, head tilting back, rising through the blood in his mouth, and it was not manic and it was not madness. It was peace. The laugh of a man with nothing left to lose because he has already, quietly, won.

The two men looked at each other. This was not a reaction they had been trained for.

The laughter subsided. He caught his breath. Spat one last time. Looked up at the first man with red, exhausted, absolutely final eyes, and drew the breath for his last sentence.

"You will never..."

THUNK.

A kunai stood in his forehead. Clean. Silent. From above.

His eyes stayed open. The sentence hung unfinished in the air where he left it. He swayed, forward, back, and dropped face-first onto the wet ground.

The two men spun, weapons half drawn, scanning the alley, the fire escapes, the roofline, and caught it for a fraction of a second: a figure on a rooftop, silhouetted against the moon. A shadow that was there, and then was not.

They stared at the empty roof. At each other. At the body.

The first man touched his earpiece.

"He's dead. Someone got to him first."

A pause. Listening.

"No... we didn't see. A shadow. That's all."

Pause.

"Understood."

They walked away, their footsteps swallowed slowly by the city.

The man lay still on the wet ground, the kunai catching one glint of streetlight. His blood found the cracks between the paving stones and followed them, the way water always finds its way, taking the paths of least resistance toward the drains of Danim.

The man who had given everything to protect the Hakai Sphere, who had passed it hand to hand across the world, who had sat on a bus beside a boy eating sweets and completed his final mission with a trembling hand, died in an alley in East Danim with half a sentence in his mouth and a laugh still fading from his face.

Nobody will ever know his name.

16. The Swallowing

Days later, on a morning built from the usual chaos, with his mum's voice rising through the floorboards and the clock running ahead of him, Kevin was rummaging across his desk when he lifted his crumpled coat off the chair, and the packet of Jewel Gems fell out of the pocket and scattered.

He looked at them, and grinned.

"Safe."

He picked up the packet and reached in, and his fingers found one sweet slightly bigger than the others. Slightly darker. He was not looking closely. He pulled it out and held it up between thumb and finger, turning it in the light.

And something breathed.

It was faint. Almost not there at all. A whisper without words, like air pulled through a crack in the world, like something exhaling very far away.

Kevin tilted his head. His eyes left the sweet and travelled the room. Left. Right. Nothing. The sound was gone, if it had ever existed.

He looked back at the sweet.

His door burst open.

"Kevin, are you even listening to m..."

His mum stopped. Saw his hand at his mouth. And Kevin, startled, did what any boy does with contraband and an audience: he popped it in.

It sat on his tongue. Hard. Heavier than a sweet has any right to be. The texture wrong in a way he had no time to think about, because his mother was staring and his brain was fully occupied with mum-management.

"Are those the sweets you came with the other day?"

He shook his head, wide-eyed, mouth full, radiating guilt at a wavelength visible from space.

"Don't you LIE to me! Those have been sitting around for days. They could be off. They could be poisonous."

She held out her hand. Open palm. The universal gesture, older than language: give it to me. Now.

Kevin looked at her hand. At the packet. At her face, which said he had one second.

He took a big gulp.

It went down fighting. His throat bulged. His eyes watered. A hard, scraping swallow that used every muscle he owned, and then he felt it drop into his stomach like a stone into a pond.

He smiled. Nervous. Sweating. He handed over the packet.

She took it, inspected it, and shook her head with the weariness of mothers everywhere.

"Honestly, Kevin."

Her footsteps went downstairs. The bin lid opened and shut.

"NOW GET READY! HURRY UP!"

Kevin exhaled, wiped his forehead, and grinned to himself like a boy who has got away with something.

He had no idea what he had just swallowed.

17. The Scare

That night the house was quiet in the way houses are quiet after midnight, when the hallway light burns dim orange and every room seems smaller. Grandad slept. The TV was off. Kevin lay in bed scrolling, eyes heavy, until the phone lost. He put it down, rolled over, rolled back, gave up, and got up.

He padded down the hallway in his socks, floorboards confessing under each step. His mum's door stood slightly open, her bedside lamp spilling warm light, her breathing soft and slow inside.

He pushed the door.

"Mum, I'm going to..."

He stopped.

In the corner of the room, by the wardrobe, where the lamplight did not quite reach, stood a figure. Tall. Still. There was nothing that should be standing there; that corner held folded laundry and a suitcase older than he was. But something was standing in front of them. Something with shoulders. And arms. And hands.

And in those hands, his mother's head.

Her body lay slumped on the bed, the neck ending in nothing. The head hung from the figure's grip by its hair, her eyes open, her mouth frozen around a sound she never finished. Blood, thick and dark, dripped and pattered softly on the carpet.

The figure turned toward him.

It had his face. Kevin's face, but older, sharper, the jaw harder, the cheekbones cut. And its eyes were black. Completely black. No white, no iris, no reflection. Two holes in a human face where a soul should have been.

It smiled.

Kevin screamed. The sound tore out of him raw and high and childlike. He stumbled back, heel catching the carpet, and went down hard on his tailbone, and felt nothing of it, because his mother's head was in that thing's hands and the thing was wearing his face.

It stepped into the doorway. Slow. Patient. Still holding her head. Still smiling. It tilted its head like a dog hearing a frequency meant only for it.

Kevin screamed again and scrambled backwards on hands and heels until the wall ended the retreat. He curled into a ball, arms over his head, knees to his chest, shaking hard enough to hum the floorboards.

A hand touched his shoulder.

He shrieked, one last throat-shredding time, and looked up.

His mum. Alive. Whole. In her dressing gown, face creased with worry, both hands on his shoulders.

"Kevin?! Kevin, what's the matter?! What happened?!"

He could not speak. His chest heaved. His eyes would not stop moving: left, right, over her shoulder, past her, behind her.

"Kevin, look at me. LOOK AT ME. What's wrong?"

Grandad appeared at the top of the stairs, one hand on the banister, the other rubbing his eye.

"What a gwaan down here?"

Their voices began to fade. He could see the words being made, but the sound lost its shape, muffled, as if arriving through a wall, through water, through something thicker than either. All Kevin could hear was his own breathing, in, out, in, out, ragged and wet, and his heartbeat filling his skull.

His mum held his face in her hands, saying his name without sound.

He looked past her, into the bedroom.

The lamp was on. The bed was a bed. The pillows were pillows. The laundry sat folded in its corner beside the suitcase. Everything exactly where it should be.

But in the far corner, where the light did not reach, where the wardrobe pooled its shadow against the wall, something was there.

A shape. Dark. Still. Almost invisible against the darkness. Almost.

The shape had eyes, catching a thread of moonlight through the curtains. And beneath the eyes, a grin. Slight. Knowing. Patient.

The grin of something with all the time in the world.

Kevin's eyes went wide, and the world flicked to black, and in the black there was only his breathing. In. Out. In. Out. And the heartbeat. Pounding.

18. The Watcher

North Danim slept. Kevin's street stood dark, the streetlights humming their electric hymn. A fox trotted across the road, stopped, read the air, and slid away under a fence.

On a rooftop across from Kevin's house, a figure stood. Cloaked. Still. Looking down at a dark bedroom window.

The house was silent now. The screaming had settled; the lights had gone out one by one, his mum's, then grandad's. The whole house breathed slow.

The figure did not move. The wind pulled at the edge of his cloak and got nothing else. A car passed streets away, its headlights sweeping and gone.

He stayed. Watching.

And if you rose up off that rooftop, higher and higher into the night, you would watch him shrink to a speck of stillness above the sleeping terraces, and the street become a block, and the block become a neighbourhood, and North Danim spread itself out beneath the sky. Beyond it the glow of Central. The darkness of the South. The forgotten sprawl of the East, where a nameless man lay in an alley. The artificial brightness of the West. And far out on the edge of everything, the distant, careful lights of Belvedire.

Danim. Beautiful. Broken.

And hiding more secrets than anyone knows.

End of Episode One.

"Welcome to Danim City"

The Reading Edition

The script, read straight through. Every beat and every line of dialogue is the script's. Dialogue is set in prose the way a novel sets it. Italics carry the production beats: camera moves, shot calls, cuts, fades, sound cues, and notes to be aware of. Everything in plain text is what you are watching happen. The script remains canonical on any conflict.

COLD OPEN

Black screen.

A single voice cuts through the silence. Refined, unhurried, the kind of accent that has never once had to raise itself to be heard.

"Welcome to Danim City."

Slow aerial shot. Mid-morning, high summer, the sun well up and the light flat and honest, the kind that leaves nothing anywhere to hide.

The camera drifts over the city, the light hard and even on everything it touches.

Red double-decker buses crawl through traffic. The underground rumbles beneath the streets. The iconic arches of Danim Bridge stretch across the river, hard-edged against a bright sky.

"Hidden away in the roots of England, United Kingdom," the voice goes on, taking its time, the way a man does when he is showing you round somewhere he knows you will never afford. "Home to some of the wonders of the world: the Danim Bridge, Danim View, and The Pendulum."

The camera glides past The Pendulum, a towering clock structure in the centre of the city, as its hands tick forward.

Pedestrians cross streets. A man sells newspapers. Kids in school uniforms mess about at a bus stop.

"Long has been forgotten about the once popular city that continues to suffer," he says, and something almost fond creeps in under the words, "bringing tourism as the years go by."

The camera descends lower. The cracks show now.

Homeless people sleeping on roadsides. Boarded-up shops. Reconstruction barriers on half-closed roads. Police sirens in the distance.

"While the economy struggles, new leaders bring new laws. New laws bring new problems."

Beat.

"And new problems..."

He lets it hang there.

A figure in a dark cloak sprints past a group of pedestrians. Fast. Too fast. They barely register what happened: a gust of wind, a blur, gone. One of them looks over their shoulder, confused.

"...bring new leaders."

The narration cuts dead.

THE FIGHT

The cloaked figure moves through the streets with silent precision, weaving between people, ducking under scaffolding, cutting through alleyways. His breathing is controlled. Not panicked. Measured. He is running, but not because he is afraid.

Without warning. BOOM.

A figure clad in black and gold drops from above, landing directly in front of the cloaked runner. The impact cracks the pavement. The black-and-gold figure rises slowly, rolling his neck.

Note: the area looks like a typical urban stretch of Danim, overhead passes, the iconic train line symbols on nearby signage, that authentic London-like feel. It is a time of day where not many people would have been around, but the ones that are just happened to be in the wrong place at the wrong time.

The air goes still. For a long moment, neither moves. The cloaked figure's hood shadows his face. The attacker's eyes burn behind his mask.

Then. Both move at once.

The fight explodes. Hands, elbows, knees: every strike is fast, sharp, precise. The ambient city noise drops to almost nothing. All that can be heard is impacts, scraping feet, and breathing.

The cloaked figure blocks a straight punch and counters with a low sweep. The attacker anticipates it, springs back, and launches a combination: two hooks and a spinning back fist. The cloaked figure takes the first hook on his forearm, slips the second, but the back fist clips him.

He recovers. Doesn't even touch where he got hit.

The attacker presses. Every strike is one step ahead. Every combination is designed to end it. The cloaked figure is on the defensive, absorbing pressure, giving ground. To anyone watching, it looks like he is struggling. Like the fight isn't going well for him.

But things keep happening that just about save him from real damage. A block that arrives at the exact right moment. A lean that takes him out of range by millimetres. A pivot that turns a direct hit into a glancing one. It is too consistent to be luck.

Then. A smirk. Small. Almost invisible under the hood.

The attacker sees it. His rhythm breaks for a fraction of a second.

He becomes enraged.

The attacks get wilder. Precision gives way to fury. His strikes start hitting the environment: a parked car's window shatters, a street sign bends, the wall of a building cracks. He is not just fighting the cloaked figure anymore. He is swinging at the world.

The cloaked figure continues to protect the area, positioning himself between the attacker and bystanders. Almost as if he knew what was going to happen. When the attacker notices the cloaked figure attempting to protect the area, something clicks. A realisation crosses his face.

The attacker fires a zipline cable from his wrist. It anchors to the side of a building and he zips upward, scaling the wall in seconds. He turns, looks down at the figure in the street below him, and somewhere under the mask there is a laugh he doesn't bother swallowing.

"Cuz..." He lets the word stretch out, savouring it. "You're a joke."

He levels his weapon at the cloaked figure. But his eyes don't stay there. They slide off, past him, down the street, and settle on a woman hauling her child towards the far corner.

"I don't think you understand what man is all about," he says, and he says it almost gently.

A crimson aura begins to ooze from the attacker. Subtle, like heat distortion. The air around him shimmers with menace.

THE RESCUE

The cloaked figure doesn't hesitate. He dashes toward the pedestrians caught in the crossfire, scanning the area for anyone else still in danger.

As he runs, weaving through debris, vaulting over a crushed car bonnet, the thought arrives without any heat in it at all.

This isn't a fight.

He spots a sharp line of bladed rope ahead of the attacker's flight path as the attacker launches from the building. The attacker spins to avoid the bladed rope, then hurls his blade at the woman and child before changing direction by ziplining to another wall.

The cloaked figure, still sprinting, pulls a knife and throws it without breaking stride. It intercepts the attacker's blade mid-air. Both fall harmlessly to the ground.

It's a temper tantrum.

He reaches the woman and her child and pushes them back against the wall, firm, but with more care than the moment deserves.

"Don't move."

He says it the way another man might tell you the time. No urgency in it anywhere.

The woman, clutching her child, looks up into the hood. Even in this much daylight the shadow inside it holds. She doesn't get a face. She gets pieces of one: the line of a jaw, the shape of a cheekbone, the mouth. Enough to build something from and nowhere near enough to describe to anyone afterwards.
