What she gets clearly is the demeanour. He is completely relaxed. Nothing in him is braced. His eyes are serene, like this is routine, like she is the most important thing in the world right now and all the rest of it is just noise happening somewhere else.

She feels safe. She doesn't understand why, but she does.

He is already moving again. The attacker has spotted new targets: more pedestrians caught in the chaos. He catapults toward them, blade drawn. The cloaked figure changes direction, cutting across the street, shoving a man out of a doorway, redirecting a teenager who is frozen in panic.

This is what happens when you give power to those who haven't earned it.

As the attacker glides toward the second group, he spots a sticky bomb on the side of the wall near where he is heading. He smirks. The bomb is about to detonate. He deviates his attack, threading metal cables through his wrist and clinging to another building wall.

The cloaked figure presses a button on his glove. The bomb stops counting down. Deactivated.

He looks up at the attacker clinging to the wall. Sees the landmines blinking around him. The attacker hasn't noticed them yet.

The cloaked figure crouches. Then launches himself upward.

He hurtles toward the attacker, cloak trailing behind him, closing the gap fast. Everything slows down. The city noise fades. His thoughts are clear, detached, almost wistful.

Life seemed easier back then. Things like this were left to the military... maybe.

The attacker sees him coming. Notices something. The cloaked figure's face, even mid-flight, even hurling through the air toward a fight, is calm. Completely and utterly unbothered. As if this is nothing to him.

The attacker scrambles to reposition. Notices the blinking landmines. His eyes go wide. Panic.

What does it matter...? All the same.

Too late.

BOOM.

The cloaked figure slams into the attacker. The collision triggers the planted devices. The explosion rips through the upper section of the building, sending glass and rubble cascading down. The impact narrowly misses the bystanders below. Just enough of the building comes down to miss them as they scramble away.

Inside the building, the attacker crashes through the office space. He rolls, skids, and finally uses his cables to stop himself. He is on one knee, breathing hard, disoriented.

He looks left. Nothing.

He looks right.

The cloaked figure is already there. Standing by the window. Calm. Ready to leave. One hand resting on the window pane, looking down at the street below.

"Please..." He doesn't turn around to say it. "Just leave."

The attacker stares. The rage drains from his face, replaced by something else: confusion. Because in this moment, with the cloaked figure's hand on the window frame, the attacker notices something. A mark on his wrist. Small. Raised. Like a burn. Old, healed, deliberate. Not a tattoo. Something done by hand a long time ago.

His face changes completely.

"What..." The word comes out of him without permission. "The... fuck?"

The cloaked figure jumps. He drops from the window and is gone into the daylight, which should be harder than vanishing into the dark, and somehow isn't.

The attacker stays on one knee. Stunned. Quietly observing. Listening to the commotion outside. Police sirens growing louder.

"Who are..." he says, to nobody, so quietly it is barely a voice at all.

He doesn't finish.

THE ROOFTOP

Wide angle. The cityscape. Emergency lights flash below. The camera drifts upward, finding the cloaked figure crouched on a rooftop, looking down at the rubble and chaos.

He watches for a moment. Bystanders being escorted away. Police securing the area. Ambulances arriving.

"What a waste," he says, and there is no anger in it, which somehow makes it land harder.

He stands. Turns. Walks away.

SHARON: ARRIVAL

Below, police cars screech to a halt. Officers pile out, shouting orders.

"Check the building!" one of them bellows.

One more police car pulls up to the scene. As the door opens, a leg steps out: heeled boot, black trousers. Sharon stands up from the car and looks up, immediately noticing the attacker looking down at the commotion from the destroyed wall above.

They briefly make eye contact.

"Sharon! I need you to call in a 4.02, now!"

Off screen.

In the brief moment Sharon glances at the person giving the order, she looks back up.

"But sir, there is a man over..."

She looks up to see the attacker had vanished.

"...there," she finishes, and the word arrives somewhere far behind the rest of the sentence.

"Sharon! Wake up!"

"Sir!"

She responds, finally alert. Snapping out of it. But her mind is somewhere else entirely.

The camera begins to rise from ground level, pulling upward along the side of the damaged building. The commotion below, officers, ambulances, witnesses, shrinks as the shot ascends. As the camera clears the rooftop line and the cityscape opens up, something catches in the distance: a dark figure in a far alley, swinging away. Escaping. Gone before anyone else could have seen it.

"We need to take some of these people in for questioning," a voice says somewhere below, already fading out of reach.

Fade to black.

CRIME SCENE: WIDER SHOT

The black fades into a slow, sweeping overhead view of the area. The full scale of the damage is revealed.

The building's upper floor is ripped open: a gaping hole exposing mangled office furniture, dangling cables, and shattered glass. Police tape cuts sharp yellow lines across the street. Three ambulances sit with their back doors open, paramedics tending to civilians wrapped in thermal blankets. A fire engine is parked at an angle, its crew standing around looking up at the building like they are trying to understand the physics of what happened.

Reporters have already arrived. A woman with a microphone stands in front of the tape, the damaged building over her shoulder, doing a piece to camera. Neighbours lean out of windows. A kid films on his phone.

The camera weaves through all of this, tight, low, moving between legs and equipment, before finding Sharon. Half in her car, one leg out on the tarmac, not doing any of the jobs happening around her.

We leave her there.

THE SOCK

The sound of a television bleeds in.

"Breaking news... A mysterious incident has been reported in Central Danim. Witnesses claim to have seen figures fighting near the scene, and a massive hole was left in the side of a building. Authorities are still investigating..."

The news is playing, but the shot is not on the TV. It is on a sock. A single sock, wedged under a pile of clothes on a messy bedroom floor.

A hand reaches for it and misses.

"Where are you..."

The room is a mess. Clothes draped over chairs, school books stacked unevenly, a game controller hanging off the edge of the bed by its cable. A boy on his knees, reaching under a pile of stuff, fishing for the sock.

He finds it. Holds it up. Sniffs it. His face scrunches. He looks at it again. Considers the options. There are no options.

"...it'll do."

He pulls it on. Grabs his shoe from under the bed and starts trying to stuff his foot in without untying the laces. It is not cooperating. He is sitting on the edge of the bed, one hand pulling the tongue of the shoe open, the other pushing his heel down, and it is just not going in.

Then he hears something. Outside. Muffled through the window. Raised voices. Not shouting exactly, but that aggressive tone that travels through glass. The sound of kids fronting.

He looks up toward the window, shoe half on, foot at an awkward angle.

He gets up and hops to the window, the shoe flapping on his foot.

THE LIT HOODIE BOY

Down the road, near the end of the block. A boy in a black hoodie, LIT printed across the front in white letters, is surrounded by four other kids. They are in his face. Circling. One of them pushes the boy's shoulder. Another is talking, pointing, getting closer.

He watches from his window. He can't hear the words, just the muffled aggression, the tone of kids who have decided something is about to happen.

The boy in the LIT hoodie doesn't back up. His posture doesn't change. He is smaller than all four of them and he is standing like he is alone in a field.

One of the bigger kids says something and shoves the boy hard. The boy stumbles back a step.

His hand goes to the window latch. He is about to open it.

The boy in the LIT hoodie moves.

It is fast. Not regular-kid fast. Something else. He sidesteps the next shove, grabs the kid's arm at the wrist, pivots underneath it, and throws him into the pavement. The kid hits the ground and slides. Before the second one can process what happened, the boy drives a short, sharp palm strike into his chest. The kid's feet almost leave the ground as he staggers backward and drops. The third one swings, a wide, panicked haymaker, and the boy ducks under it like the punch was moving in slow motion, sweeps his legs, and the kid folds. The fourth swings too, faster, smarter. The boy slips it, catches the wrist, and drives an elbow into the kid's ribs. He goes down wheezing.

The fifth kid freezes. Just stands there with his fists half raised, not committed to any decision. The boy in the LIT hoodie stares at him. Dead still. The fifth kid backs away, turns, and walks fast in the other direction.

Four kids on the ground. One walking away. Seconds.

The boy in the LIT hoodie stands there. Looking left. Looking right. Eyes moving over each of the four kids on the ground like he is checking that nobody is getting back up. Calm. Hands at his sides. He is not in a rush.

His mouth is open. His hands are still on the window latch. He doesn't blink.

Then he snaps. He looks down at his shoe, still half on, foot at an angle. He grabs it with both hands, forces his heel down with a grunt, hops twice on the spot, and gives it one final violent shove. It is on.

He bolts out of his room.

Down the hallway, family photos blur past him on the wall. Him as a toddler. Sharon in a graduation gown. A faded photo of a young boy who looks like him but older. He doesn't notice any of them. He is flying downstairs.

He hits the kitchen.

"Have you finished cleaning your room?"

"Be right back, mum." He is already past her, heading for the front door.

"Where are you going?!"

No response. The front door opens and slams shut. His mum stands in the kitchen holding a spatula, mouth open, mid-sentence.

Outside. He runs.

He goes past the end wall of the block without slowing and without looking. There is old spray-paint on it, faded so far back into the brick that it reads as texture more than lettering: a shape that might be wings, letters that lost their edges years ago. Underneath, a bunch of flowers cable-tied to the drainpipe, long dead, the cellophane gone milky.

The camera doesn't stop either. It is gone in half a second.

He carries on down the street to where the fight happened. The four kids are picking themselves up off the pavement. One is sitting on the curb holding his ribs. Another is on all fours, spitting blood. The third is leaning against a wall touching his jaw. The fourth is nowhere. Already gone.

The boy in the LIT hoodie is nowhere to be seen.

He looks left. Right. Down the side road. Up the street. Spins around. Nothing. Gone. Like he was never there.

"Where did that boy go?"

The kid spitting blood looks up at him. Wipes his mouth with the back of his hand. Spits again. Pink.

"I don't know," he says, "but he's fucked when I see him."

He barely hears the answer. He is still scanning: rooftops, alleyways, the park at the end of the road. Searching for something he has already lost.

"KEVIN!!" His mum's voice arrives from the front door at full volume.

"I'm coming, mum!"

He is still looking. One more glance down the side road. One more sweep of the street. Nothing.

He turns and walks back toward his house. But something has changed. His face is different. The wide-eyed wonder is settling into something quieter, more focused. His jaw is set. His eyes are forward. He has a question now. A burning one. And he knows exactly who to ask.

THE KITCHEN

Kevin walks back in. His mum is waiting, arms crossed. The spatula is now a weapon.

"Where. Did. You. Go."

"I just... thought I saw someone I knew."

"You THOUGHT you saw someone?" She lets the word sit there so he can hear how it sounds. "So you just run out my house without eating, without your coat, without telling me where you're going?"

"Mum, I..."

"Sit down. Eat. Now."

Kevin sits. She pushes a plate of toast toward him. He picks up a slice, takes a bite. She watches him for a second, the anger softening at the edges. She picks up a fork from the counter and pretends to eat from his plate.

"Mum!"

"What?" She doesn't even look up. "It looked lonely."

Kevin pulls the plate closer to himself, hiding a smile. She grins, quick, warm, a flash, then goes back to packing her bag for work.

Grandad is sitting at the kitchen table with a cup of tea and the newspaper. He hasn't moved through any of this.

"You know in my day we wake up before di sun," he says, without lowering the paper.

"Grandad, the sun's already up."

"Exactly."

Kevin goes back to his toast. His mum turns to the counter and starts packing her bag for work, still talking, something about the bins, something about his shoes.

The camera drifts off her and finds the shelf above the radiator.

A small photograph in a wooden frame. A boy of about eighteen in school uniform, caught mid-laugh at whoever was holding the camera. He has Kevin's face in it somewhere. Tucked into the corner of the frame, a memorial card, soft at the edges from being handled.

IN LOVING MEMORY
JADEN YOUNG

Two dates underneath. Seven years since the second one.

Beside the frame, a glass candle, the inside of the glass black from the number of times it has been lit.

His mum crosses the kitchen and, without breaking her sentence and without turning her head, straightens the card with one finger as she passes. The way you straighten a picture in a hallway you have walked ten thousand times.

Nobody looks at it. Nobody mentions it. It is furniture.

Grandad watches Kevin over the top of his newspaper. Kevin is scraping crumbs off the plate with his thumb.

"Him look more like Jaden every day," Grandad says. To Kevin's mum. Not to Kevin.

She doesn't turn around. Doesn't stop packing. Her hand pauses on the zip of her bag for maybe half a second.

"Mm."

Grandad goes back to the paper.

Kevin's eyes come up. Just for a moment. Then straight back down to the plate.

Nobody says anything else about it.

Kevin finishes the toast. Grabs his bag. Heads for the door. His mum catches him by the collar.

"Coat."

"Mum, it's not even..."

She raises the spatula. Not threateningly. Just enough.

Kevin grabs the coat off the hook.

"Straight to the barbershop and straight back! And don't..."

The door closes before she finishes.

She shakes her head.

"Him alright," Grandad says.

"Hmm."

THE BUS STOP

Kevin arrives at the bus stop. He sits down on the metal bench, bag between his feet, thinking. The question is still burning. How did that kid move like that? Where do you learn something like that? Who can teach him?

A woman approaches the bus stop. Late twenties. Tight leggings with Styles written across the thigh. Leather jacket. Hoop earrings the size of handcuffs. She is on the phone, and she is not happy.

"Ahh, you men are all the same!" She drops onto the bench next to Kevin hard enough to feel it through the metal. He shifts away slightly. "Only stick around to get what you want! As soon as you bust your nut, you..."

She stops. Looks to her left. Kevin is sitting there, rigid, eyes forward, looking like he is trying to become invisible.

The woman looks at him. Looks at her own clenched fist, which was mid-gesture, wound up like she was about to punch something.

She sighs.

"...Shit."

She puts the phone down. Flexes her hand open. Leans back.

"Fuck it."

She sits there. Silence. Kevin hasn't moved. He is barely breathing.

Then, without warning, she punches the bus stop window. CRACK. The glass shatters into a web of fractures. Not fully broken, safety glass, but ruined.

Kevin jumps up. Stands several feet away from the bench, bag clutched to his chest, eyes wide.

She looks at the shattered glass. Looks at her fist. Looks at Kevin standing five feet away like she is a grenade.

She closes her eyes. Breathes out, long and slow, the way you do when you are counting down from something. Shakes the hand loose at the wrist. Rolls her shoulders back once. When she opens her eyes the storm has gone out of them. Mostly.

"Come sit," she says, patting the bench. "What are you afraid of?"

Kevin looks at her. Looks at the smashed glass. Looks back at her.

"It's fine. I'll... I'll stand."

"Suit yourself."

She crosses her arms. Goes back to her phone. Silence.

Time passes. Buses going the opposite direction pass by. A pigeon lands near Kevin's feet. A man walks past eating a patty. Kevin's bus doesn't come.

Eventually, Kevin sits back down. The woman is scrolling her phone. She takes a sideways glance at him sitting down but doesn't say anything.

More silence. Then she looks at Kevin properly. Studies his face. He is staring at the pavement, thinking hard. Brow furrowed. Jaw tight. Miles away.

"You look like you're gonna meet your crush for the very first time."

"Huh?"

"What I mean is." She waves the phone at him vaguely. "You look like you want to crack the Da Vinci code."

Kevin doesn't respond. She keeps going.

"Does she even know your name?" the woman says, as she starts searching through her bag.

"Who?" Kevin asks, still looking forward.

"Your crush," she says, as she pulls something out and extends her hand toward him.

"I'm not going to meet a..." He looks down, puzzled. Then his face changes. "...girl."

"Oh?"

She is holding condoms. Two of them, pinched between her fingers, offered as casually as a mint. The packaging clearly reads XXL.

Kevin's eyes come back up to her face.

"Well, why would you be heading to town at this time?"

She puts the condoms back in her bag and crosses her legs. Kevin is staring at the sky, at the ground, anywhere but at her.

He thinks for a second.

"I want someone to teach me something."

"Why?"

"I... I..."

He doesn't have an answer ready. How do you explain to a stranger that you just watched a kid your age put four people on the ground in seconds and now you need to know how that is possible?

The bus approaches in the distance.

"Finally!"

She stands up with relief, waving the bus down. Kevin turns as the bus pulls up. They get on. She taps her card and immediately starts going off at the bus driver.

"Do you know how long I've been waiting? The app said three minutes. THREE MINUTES. That was fifteen minutes ago. What were you doing back there? Playing with your fucking balls?"

Kevin taps his Clam card and walks past her while she is still going. He heads straight upstairs to the top deck. Behind him, her voice continues, getting louder.

"No, don't give me that fucking look. I pay for this service! I PAY! You think I'm standing out there in this heat so you can finish your wank break?!"

Kevin sits down by the window. From downstairs he can still hear her going. Muffled. Relentless. He listens for a second. Shakes his head slightly.

Danim.

He puts his earphones in. The city starts to move past the window.

THE BUS AND THE CAR

Intercut. Two places, one stretch of time. Neither of them knows about the other.

Kevin, top deck, window seat, earphones in. His own reflection sits on the glass, half there and half not, the streets running straight through his face.

Growing up in this part of Danim was never easy.

Sharon, half in the police car, one leg out on the tarmac, looking up at what is left of the fifth floor. She raises her phone and takes a picture of it.

"What is going on in this city?" she says, to nobody but herself. "Am I just seeing things? Impossible things."

She has a slight flash of the eye contact she made with the attacker moments earlier. Blinks it away. Looks at the photo on her screen.

A parade of shops slides past Kevin's window. Half of them shuttered. A man asleep in a doorway with his coat over a dog.

My dad passed when I was young. And my older brother...

His eyes stay on the window.

Murdered. In cold blood.

Sharon, still looking at the photo. Then, without deciding to, she comes out of it, opens her contacts, and dials.

It rings.

Worst of all, they never found his body.

In Kevin's coat pocket, against his leg, the phone starts to buzz. Short pulse. Pause. Short pulse.

He doesn't feel it. Or he feels it and it doesn't register, because there is music in his ears and a window in front of him and he is thirteen.

They never found who did it. No witnesses. Never got close.

Sharon, the phone at her ear. Ringing. Her eyes somewhere on the middle distance.

"Come on," she says, under her breath. "Come on, pick up."

The buzzing in Kevin's pocket stops. The reflection holds. He has not looked down once.

My sister left after that.

She is on screen as he says it. Phone to her ear. Waiting.

Joined the police. Said she was going to get justice for him, and that was the only thing she wanted.

Traffic lights. The bus stops. A woman crosses with a pram. The bus moves again.

Years went by. The case went cold.

Sharon. Still ringing. She has not moved.

That was a long time ago, though. We all found our own way to cope.

The bus turns a corner and the light swings across his face.

Mine was a barbershop.

UNCLE JON'S

The bus crosses the invisible border between Central and South Danim. The streets get quieter. Less traffic. Smaller buildings. Kevin gets off at his stop and walks down a side road that leads to another side road that leads to a narrow street lined with old shops: a dry cleaner's, a newsagent with faded window displays, and tucked between them, a barbershop.

The sign reads UNCLE JON'S.

Kevin stops in front of it and looks up at the letters like he is checking they are still there.

I've been coming here since before I can remember. Mum used to drop me off and go about her day.

It's mad how much time you can spend somewhere before you notice how much it matters.

He pushes the door. The bell rings.

We do not follow him in.

SHARON: NELSON

Straight off the bell.

Sharon, half in the car, one leg out. The phone comes down from her ear. The screen is dark. It rang out.

She looks at it.

"...Shit."

She drops her head back against the door frame and shuts her eyes.

"Sharon!!"

The shout comes from somewhere behind her. A policeman is already approaching: Nelson. London cockney accent. The kind of man who takes up more space than he has earned.

"Sir!" Sharon jerks to attention, stepping out of the car.

"What do we pay you for, aye?" He stops in front of her. Close. Too close. "Why is it, you, I always have to cover for? Boateng's on my back about your disclosure again, and it ain't her I'm gonna hear it from, is it. If it were up to me you wud'a been out this force before the morning cock-a-doodles."

Sharon stares ahead. Jaw tight. Eyes forward. Professional. Taking it.

"What is it the Super sees in you?" he asks, and he starts to walk around her, slowly, like an inspection. His eyes drop. "...Or what is it he wants to put in you?"

He is looking at her body. Not even hiding it. Another policeman approaches and stands next to him.

"Wouldn't mind mashing my gravy all over them bangers," Nelson says to him, barely bothering to lower his voice.

The other officer stifles a laugh. Sharon doesn't move. Her face is stone. But her hands, at her sides, are trembling slightly. Not from fear. From rage.

She walks away. Steady. Controlled. Every step deliberate.

"Stupid Nelson," she says under her breath.

She keeps walking toward the building. Ambulances on either side of her, paramedics loading stretchers, officers interviewing witnesses.

"Probably why you never got a promotion," she mutters.

She passes a police officer interviewing a woman, the same woman the cloaked figure protected. The woman is sitting on the back of an ambulance, thermal blanket around her shoulders, child on her lap.

Sharon is walking past when she hears it.

"...and he just said 'don't move.'" The woman shakes her head slowly, like she is still trying to make the words fit. "That's all he said. Just... 'don't move.' And the way he said it... I can't explain it. Like nothing was wrong. Like everything was going to be fine. I've never felt so..."

Sharon stops walking.

Her breathing changes. Something behind her eyes shifts. Like a door opening in a room she forgot existed.

Flashback: quick, fragmented, half a memory. Everything in it is from her eyeline and nothing in it is complete.

Sound arrives before picture. Running feet on pavement. A shout, too far off to make out. Breathing, fast and shallow, and it is hers.

Daylight. A gap between two buildings. A small hand closes around her wrist and pulls, hard, and the world swings.

They come round the corner. Brick against her back. She is small. Her bag is still on one shoulder and she cannot make herself let go of the strap.

A boy. Younger than her. He barely comes up to her shoulder. He puts one hand flat on her chest and holds her against the wall, not roughly, the way you would steady something that might fall.

"Don't move," he says, quietly.

He isn't looking at her. He is looking past the corner, leaning out just enough to see, his weight forward on one foot.

She is shaking. She can hear it in her own breath. She looks up at him and she wants to ask, and half the question gets out.

"What are yo..."

He lifts one finger. Still not looking at her.

"Shhh."

Beyond the corner, something happens. We do not see it. We only get the sound of it, and we get it the way she got it, which is muffled and out of order.

The hand stays on her chest. Steady. Not one tremor in it.

And then he starts to turn back toward her.

The light is behind him. His face begins to come round out of the shadow, and the memory is already going, thinning at the edges, the sound draining out of it.

She never sees it.

"Don't move," somewhere far off, echoing after her.

Flashback ends.

Sharon is breathing heavily. Standing in the middle of the crime scene, eyes unfocused, one hand on her chest.

She shakes it off. Physically shakes her head. Then turns and approaches the witness. Fast. Intense.

"Wait, what did you say?" The questions come out of her in a rush, one climbing over the next. "What did he look like? Did you see his face? How tall was he? What was he wearing? Did he say anything else?"

The witness recoils slightly, startled by the intensity. The police officer interviewing her puts a hand up.

"Sharon, relax. I've got the notes right here..."

Sharon snatches the notepad out of his hand.

"Hey? You can't just..."

She isn't listening. She is reading. Her eyes scan the handwritten notes, lips moving slightly.

"Cloaked figure..." she mumbles. "Don't move..."

She looks up. Still thinking. Looks at the witness.

"Can you tell me anything else? Anything at all?"

"Ahhh well..." The witness lifts a hand and points up at the hole in the building. "He hurled into the building."

"Wait..." Sharon follows the finger, and her face empties out. "What do you mean? He made that?"

"That's what I keep telling this gentleman."

"Ma'am, like I told you before," the officer says, in the flat, patient voice of a man who has said it several times already, "sometimes when you are in these types of situations, the body goes through shock. We see things our mind is telling us. Now Sharon, can I have my..."

He stops. Sharon has pulled out her phone.

SNAP.

She photographs the notepad pages, both sides, close-up, making sure every word is captured. Then she tosses the notepad back to the officer without looking at him.

"Hey..."

He fumbles the catch. The notepad hits his chest and he scrambles to grab it. He looks at the witness. They both stare at Sharon, who is already walking away.

SHARON: THE CALL

Walking. Fast. Through the tape, past the ambulances, her eyes fixed on the building ahead of her and the two men standing at its entrance. The phone is already at her ear.

It connects on the third ring.

"Sharon?"

"Mum. Is Kevin with you?"

There is a pause on the line. Her mum has heard something in her voice already.

"No. He's gone to get a haircut. Why? What's happened?"

She keeps walking. Her eyes go up the front of the building to the hole five floors up.

"I can't explain right now. It's police business. But when he gets in, I want him in. Tell him to stay in the house."

"Sharon, you're scaring me."

"Mum. Please."

Silence on the line. Then, quietly:

"...Alright. I'll tell him."

Sharon closes her eyes. Just for a second. Still walking.

"Thanks, Mum."

She hangs up. And she stops. Twenty feet short of the entrance, phone still in her hand, looking at the two men in black suits standing either side of the door.

They have already clocked her. Neither of them moves.

JON'S BARBERSHOP

Back inside, picking up where the bell left off.

Inside, the shop is warm. Not fancy. Three barber chairs, mirrors, a counter with products that haven't been rearranged in years. A radio plays softly. The kind of place where time moves slower than the rest of the city.

Jon is standing behind the first chair, clippers in hand, working on a customer. He looks up when the bell rings.

"Kev."

"Uncle Jon."

Kevin drops his bag and sits in the waiting area. He is thinking. The question is right there, sitting behind his teeth, ready to come out. He has been rehearsing it the whole bus ride. Something like Uncle Jon, can you teach me how to fight? Or maybe Do you know anything about fighting? Or maybe just How did that kid do that?

He is working up to it. Organising the words. Finding the courage.

The bell rings.

The door swings open. Sleeze walks in like he owns the place. Tattoos from his neck to his wrists, gold chain, tracksuit bottoms, fresh trainers. He is grinning at nothing in particular. Behind him come two of his boys, matching his energy, matching his tracksuits, matching his swagger: a tall one who stations himself by the door, and a shorter, rounder one who goes straight to the product counter and starts picking things up he has no intention of buying.

"Jon-Jon-Jon." Sleeze spreads his arms wide enough to take in the whole shop. "My guy."

"Sleeze." Jon doesn't look up from the clippers.

"You busy?"

Jon glances at the customer sitting in his chair, half-cut, then back at Sleeze.

"What does it look like?"

"Looks like you need some better customers, fam." Sleeze tips his chin at the chair. "Look at this man's head. Bro, your head is shaped like a Tic Tac."

The customer stiffens under the cape. Jon's hand doesn't pause. Kevin presses his lips together and studies the floor very hard.

"Sleeze, man." The tall one by the door says it wearily, like a man who has made this exact request many times. "Leave the guy alone."

"I'm being nice!" Sleeze rounds on him, wounded. "I'm saying he needs Jon more than most. That's a compliment."

He drops into the waiting chair next to Kevin, leans back, and spreads both arms along the seat backs like a man on a throne. Then he notices who he is sitting next to.

"Yo, little man." He leans in. "You here again? You practically live here, fam."

"Just getting a trim," Kevin says.

"A trim? A TRIM?" Sleeze sits forward, genuinely offended on behalf of the entire concept. "Bro, you come here every other week. What trim are you getting? You've barely got hair to trim." He twists round towards the mirror. "Jon, what are you even cutting on this yout's head?"

"More than I'd cut on yours if you're not paying," Jon says, still not looking up.

"See, that's cold." Sleeze appeals to the room. "That is cold, Jon. After everything I've done for this shop."

"What have you done for this shop?"

"I bring the vibes, bro." He says it as though it settles the matter. "You can't put a price on vibes."

"He's got a point still," the short one offers from the counter, turning over a tub of pomade.

"I can put a price on a haircut though." Jon flicks the clippers off for a second. "Fifteen pounds."

Sleeze clutches his chest like he has taken a round.

"Fifteen?! Fifteen?!" He looks left and right for witnesses. "You hear this? Man's out here robbing people in broad daylight and he's meant to be one of the good ones."

Kevin is grinning now. He can't help it, and Sleeze catches it instantly.

"See?" He jabs a thumb sideways at Kevin without looking at him. "Little man gets it. He knows the struggle."

"Yeah but little man doesn't pay either, does he?" the tall one says from the door.

"That's different." Sleeze doesn't even turn round. "Little man is family. He's like a nephew. You ever see Jon kicking a nephew out for a fiver short? No."

"You've never paid full price in your life though, Sleeze." The short one says it to the pomade, mildly, and puts the tub back on the wrong shelf.

"And? I'm consistent." Sleeze delivers it like a man laying down a philosophy he expects to be quoted on. "Loyalty is a price too, you know what I'm saying?"

Jon shakes his head at the mirror. The customer in the chair is desperately wishing he was anywhere else in Danim. Kevin is fully laughing now. And whatever question he walked in here carrying, and there was a question, a burning one, is gone. Dissolved into Sleeze's circus.

Jon finishes with his customer. The man pays, gives Sleeze a wide berth, and leaves. Jon dusts off the chair and nods at Kevin.

"Come."

Kevin sits in the chair. Jon throws the cape over him, adjusts the height, and starts working. Sleeze hasn't stopped talking. He has moved on to a story about a girl who blocked him on three different platforms. His boys are on their phones, occasionally laughing at the wrong parts, which makes Sleeze louder.

While Jon works, Kevin watches the mirror. His eyes drift. He notices things. He always notices things.

The door to the back room. It is closed. There is a small deadbolt on it that Kevin has never seen on any other barbershop door. As he watches, a man comes through the front door, nods at Jon, and walks straight to the back without sitting down. Jon nods back without breaking his conversation. The man disappears through the door. It closes behind him.

Kevin watches this happen in the mirror's reflection. Nobody else reacts. Like it is normal.

Kevin files it away.

"How's your mum?"

"Same. Stressing."

"And your grandad?"

"He's good. Told me in his day they woke up before the sun."

"Smart man."

"The sun was already up."

Jon smirks. Barely. Just the corner of his mouth.

Kevin's phone goes in his pocket, under the cape, and he does the whole awkward operation of getting to it without moving his head: elbow up, hand fishing, cape rustling. Jon lifts the clippers away and waits, patient, like a man who has done this a thousand times.

Kevin looks at the screen. Answers it.

"Mum."

A beat.

"Yeah. Yeah, I'm there now."

A beat. He rolls his eyes at nothing.

"Will do."

A beat.

"Okay, mum."

He hangs up, puts the phone back under the cape, and Jon brings the clippers in again.

"Everything alright?"

"Yeah. Mum's just saying come back home."

Jon nods and carries on cutting. Nothing in his face changes.

Neither of them thinks about it again.

Sleeze leans forward.

"Yo, Jon, you hear about what happened in Central this morning? Some madness went down. Building got a hole in it the size of a bus. News saying gang activity, but bro..." He shakes his head slowly. "That weren't no gang. I'm telling you. Something's going on in this city."

Jon's clippers pause. A fraction of a second. So brief that Sleeze doesn't catch it. His boys don't catch it. But Kevin, watching in the mirror, catches it. The hesitation. The slight tightening of Jon's grip on the clippers.

Then he continues cutting. Smooth. Like nothing happened.

"People talk too much."

"I'm just saying..."

"And I'm just saying people talk too much."

Sleeze holds his hands up. Message received. He changes the subject. Something about new trainers, something about a debt. The moment passes.

But Kevin caught that pause. He stores it in the same drawer as the back room door and the man who walked straight through without getting a haircut.

SHARON: THE BUILDING

Same spot. She hasn't moved. She is looking down at her phone, thumbing back through what she has: the notepad pages, both sides, the handwriting. The hole in the building. The notepad again.

She stops on one. Reads it. Her jaw sets.

She looks up. The two men are still there. Still watching her.

A long beat.

"...Fuck it."

She pockets the phone and walks straight at them. Two men in black suits step into her path. Not police. Something else. Their posture is military. Their faces are blank.

"Sorry ma'am." The first one doesn't move an inch as he says it. "I can't let you through. This investigation is out of your jurisdiction."

"Where are you guys from?"

The two agents don't reply. They just stare at her. Sunglasses. Earpieces. Stone faces.

"What the hell is going on?"

Silence.

"You're not gonna tell me. Fine." She holds the look a second longer than she needs to. "I'll be back."

She turns to walk away.

"Don't waste your time," the second one says.

They look at each other.

"Haha. Good one."

They pound fists, chuckling. In the background behind them, Sharon makes a left into an alleyway around the side of the building. They don't notice.

Sharon moves through the alley, quick, quiet, pressing herself against the brickwork. The further she gets from the main road, the quieter it becomes. Dripping pipes. The hum of an air conditioning unit. A cat bolting across her path makes her flinch.

She reaches the back of the building. Presses her back against the corner wall and peeks around.

One more agent. Guarding the back door. Standing with his hands clasped in front of him, scanning the alley.

"Shit," she whispers.

She looks around desperately for an idea. There is a fire escape above her, a stack of old pallets, a wheelie bin. Nothing useful.

Then the back door opens. A woman steps out. Late forties, sharp blazer, heels that click on the concrete, phone pressed to her ear. She walks like the ground adjusts to her, not the other way around.

"...No we don't have time... I need that report yesterday... That means you are running out of time..."

She walks away from the door, the agent following her like a shadow.

"...And make sure you keep reporters from this, otherwise it's my tits on the line..."

They round the corner. Their footsteps fade.

Sharon's eyes lock on the door. It is closing. Slowly. The hydraulic hinge giving her seconds.

She moves. Fast. Slipping around the corner and catching the door with her fingertips just before it clicks shut. She slides through the gap and she is inside.

Dark corridor. Emergency lighting casting everything in a sickly green. She spots the stairwell sign.

"Judging where the hole is," she says to herself, "it should be about the fifth floor."

She starts climbing. Two steps at a time. Her heels are loud on the metal stairs. She pauses, slips them off, carries them. Bare feet on cold metal. She feels every ridge, every bolt. Her toes curl against the chill.

She has a brief flash of the witness's words. He hurled into the building.

Is that even possible? I'm having a hard time just imagining it.

Fifth floor. She presses herself against the wall and peers around the corner. Three agents are blocking the corridor leading to the destroyed office. They are having a conversation.

"Great."

She leans back against the wall, rolls her eyes, blows air through her lips.

Down the corridor, the agents' conversation is already in full flow.

"Then I told him, nah you ain't finished. You ain't washed behind your ear or..."

"Where are you?!" The voice comes echoing down the corridor and lands like a dropped tray. "I said get here NOW!"

The three agents freeze mid-conversation.

"Was that the chief?"

"Did you hear what I said?!" she calls again, louder. "I said get here NOW!"

"Yes ma'am!" all three say at once.

They scramble. All three of them rushing around the corner in a panic, their conversation forgotten, nearly tripping over each other.

The corridor is empty.

Above where the guards were standing, a ventilation grate slowly opens. Sharon's fingers curl around the edge. She lowers herself through, arms shaking, abs burning, sweat running down her temple. Her blouse catches on the metal edge and tears slightly. She drops the last foot and lands softly, wincing as her bare feet hit the cold floor.

She looks down at the tear in her blouse.

"Great," she whispers. "That was new."

She turns to the door. The destroyed office. She pushes it open slowly and peers inside.

Her eyes widen.

The camera does a slow rotation around her, revealing what she sees.

The hole is massive. Far bigger than it looked from the ground. Half the floor is gone. Office desks are piled up like matchsticks. The ceiling has partially collapsed. Wind blows through the gap, carrying dust and the distant sound of sirens from below. Through the hole you can see the Danim skyline, the river, the bridge. It is almost beautiful if you ignore the destruction.

Sharon steps inside carefully. Glass crunches under her bare feet. She winces, picks a route between the debris, stepping where the carpet is still intact.

She hears voices approaching from the corridor. Getting louder. Fast.

Sharon ducks behind a pile of toppled office desks and overturned filing cabinets. She presses herself flat. Pulls her knees in. Holds her breath.

The door slams open.

"...And where's Adam?!" the woman demands, storming in, heels crunching on glass she clearly does not care about, walking across the debris like it personally offended her. "He was supposed to be here before I showed up!"

"I... don't know ma'am. I think..."

"Ahhhhh!"

She palms her forehead. Closes her eyes. Takes a breath. Then starts massaging her temples with both hands, slow circles.

The agent stands there. Waiting. He has learned not to speak when she is like this.

"So..." he tries eventually. "Do you want me to take the footage to review?"

The Boss Lady exhales. Long. Controlled. Like she is deciding whether to fire everyone in the building or just this one.

"Yes."

"Copy."

He turns to leave. Gets two steps.

"Wait."

The agent stops. Turns his head. Waiting for further instructions.

"Put it down for now and come here."

The agent places the mini USB hard drive on a nearby office desk, one that is still standing, barely, and turns around. He walks toward her.

The Boss Lady takes off her blazer. Drapes it over a chair. Then unbuttons her shirt. One button. Two. Not rushing. Not embarrassed. Like this is as routine as filing a report.

"One thing I love above all in this God-forsaken job is..."

She reaches out and strokes the agent's crotch. Casual. Possessive. Like adjusting a tie.

"...I'll always have one of you clumsy idiots to take my anger out on."

Sharon, peering through a gap in the toppled desks, has one eyebrow raised. She watches the Boss Lady finish her sentence and the eyebrow drops. Her expression shifts from curiosity to a flat yeah, right.

"Yeah right, you horny bitch," she says, barely audible even to herself.

The Boss Lady slowly unbuckles the agent's trousers. They drop to the floor. Sharon's eyes, which had been watching with detached professionalism, slowly widen. Wider. Wider. Her mouth opens slightly. Then, involuntarily, a tiny smile crosses her face.

"Jackpot," the Boss Lady says, her face in shadow, grinning.

The camera floats away from them. Drifting across the rubble.

The sounds of sex fill the destroyed office: gasping, moaning, the Boss Lady giving orders like she is running a military operation. The agent barely gets a word in.

Back to Sharon. She is pressed against the desks. Her breathing has changed. The sounds are everywhere in the acoustics of the destroyed room. She stares at the ceiling. Her jaw tightens. Her hand moves. First to her chest, gripping her blouse. Then lower.

Quick flash: images stacking on top of each other. Different people. Different places. A woman's neck. A man's back. A club bathroom. A car park. A hotel room that charges by the hour. The images come faster, layering, breathing, the flash of a lighter, a hand on glass, a gasp.

Sharon snaps out of it.

Her eyes go wide. She looks down at herself. One hand is holding her breast through her blouse. The other is down her trousers. She freezes. Looks left. Looks right. The sounds are still going on in the background.

She slowly pulls her hand out. Opens her legs slightly. Sees the wet patch between her thighs. Closes her legs. Wipes the hand that was down her trousers on her already torn blouse.

"...Whatever," she says, flat, to nobody, and files the whole thing away.

She refocuses. The drive is right there on the desk. Maybe ten metres away. Between her and it: a minefield of debris, and two people who are very much occupied.

Sharon starts to crawl. Slowly. Behind the toppled desks. Under a dangling cable. Over a shattered monitor. Glass presses into her knees and palms. She grits her teeth, keeps moving. A bead of sweat runs from her hairline down her nose and drops onto the carpet.

From the perspective closest to the couple, the Boss Lady is bent over with both hands on the wall, getting her hair pulled. And in the distance behind them, Sharon's hand, slowly, carefully, reaching across the desk surface toward the drive.

Her fingers close around it. She slides it off the desk and tucks it into her waistband.

"Harder. HARDER." The Boss Lady's head is against the wall, and she is still somehow issuing instructions. "You think I'm made of glass? Move. That's it. That's it right there. Don't you fucking stop."

"Say my fucking name," the agent says, leaning into her ear.

"I don't give a shit!"

She is on the edge. The sounds intensify.

"Oh my God!... I'm... oh shit... I'm about to... oh shit oh shit oh SHIIIIT!!"

Sharon is already out the door. Moving through the corridor fast now, not worrying about noise. They can't hear anything over themselves.

She spots the stairs sign. Pushes through the door. Starts descending, bare feet slapping on metal steps, the drive tucked in her waistband pressing cold against her skin.

Voices. Coming up the stairs. Agents. She can hear their conversation getting louder with every step.

One floor below her, a window. She rushes to it. Pushes it open. Cold air hits her face. She looks down. There is a square industrial bin directly below, and an air conditioning unit jutting out from the wall between her and it.

No time to calculate. She hears the agents rounding the stairwell below her. She climbs onto the windowsill and hangs from the ledge, feet dangling, fingers white on the frame.

The agents pass the floor above her. Their conversation drifts down.

"I tried proposing. He said no. But every time I..." He stops himself. "Are those fingers?"

Sharon gasps. She looks down at the bin below. Looks at the air conditioning unit between her and it. Lets go.

She drops. Her hip catches the air conditioning unit on the way down. She yelps, spins, and crashes onto the top of the bin. The lid buckles. She rolls off the side and hits the ground, landing in a heap on the wet concrete.

For a second she doesn't move. She is on her back, staring at the sky, trying to remember how breathing works. Her blouse is torn. Her knees are bleeding. Her feet are black with grime. The drive is still tucked in her waistband.

She gets up.

"We have a perimeter breach!" someone shouts from above.

Footsteps. One agent running up the stairs, another running down.

Sharon runs. Bare feet on wet alley concrete. Through the gap between two bins. Around a corner. Into a side street. She doesn't look back.

The agent bursts out the back door seconds later. Scans the alley. Empty. Sharon is gone.

SPIKE'S SAFE HOUSE

A different part of the city. A rooftop structure. Not fancy, industrial, hidden. A staircase leads to its entrance. The attacker from the fight, Spike, pushes the door open and walks inside.

He is barely through the door when a girl slides out of the shadows on rollerblades. Purple matching outfit. Short dress, belt of gadgets. She glides toward him backwards with a sinister grin.

"What the fuck..." She lets the pause do the work, still gliding, still grinning. "Was you thinking?"

She chuckles. Spike rolls his eyes. Doesn't respond. Keeps walking.

She starts roller-skating backwards alongside him, hands behind her back, matching his pace.

"Aw, talk to me, pumpkin," she coos, pitching her voice up into something sweet enough to be an insult.

Spike ignores her.

"You have blue balls? I mean, I can help you out with that." She tilts her head, still skating backwards, and holds the look.

Spike keeps his eyes forward.

"Shut up."

The corridor leads to spiral descending stairs. The girl splits her legs, placing each skate on each railing, and slowly grinds down. Her back is turned to Spike as she descends.

"Well, darling, I just want you to know that whatever the case..."

She bends over, leaning mainly to her right, looking back at him over her shoulder.

"A queen bee always gets the honey."

She lands at the bottom and halts at the entrance of a door. Opens it. Lifts her hand to show him in, like a hotel concierge.

"Tss."

He walks through.

Inside, the den. An open space converted into a hideout. Makeshift furniture, monitors, weapons on surfaces. Ninjas scattered around: some cleaning blades, some eating, some talking in corners. The moment Spike walks in, the room reacts.

"Spike?! What the fuck, fam?!"

"Broad daylight?"

Laughter. More of them gathering.

"Brooo!!"

"Shut up."

"Tell your momma to shut up, brudda."

He walks away laughing with the others. Spike stands there, jaw tight, eyes down.

The ninja who tried to silence the room, Spike's comrade, approaches.

"Come with me."

They go into a side room. A makeshift boardroom: one long table, mismatched chairs, one window with shutters letting in strips of daylight.

"Sit."

"I'll stand."

He crosses his arms and leans on the table.

The comrade looks at him. Starts walking slowly around the room.

"A battle with an enemy should always be strategic and well thought through. A battle without a plan is suicide." He takes his time with it, in no hurry to arrive anywhere. "I'm not gonna question why you are still alive because that goes without saying."

He arrives at the window. Looks through the shutters.

"I always want to know the motives of my comrades, so before you got here I did a fair share of brainstorming. Even gone as far as thinking someone killed your family."

He turns from the window.

"I want to see this town go down just as much as the next man, and I know you know everything the Hood stands for. So I'm still left with the same question..."

He faces Spike.

"Why?"

Spike is still leaning on the table. Arms crossed. Eyes shut.

"It wasn't supposed to turn out that way."

He opens his eyes.

"The family was low in cash and rent was due. I just wanted to get some cash and that was it."

SPIKE'S FLASHBACK

Another day. Summer, around eight in the evening, and the sun is still well up, throwing long gold light down a quiet parade of shops in Danim. Shutters coming down. The street emptied out to the last few stragglers heading home. An electronics shop, still open. Through the window, a customer is finishing up at the counter. Spike is around the corner, pulling a mask over his face. Black cloak, mask covering up to his nose. He peeks around the corner. The customer leaves. The sound alert beeps as they pass through the door.

Spike moves. Fast. He vaults over the counter in one fluid motion while the cashier is looking down, about to close the register. Spike catches him in a chokehold from behind and presses a blade, his signature sting, against the cashier's back.

"Stay still."

The cashier's hands shoot up. He gasps.

"Now walk away or die. Your choice."

He loosens the chokehold. The cashier looks at the exit. Runs. His footsteps and panicked breathing fade out the door.

Spike turns to the register. Starts pulling out cash. Stuffing it into his cloak. Focused. Quick.

A shadow falls across the counter.

Spike looks up.

A cloaked figure is standing at the entrance. Still. Calm. Holding a sandwich from the corner shop next door. One bite taken. He is just standing there. Looking at Spike. Chewing.

"Jog on, bro." Spike points the blade at him without much conviction. "Nothing to look at."

The cloaked figure doesn't move. Just keeps looking at him. Takes another bite of the sandwich.

"What? You want some P too, brudda?"

The cloaked figure chews. Swallows. Doesn't speak.

"Don't worry, I got you."

Spike looks down for a split second to grab more cash.

A flash of light. Something coming toward him. Time slows down.

Spike's eyes go wide. His brain processes it in fragments: metal. Spinning. Knife. Coming at his face.

His hand rises on instinct. Years of training condensed into a reaction. His palm catches the edge of the blade and deflects it upward. The knife spins into the air above him.

Spike opens his eyes.

The cloaked figure is standing directly in front of him. Right there. Across the counter. He didn't make a sound. Not a footstep. Not a breath. He is holding Spike's wrist, the one with the blade, firmly but without strain. Like holding a pen.

Spike looks into the cloaked figure's face. The hood shadows most of it, but the eyes are visible. They have no emotion. No anger. No excitement. Nothing. Just calm. The kind of calm that comes from being so far above a situation that the outcome was never in question.

Spike tries to speak. His mouth opens.

The deflected knife drops back down from above. On its way down, the blade slices through Spike's mask. A clean cut diagonally across the fabric. The mask falls away in two pieces, exposing Spike's face.

The cloaked figure releases Spike's wrist and catches the falling knife. Same hand. Without looking up. He tucks it away.

"I have triggered the alarm."

Spike glances down. Under the cash register, a small red light, blinking. The panic button. The cloaked figure pressed it. When? How? He was across the room a second ago.

"...And your face is exposed."

He turns and walks out of the shop. Casual. Like leaving a newsagent after buying a paper.

Spike stands behind the counter. Mask on the floor. Alarm blinking. Face out. He has been completely dismantled in under ten seconds and the man responsible just walked away eating a sandwich.

Spike chuckles. Not because it is funny. Because it is absurd.

He shoots his metal cable through the shop entrance. It clamps onto a wall outside. Spike hurls himself through the front of the shop, glass fragments scatter, and deviates his path upward, zipping to the top edge of a building. He lands on the roof. Turns around. Looks down.

The cloaked figure is walking out of the shop below. He looks up at Spike on the rooftop. Still holding the sandwich.

Spike points down at him. Opens his mouth to say something.

Beeping.

Spike looks left. Nothing. Looks right. Nothing. Looks down at the bottom of his cloak.

A tiny device. Stuck to the fabric. Blinking.

Four seconds.

Three seconds.

"Shit!"

He rips his cloak off, wraps it into a ball, and launches it upward with his cable. The cloak sails into the air.

BOOM.

The explosion punches a ball of orange into a bright blue sky, smoke unspooling above the rooftops in full daylight where half of Danim can see it. Scraps of black fabric rain down like confetti.

Below, the cloaked figure watches the debris fall. He takes another bite of the sandwich.

"Now you've completely caused attention to yourself," he says, quietly, to himself, the way a man notes the weather.

BACK IN THE ROOM

The flashback ends. Back in the makeshift boardroom. Spike is standing in the same position, arms crossed, leaning on the table. His comrade is staring at him.

"Wait... what?" He steps forward. "Your face was exposed? Rule number one. Destroy all..."

"It's destroyed."

Quick flash: the CCTV mainframe in the shop, ripped apart, electrical wires sticking out, sparking.

"Oight. Kool. Kool. Calm. Calm."

He paces. Takes it in.

"I'm still trying to work it out, though." Spike looks at his fist. Clenches it. Opens it. "How did my man do it?"

"Do what?"

"Blood, have you heard a word I said?!" He pushes off the table, animated now. "You can take an L... but this brudda... I don't know. He left no openings, even when times were bad. Everything he did was necessary."

As Spike explains, the camera shifts: zooming, rotating, showing replays of the flashback from new angles. Bullet-time. The audience sees what Spike saw, but broken down.

"The blade he chucked at the beginning to get me distracted..."

Replay: the knife spinning toward Spike's face. But now from above. The angle was never aimed to kill. It was aimed to draw Spike's hand upward, exposing his wrist, giving the cloaked figure the opening to grab it.

"I don't even know how he knew I would survive that."

Replay: the cloaked figure's eyes tracking the knife's trajectory. He calculated the exact speed, the exact angle, the exact moment Spike would react. If Spike was slower, even by a fraction, the knife would have hit. But the cloaked figure knew he wasn't.

"From my block, how did he get to me that quick?"

Replay: the entrance of the shop to the counter, maybe six metres. The cloaked figure covers it in the time it takes Spike to deflect the knife. No sound. No steps. Just displacement.

"I don't know what's even more impressive, the fact that I didn't hear the sound for a customer coming into the store, or the fact that he knew exactly how his blade would end up revealing my face."

Replay: the knife deflected upward. The exact rotation calculated so that on its way back down, the blade would slice the mask. Not Spike's face. Not his neck. The mask. Precise enough to expose him without harming him. That is not skill. That is something else.

"Not to mention he also pressed the trigger alert panic button."

Replay: the cloaked figure's hand, visible for a single frame, tucked under the counter, pressing the button, while his other hand held Spike's wrist. Two actions at once. Neither of them visible in real time.

"It was never my plan to leave the shop through the front, but in a way... I got excited."

Replay: Spike launching through the shop entrance. And there, in the blur of the exit, the cloaked figure's hand, planting the tiny bomb device on Spike's cloak as he zips past. One touch. Less than a second of contact.

"When I zipped past him was the final icing on the cake to fully expose me."

The replays end. Back to the room. Spike is shaking his head slowly.

"I can't keep thinking about..."

The door swings open.

"He's here."

THE MAN THEY ALL STAND UP FOR

The energy in the den shifts immediately. Every ninja stops what they are doing. Conversations die. Blades stop being cleaned. Phones go down. The room reorganises itself: bodies straightening, eyes forward, a collective intake of breath.

A man walks in.

Nobody says his name. Nobody needs to. He doesn't rush and he doesn't announce himself, and he moves through the room the way gravity moves through a room, which is to say that everything in it adjusts to him without being asked. The ninjas part. He sits in his chair, a worn leather armchair at the head of the room, the only piece of furniture in the place that looks like it was chosen rather than found.

He sits. Takes a deep breath. Leans back. Rests his chin on his hand. His eyes move slowly around the room: scanning every face, reading every posture, missing nothing.

His eyes find Spike.

He closes his eyes.

"What happened?"

His voice is calm. Quiet. The kind of quiet that is louder than shouting.

Everyone looks at Spike. Waiting.

Spike looks around the room. All eyes on him. He catches the roller-skate girl across the room. She is leaning on another ninja, looking at Spike, grinning. She makes an obscene gesture with her hand and her mouth. Spike's eyes drop back to the floor. She smirks and keeps watching.

"Tsh." He grunts it out. "I got jumped."

"Jumped by who?"

"I couldn't see his face."

"Well, ain't he lucky." The man in the chair doesn't open his eyes. "Why is that then?"

"He had a hood on."

"That doesn't seem much of a disguise. All this commotion and you couldn't give any sort of description?"

Silence. Spike is still crossing his arms. Eyes shut. Jaw clenched.

"...He had a mark."

"Great. That narrows it down."

"On his wrist. Some sort of..."

The man's eyes, which had been half-closed, start to open. Slowly. The hand supporting his chin lowers slightly.

"...Burn mark. Like it was done on purpose. Old. Healed."

The room is silent. The man doesn't move. But something has shifted behind his eyes. His other hand, the one resting on the arm of the chair, drifts to his own wrist. His fingers brush the inside of his wrist, where his sleeve covers his skin. It is not a conscious movement. He doesn't even notice he is doing it.

For one second, maybe two, something flickers across his face. Not recognition. Not memory. Something deeper and more broken than that. Like a word on the tip of your tongue that dissolves before you can speak it.

Then it is gone. His hand returns to the armrest. His expression resets.

"What did you just say?"

His voice is different now. Harder. The calm is still there but there is something underneath it. Something that wasn't there before.

Spike opens his eyes. Looks at his leader. Sees something in his expression he has never seen before.

The room holds its breath.

Cut.

CHECKING THE TIME

Jon finishes. Kevin looks at himself in the mirror. Tilts his head left, right. Fresh.

"Good?"

"Yeah. Safe, Uncle Jon."

He pays. Grabs his bag. Checks his phone. His face drops. He has been in here well over an hour, and he was told twice.

"I gotta go."

"Straight home."

"Yeah yeah."

He is already out the door. The bell rings behind him.

He half-jogs to the bus stop. Checks the display. The next bus is in eight minutes.

Eight minutes. He looks at the display. Looks across the street. There is a corner shop. One of those little ones with the faded ice cream poster in the window and the bell that doesn't quite ring properly.

He looks at the display again. Eight minutes.

"...I've got time," he tells himself, which is how most of it starts.

He ducks into the shop.

THE CORNER SHOP

Strip lighting. Narrow aisles. The shopkeeper behind the counter watching a tiny TV. Kevin walks past the crisps, past the drinks, straight to the sweets. He grabs a packet of Jewel Gems: small, round, colourful hard sweets in a cellophane bag. Pays. Change rattles on the counter. He stuffs the packet in his coat pocket and heads back to the bus stop just as the bus rounds the corner.

He gets on. Taps his Clam card. Upstairs. Window seat.

He tears open the Jewel Gems and pours a few into his hand. Pops one in his mouth. Watches the city go by. The open packet sits on his lap.

THE HANDOFF

The bus pulls up to a stop. Footsteps on the stairs. Someone coming up to the top deck in a hurry.

A man appears. Japanese, late forties, thin, wearing a crumpled jacket that looks like he has been wearing it for days. His hair is messy. His eyes are everywhere: darting left, right, down the stairs, out the window, back to the stairs.

The top deck is busy. Almost every seat is taken. The only one available is next to Kevin, who is sitting by the window with his open packet of sweets on his lap.

The man hesitates. Sits down.

Kevin glances at him. Pops another sweet. Goes back to the window.

The bus pulls off. The man's leg starts twitching. Right knee bouncing fast. His fist clenched on his thigh. He keeps looking toward the stairs: checking, checking, checking. His head turns: stairs, window, stairs, window, stairs.

Kevin notices. His eyes slide sideways. He takes in the twitching leg, the clenched fist, the sweat on the man's temple, the vein pulsing in his neck. Kevin's face doesn't change. One eyebrow drifts upward. The slightest expression, somewhere between what's your problem and whatever, man.

The bus slows. Next stop. The doors open below. People getting on. The man's whole body goes rigid. He gulps. Loud enough that Kevin hears the click in his throat. His Adam's apple bobs.

Two men get on the bus. They come upstairs. Big. Broad. Dark clothes. They don't look like commuters. One of them says something to the other. Short, clipped, purposeful. They walk to the back of the top deck and sit down.

The man next to Kevin has stopped breathing. His eyes are locked on the stairs. His hands are gripping his knees so hard his knuckles are white. He looks at Kevin. Looks at the stairs. Looks back at Kevin. There is something in his face: desperation. Maybe an apology.

Suddenly, commotion at the back of the bus.

"WAIT! WAIT! This is our stop! Hold on, bus driver!"

Three or four people jump up and rush down the aisle. Bags swinging, elbows bumping seats, voices raised. They squeeze past Kevin and the man, pushing and stumbling their way to the stairs.

In those three seconds of chaos, while everyone is moving and nobody is looking, the man's hand moves. Quick. Precise. Practised. He drops something small into Kevin's open packet of Jewel Gems.

Kevin doesn't see it. He is pulling his knees in, annoyed, letting the passengers squeeze past.

The commotion dies down. The two men at the back of the bus are still seated. One of them is scanning. The other stares straight ahead.

The man next to Kevin is rigid. Jaw locked. Staring forward. Trying to be invisible.

Kevin looks at him sideways again. Same face. One eyebrow. Unbothered.

Stops pass. The bus rocks and sways. The man's stop comes. He stands. Stiff. Mechanical. Doesn't look at Kevin. Doesn't look back. He walks to the stairs like his legs are made of concrete.

He goes downstairs. The bus stops. Doors open.

As soon as his feet hit the pavement, he runs.

Kevin watches from the top deck window. The man sprinting. Arms pumping. Not looking back.

The two men from the back stand up. Move calmly. Down the stairs. Off the bus. They walk fast, purposeful, in the same direction. Then, once clear of the bus, they break into a sprint.

Kevin watches all of this. Three men running down a street in Danim. His face doesn't change.

He shakes his head slightly.

Danim.

He pops another sweet. Looks out the window. His stop comes. He grabs his bag, stuffs the half-eaten packet into his coat pocket, and heads home.

THE ALLEY

East Danim. Late. The streets are dead. Orange streetlights cast long shadows down a narrow alley between two buildings. Water drips from a pipe somewhere. A rat moves along the base of a wall.

The Japanese man from the bus is on his knees. His jacket is torn worse than before. His lip is split. Blood runs from a cut above his eye. He has been here a while.

The two men who chased him stand over him. Up close, they are imposing: military posture, earpieces, the build of people who are paid to be dangerous. One of them crouches in front of the Japanese man.

"Where is it?"

The Japanese man coughs. Spits blood onto the wet concrete. Wipes his mouth with a shaking hand.

"I don't... I don't know what you're talking about."

"Don't insult me."

"I'm telling you the truth. I don't know what you want."

Man 1 looks at Man 2. Man 2 steps forward. He produces something from his coat. Something that clicks, something that glows at the tip. He presses it against the Japanese man's shoulder.

The man convulses. Grits his teeth. A strangled sound escapes through his clenched jaw. The device pulls away. He slumps forward, breathing hard, steam rising from the point of contact.

"You were the last carrier. We've tracked every hand it passed through. Every single one. You are the end of the chain." He leans in closer. "So I'll ask again. Where. Is. It."

"You've made a mistake." He is gasping it out now. "I'm... I'm just a tourist. Wrong place, wrong time."

"A tourist."

"Yes. Visiting family."

"Your family is in Osaka. We checked."

"My cousin lives here. In Danim. I came to see him."

"What's his name?"

"Hiroshi."

"Last name."

A beat. The Japanese man's eyes flicker.

"Tanaka."

Man 2 presses the device against him again. Longer this time. The man's whole body locks up. When the device pulls away, he sags forward, gasping, drool mixed with blood hanging from his lip.

"There is no Hiroshi Tanaka. We checked that too. You've been in this country for eleven days. You've made contact with seven individuals across four cities. We have all of them. Two of them are already dead. The other five gave us your name before they went." He waits until the man's eyes come back up. "So I am not going to ask you a third time."

The Japanese man laughs. Quiet at first. Wet. Broken. He spits more blood.

"You're a long way from finding it. You know that, don't you?"

"Where. Is. It."

"Gone."

"Where."

"Somewhere you'll never look."

Man 2 grabs him by the collar. Lifts him. Slams him back down onto the wet ground. The Japanese man's head hits the concrete. He coughs again. Spits. His breathing is ragged but his eyes are clearer now. Like he has made peace with something.

Then something changes in his face.

He is laughing.

Quiet at first. A chuckle. Broken and wet, bubbling through the blood in his mouth. Then louder. His head tilts back. The laugh builds. Not manic, not crazy. Something else. Something peaceful. The laugh of a man who has absolutely nothing left to lose because he has already won.

The two men look at each other. This isn't the reaction they expected.

The Japanese man's laughter slowly subsides. He catches his breath. Spits one more time. Then he looks up at Man 1. His eyes are red and exhausted but there is something in them now: clarity. Finality. The look of someone who has finished running.

He opens his mouth. Draws a breath. Starts to speak.

"You will never..."

THUNK.

A kunai embeds itself in his forehead. Clean. Silent. From above.

His eyes stay open. The beginning of his sentence hangs in the air, unfinished. His body sways, forward, backward, and then drops face-first onto the wet ground.

The two men release him and spin around. Hands reaching for weapons. Eyes scanning the alley, the rooftops, the fire escapes above.

There, for a fraction of a second, movement. A figure on a rooftop, silhouetted against the moon. A shadow that was there and then wasn't. A shape that doesn't belong to the city's geometry. And then, gone.

The two men stare at the empty rooftop. Then at each other. Then down at the body.

Man 1 touches his earpiece.

"He's dead. Someone got to him first."

He listens.

"No... we didn't see. A shadow. That's all."

He listens again.

"Understood."

They walk away. Their footsteps echo down the empty alley until the sound is swallowed by the city.

The Japanese man lies still on the wet ground. The kunai catches a glint of streetlight. The blood from his forehead runs along the cracks between the paving stones, following the paths of least resistance, the way water always does.

The man who gave everything to protect the Hakai Sphere, who sat on a bus next to a boy eating sweets, twitching with fear, completing his final mission with a trembling hand, dies in an alley in East Danim with a half-finished sentence in his mouth and a laugh still fading from his face.

Nobody will know his name.

DAYS LATER: THE SWALLOWING

Kevin's room. Morning. The usual chaos. His mum's voice from downstairs, the clock running late, the routine.

He is looking for something on his desk, rummaging through stuff. He picks up his coat from the other day, crumpled on the back of his chair. As he lifts it, the packet of Jewel Gems falls out of the pocket and scatters across the desk. A few sweets roll. The packet is still half full.

Kevin looks at them. Grins.

"Safe."

He picks up the packet. Reaches in. His fingers find one, slightly bigger than the others. Slightly darker. But he is not looking closely. He pulls it out and holds it between his thumb and finger.

He looks at it for a second. Turning it slightly in the light.

Something sounds. Faint. Almost imperceptible. A whisper, not a word, just a sound. Like air being pulled through a crack in the world. Like something exhaling from very far away.

Kevin tilts his head. Did he hear something? His eyes drift from the sweet to the room. He looks left. Right. The sound is gone. Was it even there?

He looks back at the sweet in his fingers.

His bedroom door bursts open.

"Kevin, are you even listening to m..."

She stops. Sees him holding the sweet. Kevin, startled, pops it into his mouth. Reflex. Panic.

It sits on his tongue. Hard. Heavier than a sweet should be. Not quite the right texture. But his mum is staring at him and his brain is doing mum-management, not sweet-analysis.

"Are those the sweets you came with the other day?"

Kevin, mouth full, shakes his head. Wide eyes. Comically guilty. The Sphere is sitting on his tongue, too hard to chew, too big to hide.

"Don't you LIE to me! Those have been sitting around for days. They could be off. They could be poisonous."

She holds out her hand. Open palm. The universal mother gesture for give it to me, now.

Kevin looks at her hand. Looks at the packet. Looks at her face. Her expression is clear. He has one second.

He takes a big gulp.

The Sphere goes down. His throat bulges. His eyes water slightly. A hard, scraping swallow that takes everything he has got. He feels it drop into his stomach like a stone into a pond.

He smiles. Nervous. Sweating. Hands the packet over.

She takes it. Inspects it. Shakes her head.

"Honestly, Kevin."

She walks out. Her footsteps go downstairs. The sound of the bin lid opening. Closing.

"NOW GET READY! HURRY UP!"

Kevin exhales. Wipes his forehead. Grins to himself like he got away with something.

He has no idea what he just swallowed.

THE HAKAI SCARE

Night. The house is quiet. TV off. Grandad asleep. The hallway light is dim. That orange glow that makes every house feel smaller after midnight.

Kevin is in bed, scrolling on his phone. Eyes heavy. He yawns. Puts the phone on the bedside table. Rolls over. Rolls back. Gets up.

He pads down the hallway in his socks. Floorboards creak under his weight. His mum's bedroom door is slightly open. Warm light from her bedside lamp spills into the hallway. He can hear her breathing. Soft, slow, asleep.

He pushes the door open.

"Mum, I'm going to..."

He stops.

In the corner of the room. By the wardrobe. Where the lamplight doesn't quite reach. A figure. Tall. Still. It shouldn't be there. Nothing should be there. That corner has a stack of folded laundry and a suitcase that has been there since before Kevin can remember.

But something is standing in front of them. Something that has shoulders. And arms. And hands.

And in those hands: his mother's head.

Her body is slumped on the bed. The neck ends in nothing. The head hangs from the figure's grip by the hair. Her eyes are open. Her mouth is frozen mid-sound. Blood, thick, dark, drips from the neck and patters softly on the carpet.

The figure turns toward Kevin.

It has his face. Kevin's face. But older. Sharper. The jaw more defined, the cheekbones harder. And the eyes: completely, utterly black. No white. No iris. No reflection. Nothing. Two holes in a human face where a soul should be.

It smiles.

Kevin screams.

The sound rips out of him: raw, high, childlike. He stumbles backwards. His heel catches the hallway carpet. He goes down. Hits the floor hard, tailbone first, pain shooting up his spine, but he doesn't feel it because his mother's head is in that thing's hands and it has his face.

The figure steps into the doorway. Slow. Patient. Still holding the head. Still smiling. It tilts its head like a dog hearing a frequency only it can hear.

Kevin screams again, louder, and scrambles backward on his hands and heels, dragging himself across the hallway floor. His back hits the wall. Nowhere to go. The figure keeps coming.

Kevin curls into a ball. Arms over his head. Knees pulled to his chest. Screaming into himself. His body shaking so violently the floorboards vibrate.

A hand touches his shoulder.

Kevin screams, one final, desperate, throat-shredding shriek, and looks up.

His mum. Alive. Whole. Standing over him in her dressing gown, face creased with worry, both hands on his shoulders.

"Kevin?! Kevin, what's the matter?! What happened?!"

Kevin can't speak. His chest is heaving. His eyes are darting: left, right, over her shoulder, past her, behind her, everywhere. His pupils are massive.

"Kevin, look at me. LOOK AT ME. What's wrong?"

Grandad appears at the top of the stairs. One hand on the banister, the other rubbing his eye.

"What a gwaan down here?"

Their voices start to fade. Kevin can hear them, his mum asking questions, grandad asking what is happening, but the words lose their shape. They become muffled. Like hearing people talk through a wall. Through water. Through something thicker than either.

All Kevin can hear is his own breathing. In. Out. In. Out. Ragged. Wet. And his heartbeat. Pounding. Filling his skull. Thudding behind his eyes.

His mum is holding his face in her hands. Saying his name. He can see her lips moving but the sound isn't reaching him.

He looks past her. Into the bedroom.

The lamp is on. The bed is normal. The pillows are there. The laundry is stacked in the corner. The suitcase. Everything exactly where it should be.

But in the far corner. Where the light doesn't reach. Where the wardrobe casts a shadow that pools against the wall.

Something is there.

A shape. Dark. Still. Almost invisible against the darkness. But not quite.

Kevin's eyes strain. His breathing is ragged. His hands are trembling.

The shape has eyes. Catching the faint moonlight through the curtains. And beneath the eyes: a grin. Slight. Knowing. Patient. The grin of something that has all the time in the world.

Kevin's eyes go wide.

Flick to black.

His breathing continues over the darkness. In. Out. In. Out. His heartbeat pounding.

THE WATCHER

North Danim. Kevin's street. Late night. The houses are dark. Streetlights hum their electric hymn. A fox trots across the road, stops, sniffs the air, and disappears under a fence.

On a rooftop across from Kevin's house, a figure stands. Cloaked. Still. Looking down at Kevin's bedroom window.

The light in Kevin's room is off now. The house is silent. The commotion from earlier has settled. His mum's bedroom light is off too. Even grandad's. The whole house is asleep.

The figure doesn't move. The wind catches the edge of his cloak, tugging it sideways, but his body stays rooted. A car passes in the distance, its headlights sweeping across the far end of the street and then gone.

He stays.

Watching.

The camera slowly pulls back.

The figure grows smaller against the rooftop. Kevin's house shrinks into the row of terraced homes. The street becomes a block. The block becomes a neighbourhood. North Danim stretches out beneath the night sky. Beyond it: the glow of Central Danim. The darkness of South. The forgotten sprawl of East. The artificial brightness of West. And somewhere on the outskirts, the distant lights of Belvedire.

Danim. Beautiful. Broken. And hiding more secrets than anyone knows.
