She walks out. Her footsteps go downstairs. The sound of the bin lid opening. Closing.

MUM (O.S.):
"NOW GET READY! HURRY UP!"

Kevin exhales. Wipes his forehead. Grins to himself like he got away with something.

He has no idea what he just swallowed.

THE HAKAI SCARE

Night. The house is quiet. TV off. Grandad asleep. The hallway light is dim. That orange glow that makes every house feel smaller after midnight.

Kevin is in bed, scrolling on his phone. Eyes heavy. He yawns. Puts the phone on the bedside table. Rolls over. Rolls back. Gets up.

He pads down the hallway in his socks. Floorboards creak under his weight. His mum's bedroom door is slightly open. Warm light from her bedside lamp spills into the hallway. He can hear her breathing. Soft, slow, asleep.

He pushes the door open.

KEVIN:
"Mum, I'm going to..."

He stops.

In the corner of the room. By the wardrobe. Where the lamplight doesn't quite reach. A figure. Tall. Still. It shouldn't be there. Nothing should be there. That corner has a stack of folded laundry and a suitcase that's been there since before Kevin can remember.

But something is standing in front of them. Something that has shoulders. And arms. And hands.

And in those hands: his mother's head.

Her body is slumped on the bed. The neck ends in nothing. The head hangs from the figure's grip by the hair. Her eyes are open. Her mouth is frozen mid-sound. Blood, thick, dark, drips from the neck and patters softly on the carpet.

The figure turns toward Kevin.

It has his face. Kevin's face. But older. Sharper. The jaw more defined, the cheekbones harder. And the eyes: completely, utterly black. No white. No iris. No reflection. Nothing. Two holes in a human face where a soul should be.

It smiles.

Kevin screams.

The sound rips out of him: raw, high, childlike. He stumbles backwards. His heel catches the hallway carpet. He goes down. Hits the floor hard, tailbone first, pain shooting up his spine, but he doesn't feel it because his mother's HEAD is in that thing's HANDS and it has HIS FACE...

The figure steps into the doorway. Slow. Patient. Still holding the head. Still smiling. It tilts its head like a dog hearing a frequency only it can hear.

Kevin screams again, louder, and scrambles backward on his hands and heels, dragging himself across the hallway floor. His back hits the wall. Nowhere to go. The figure keeps coming.

Kevin curls into a ball. Arms over his head. Knees pulled to his chest. Screaming into himself. His body shaking so violently the floorboards vibrate.

A hand touches his shoulder.

Kevin SCREAMS, one final, desperate, throat-shredding shriek, and looks up.

His mum. Alive. Whole. Standing over him in her dressing gown, face creased with worry, both hands on his shoulders.

MUM:
"Kevin?! Kevin, what's the matter?! What happened?!"

Kevin can't speak. His chest is heaving. His eyes are darting: left, right, over her shoulder, past her, behind her, everywhere. His pupils are massive.

MUM:
"Kevin, look at me. LOOK AT ME. What's wrong?"

Grandad appears at the top of the stairs. One hand on the banister, the other rubbing his eye.

GRANDAD:
"What a gwaan down here?"

Their voices start to fade. Kevin can hear them, his mum asking questions, grandad asking what's happening, but the words lose their shape. They become muffled. Like hearing people talk through a wall. Through water. Through something thicker than either.

All Kevin can hear is his own breathing. In. Out. In. Out. Ragged. Wet. And his heartbeat. Pounding. Filling his skull. Thudding behind his eyes.

His mum is holding his face in her hands. Saying his name. He can see her lips moving but the sound isn't reaching him.

He looks past her. Into the bedroom.

The lamp is on. The bed is normal. The pillows are there. The laundry is stacked in the corner. The suitcase. Everything exactly where it should be.

But in the far corner. Where the light doesn't reach. Where the wardrobe casts a shadow that pools against the wall.

Something is there.

A shape. Dark. Still. Almost invisible against the darkness. But not quite.

Kevin's eyes strain. His breathing is ragged. His hands are trembling.

The shape has eyes. Catching the faint moonlight through the curtains. And beneath the eyes: a grin. Slight. Knowing. Patient. The grin of something that has all the time in the world.

Kevin's eyes go wide.

Flick to black.

His breathing continues over the darkness. In. Out. In. Out. His heartbeat pounding.

THE WATCHER

North Danim. Kevin's street. Late night. The houses are dark. Streetlights hum their electric hymn. A fox trots across the road, stops, sniffs the air, and disappears under a fence.

On a rooftop across from Kevin's house, a figure stands. Cloaked. Still. Looking down at Kevin's bedroom window.

The light in Kevin's room is off now. The house is silent. The commotion from earlier has settled. His mum's bedroom light is off too. Even grandad's. The whole house is asleep.

The figure doesn't move. The wind catches the edge of his cloak, tugging it sideways, but his body stays rooted. A car passes in the distance, its headlights sweeping across the far end of the street and then gone.

He stays.

Watching.

The camera slowly pulls back. The figure grows smaller against the rooftop. Kevin's house shrinks into the row of terraced homes. The street becomes a block. The block becomes a neighbourhood. North Danim stretches out beneath the night sky. Beyond it: the glow of Central Danim. The darkness of South. The forgotten sprawl of East. The artificial brightness of West. And somewhere on the outskirts, the distant lights of Belvedire.

Danim. Beautiful. Broken. And hiding more secrets than anyone knows.

Cut to black.

Breathing fades.

Heartbeat fades.

Silence.

Outro music.

END OF EPISODE 1

Episode Two: Good Family

The Book Edition

Novelised from the final script. The script remains canonical on any conflict.

1. Two Sets of Books

Every empire keeps two sets of books.

The first records what happened. The second records what we have agreed to say happened. Tonight's programme concerns the second kind. Fourteen years before the events you have already witnessed. Do try to keep up.

South Danim, in the late-afternoon gold that forgives nothing and flatters everything. Council blocks stacked like bad teeth. Washing lines strung between balconies. A chicken shop sign with three of its letters dead. Kids on bikes circling a corner like slow birds.

Outside a corner shop stood three teenage boys, laughing. Two of them were exactly what they looked like: mates. Random South Danim boys, one loud and leaning on the shop window, one laid-back with folded arms and half a smile. Local boys. Nobody this story ever needs again.

The third was seventeen, and tall for it.

School shirt open over a vest, tie stuffed in a pocket, and a scar running his cheek that he had long since stopped explaining. He was mid-story, mid-laugh, hands drawing something enormous in the air, and the laugh was easy, and there was nothing in his face yet that anybody in Danim would have been afraid of.

Then he stopped laughing.

Across the road, walking alone against the flow of the pavement, was a girl. School uniform, but not a local school; the blazer was too good for this postcode. Skirt rolled at the waist in the way that gets you sent to the head of year. She walked like the street was a catwalk that owed her money.

The camera stays on him rather than on her. The smile going soft and stupid. The story dying in his hands.

"Oi oi," said the loud mate. "Devon's buffering."

"Say nothing."

"Bro, look at the blazer. That's Belvedire. Girls like that don't give out numbers, they give out restraining orders."

"Let him find out," said the laid-back one, softly.

Devon handed him his bag without looking, straightened nothing, fixed nothing, and crossed the road exactly as a bus hissed past behind him, using its cover like a stage curtain.

"Walk nicely, yeah!" the loud one called after him. "Left, right, left..."

Devon landed on the pavement a stride ahead of her, turned, and walked backwards in front of her. She did not slow down. He had to keep moving or get walked through.

"You're lost," he said.

"You're in my way."

"Can't be both true. If you're lost, there is no way. I'm just... here. Scenery."

She looked at him properly for the first time then. Fifteen, though he did not know it yet, and would not have cared if he had known better. The look was an audit: shoes, hands, mouth, eyes... scar.

Her eyes crossed the scar the way you cross a road you have crossed all your life. No flinch. No lingering. Nothing.

Something in Devon's walk changed. Only the street noticed: he had been braced for the flinch, the way he was always braced for it, and it never came.

"Scenery moves out of the way," she said. "Or it gets developed."

"Developed."

"Knocked down. Built over. Turned into flats."

"Rah. You talk like a landlord."

"You talk like scaffolding. Loud, temporary."

He barked a laugh, genuine and delighted, and finally fell into step beside her instead of in front. She allowed it the way royalty allows weather.

"Devon."

"Didn't ask."

"You were about to."

"I really wasn't."

"You were gonna ask something."

"I was gonna ask if the two behind us are your carers."

Fifty metres back, the two mates were following at a shameless stroll.

"Them?" Devon said, not looking back. "Never seen them before in my life."

"DEV!" came the distant bellow, hands cupped. "ASK IF SHE'S GOT FRIENDS!"

Devon closed his eyes. And her mouth betrayed her: one corner lifted, a real one, arrested almost in time.

"...Brothers," he said. "Adopted. Against my will."

"Mm. They seem like the smart ones."

They walked. A rhythm had started that neither of them was admitting to. She stopped at the corner where the high road met the bus lane. Her stop. He clocked it and pretended he had not.

"So what's Belvedire doing walking through my ends in school shoes?"

"Your ends?" Mock surprise. "You own all this?"

"Every brick you can see."

"The chicken shop as well?"

"That's the crown jewel. Keep up."

She turned to face him then, and gave him the whole of her attention for the first time, and it landed on him like weather.

"I get off two stops early. I walk through. It winds my dad up and I like the noise. Everything where I live is carpets. Carpets and doors that don't slam. You can hear yourself think and it's boring, it's SO boring."

"And here?"

"Here it's loud. Nobody's watching me. It's the only hour of my day that's mine."

Devon nodded slowly. And he did not do the thing. He did not sell the ends, did not perform the danger. He just told the truth, quietly.

"It's less fun when you can't leave it."

That landed. She studied him again: the scar, the eyes, the sudden stillness underneath all that mouth.

Her bus rounded the far corner. She saw it. He saw her see it.

"There's a thing Friday," he said, fast, casual, far too casual. "Nothing deep. Music. My lot. You'd hate it."

"I'd hate it?"

"Guaranteed. Loud, no carpets, doors slamming everywhere."

The bus pulled in. She stepped backwards onto it without breaking eye contact, and at last she gave it to him: the relaxed eyes, the soft voice, pitched down low where only he could hear.

"Sounds like the only hour of my day that's mine... I like your face, scenery. Friday."

The doors closed on his expression.

Hold there, on a seventeen-year-old boy through bus-door glass: a boy with a scar he had been fighting his whole life, being told, by the most impossible girl he had ever met, that the face was what she liked.

His mates arrived either side of him, and all three watched the bus go.

"You didn't get a number."

"Don't need one."

"He didn't get a number, you know."

"He got a day," said the laid-back one.

The bus shrank to nothing. Devon was still smiling at it.

2. Friday

A front door closed on a party's noise, muffling it to a heartbeat through walls.

Then the picture of that night flicks, like a channel changing, and the room is dark and the sound is everything.

What happened next is heard and suggested, never shown, and it is frantic:

"Some doors, once closed," Archer says, almost gently,

over a bare shoulder, out of focus, a hand pressed flat against peeling wallpaper.

"do not open again in the same way."

A shadow thrown huge and doubled across a wall, two silhouettes made one, moving.

"Youth mistakes intensity for permanence."

The corner of a single bed, its legs walking themselves a centimetre at a time across bare floorboards; a trainer falling off the end of it.

"It is a common, and usually expensive, error."

A light fitting swaying. In the next room a framed picture knocking against the wall in time, and from somewhere half a laugh, hers, then his, then neither.

And then the night itself seemed to rise: up through the ceiling, up through the roof, up over the rooftops of South Danim with the city glittering all the way out to the black band of the river, the party bass shrinking to a pulse, until, tiny beneath the whole sky, two voices reached one final note together and went quiet.

A fox trotted across an empty road.

3. The Queen B

Morning, and a different world entirely: a school, all glass and honey-brick, the kind of school with a rowing team. Corridor traffic. Blazers everywhere.

The girl in the Belvedire blazer stood at her locker, putting books away, somewhere else entirely. She closed it. SLAM.

Standing exactly where the door had been was a girl. Fifteen, box braids, prefect badge worn upside down, and already mid-sentence, as if the conversation had been running since birth.

"...so THEN he says he can't do Saturday because of football, football, Hella, a friendly, not even a real match, and I said okay cool enjoy your friendly, and he said what's that supposed to mean, and I said nothing, WHICH MEANS EVERYTHING, obviously, everyone knows that, and then he liked Priya's photo at eleven forty at NIGHT, the audacity, the sheer..."

She caught herself. Squinted.

Hella was smiling. Not at anything. At the middle distance. A private, fully glazed, out-of-office smile.

"Tskk." She kissed her teeth. "Are you even listening to me?!"

"Oh. Yeah, yeah, my bad, Mele. I'm just tryna get to class."

Hella gave her a glance, a glimpse, sliding past eye contact, and walked. Mele stayed put, staring after her.

And then Mele noticed the walk.

Her face assembled the data by degrees, the eyes widening like a dial being turned.

"Oh... my..."

She DASHED, overtook half the corridor, cut Hella off, and landed a hand on each shoulder.

"You cheeky shit. Look at me."

Hella slowly lifted her eyes. The smirk was still there. Her whole face was in la la land, happy in a way that had no defences left.

Mele's gasp pulled heads three lockers down.

"You've been BANGED," she whisper-screamed.

She looked left. Looked right. Grabbed Hella's wrist and towed her down the corridor, out through a fire door, gone.

The flat roof above the science block had a milk crate, a vent to lean on, and a view of the pitches, and it had clearly hosted these two before. A joint travelled between them.

"Seven times?? SEVEN???"

"Mm hmm."

Hella took her pull and held it like a professional. Exhaled slow.

"I can still feel my legs shaking and twitching, you know."

Her legs were stretched out on the roof felt, and there it was: the faintest tremor, a muscle spasming small under the skin. She watched them like they belonged to someone else. She was proud of them.

"You know he can go to jail, right?" Mele took the joint off her.

"Bitch, I'm sixteen in ten months. I'm straight."

"That's NEXT YEAR, you plum."

"Don't be acting like you ain't had sex."

"I'm sixteen."

"So... I know what you were doing at MY age..." Hella turned her head and delivered it deadpan, like a newsreader.

"...Heather Brooke."

A beat.

Mele was mid-pull. The cough detonated. Smoke everywhere, eyes streaming, half laughing, half dying, one hand flapping.

"I'm DEADDD," she wheezed. "How do you even know about the queen B..."

And the roof fell away below them, two girls shrinking on a school roof, Mele's voice fading under the wind and a bell ringing somewhere beneath.

"...nah, seriously, who showed you that, you're actually moving like..."

Black.

4. Five Weeks

Sound first: retching. Hard, hollow, echoing off tile.

A bathroom fit for a hotel. Marble, brass, a mirror wider than most beds. A girl crouched over the toilet with her back to the room, one hand white-knuckled on the seat. It went on longer than was comfortable. It was meant to.

It stopped. She stayed folded a moment, breathing. Then, in stages, she got herself up: knees, hand on the wall, standing. She ran the tap and faced the mirror.

Hella. Rough. Grey around the mouth, eyes glassed, a fleck of sick at the corner of her lip that she wiped away with the back of her wrist.

FIVE WEEKS LATER.

She got herself ready, and when she stepped out of the bathroom the episode quietly played its card, because the corridor was not a corridor. It was a gallery. High-end and modern, glass balustrade, art with its own lighting, a cleaner moving a hoover somewhere far away like a figure in a landscape painting. New money, sharpened daily.

This was where the girl in the rolled skirt lived. The uniform, the blazer, Belvedire: it assembled.

Her bedroom was enormous and beautiful, a teenage girl's room art-directed by an interior designer and then fought back into life by the teenager: clothes over a chair the housekeeper kept losing to, photo strips in the mirror frame, one wall of trainers. She dressed in quick, quiet stages, the practised face going on over the grey one, every mirror check a little longer than it needed to be. Once, briefly, a hand rested flat on her stomach, and was taken away like it burnt.

In a kitchen the size of Devon's whole flat, her little sister Tammy sat swinging her legs on a stool, six years old, cereal, cartoons, talking the way six-year-olds talk: constantly, about everything.

But the words arrived the way Hella heard them: distant, underwater, fuzzed at the edges, a radio between stations.

"...and Miss Okafor said if the caterpillars hatch on the weekend then NOBODY gets to see it and that's not fair because I fed them, Hella, I fed them the MOST..."

Hella stood at the counter, cereal untouched, staring at a spoon.

What the fuck is wrong with me?

"Hellooooo," said Tammy, surfacing through the fuzz, waving a small hand.

Black.

"You're pregs."

The roof again. Same crate, same vent. Mele lay back against the slope of the vent housing, sunglasses on, joint lit, one arm stretched sideways, offering it. Holding the pose. Waiting.

"WHAT?!"

Mele did not move. Just waited, hand out, the joint smoking gently between two fingers.

Hella looked at it. Looked at it properly. Then shook her head. Small. Twice.

A beat. Mele clocked the refusal, and the refusal confirmed everything. She shrugged and took it back.

"The fuck you mean 'what'," she said, smoke riding the words. "You are pre-g-nant. Didn't you use a condom?"

"Yes. We had six."

A beat.

"Ha!" Mele looked at the sky, smirking, smoke escaping through the grin, a small cough riding it. "Seven times."

Silence. A plane drew its chalk line across the blue. Hella pulled her knees up to her chest and hugged them.

"So... what should I do?"

"Abort it." There was no cruelty in it; the speed was the kindness, to her mind. "It's easy. No one has to know. Take like two secs."

A long moment. Hella curled smaller, arms locked around her legs, chin down onto her knees. The wind moved her hair. She was fifteen, and suddenly, completely, she looked it.

Mele watched her from the corner of her eye, still flat on her back, the clouds crossing her sunglasses.

"You're not thinking of keeping it... are you."

It was not a question. Hella did not move. Did not flinch. Stared at nothing.

Mele sat up. Slowly. Sunglasses off. This was Mele serious, and Mele serious was a rare exhibit.

"Bitch. Don't tell me you're keeping that thing."

Hella stayed curled, thinking, and the silence stretched until it became the answer.

"You... are... FUCKED."

Mele lay back down. Sunglasses on. She took the longest pull of her life and spoke it to the sky, filthy and loyal and afraid, all three at once.

"This is why I swallow mines."

The words hung there as the roof faded, two small figures under a big sky, the bell ringing somewhere below.

5. Five Months

BANG. A pot hit the wall, clattered onto the stove top, spun, and settled.

The kitchen's geometry was all wrong now, because the sound coming through from the next room was enormous.

"You are fucking FIFTEEN! FIFTEEN years old! This is the person you want to be! HUH?! A fucking MOTHER at FIFTEEN fucking years old!"

Hella sat on a chair against the wall, feet up on the rung, shrunk to nothing. There was the smallest curve to her now, five months of it, under a school jumper she was still wearing like the costume of a former life.

The maid came to her quickly and got down to her level. Audrey. Forties, kind eyes, a face that had worked in this house long enough to know all its weathers. She took Hella's hands in hers.

"Everything is going to be alright."

But Hella could see it on her face: Audrey was exactly as frightened as she was. The comfort was a costume too. They held hands anyway. It was what there was.

BOOM. The door. Her father entered the kitchen.

Fourteen years younger than the man this city would come to know: mid-forties, shirtsleeves, a watch worth more than the street Devon lived on. The rage had gone quiet somewhere between the rooms, which was worse.

Audrey stood. And she put herself, without one gram of drama, between him and the chair. Shaking. Doing it anyway.

"You," he said, low. "Get the fuck out."

Audrey looked at him. Looked back at Hella, one long look, a promise she had no power to keep. Then back at the man, whose face had not moved.

She left in silence, and the door clicked behind her like a verdict.

He slid the bolt across. He walked, unhurried now, to the sink, took a glass from the drying rack, crossed to the water dispenser, and pressed. The room was so quiet you could hear the water climbing the glass, the note rising as it neared the top.

"FUCK!"

He flung it. The glass detonated against the counter edge, water and fragments everywhere. Hella jolted, hands flying up over her head.

Then, calm again, that obscene instant calm, he pulled out a stool at the kitchen island and sat. Laced his fingers. Rested them against his lips, elbows on the marble.

And stared at her.

The tap dripped. He stared. She shook.

His gaze descended, deliberately, from her face to her stomach.

FIVE MONTHS.

The gaze came back up to her eyes, and somewhere under the floor of the scene a pressure had been building, strings winding tighter and tighter, up and up, until something had to break.

SNAP. Black. Silence.

6. The Ward

In the black, a baby crying. Close. New. That first furious, astonished sound.

Light bled in, blurry, overexposed, swimming. Shapes in scrubs. A ceiling light like a halo. Everything echoing down a long tube.

"It's a beautiful baby boy..."

The halo smeared. Black again.

Then a private room, machines idling, evening light, and Hella asleep and small in the pillows. She stirred. Opened her eyes. Ceiling. Drip stand. Where...

She snapped upright.

"My baby! Where's my baby!"

"He's fine, Hella." The nurse was fifties, sleeves at her elbows, with the calm of ten thousand nights like this one. She nodded to the left of the bed. "He's having a nap. Working hard at it, too."

Hella looked. Beside the bed stood a clear-sided hospital cot, and inside it, swaddled to the chin, impossibly small, was a baby. The baby. A shock crossed her eyes, a physical thing, and then her whole face softened, muscle by muscle, into an expression she had never worn in her life.

She lay back slowly, eyes never leaving the cot.

"You had us worried," the nurse said. "You've been blacking out. Anyone home when you faint like that?"

"...He's so small."

"Six pounds nine. That's a decent size, that."

"No, I mean... he's SMALL. Like. What's he supposed to do like that?"

The nurse laughed softly, tidying the blanket edge.

"Nothing. That's the arrangement. He does nothing, you do everything, and somehow he's still in charge."

Hella almost smiled. Then it collapsed.

"I don't know how to do... any of it. I don't know anything."

"Nobody does. First-time mums arrive knowing precisely nothing, same as first-time babies. You learn each other."

She checked the drip line, talking easily, not lecturing, just laying it down like fresh sheets.

"Here's the whole trick, so you can stop being scared of the wrong things. He doesn't need you clever. He doesn't need you rich. He needs you THERE. Fed, warm, held, that's the entire curriculum for the first bit. And when he cries at three in the morning and you're crying with him, that's not failing. That's the two of you having the same conversation."

Hella listened like it was scripture. Her eyes shone.

"And I'll tell you something for free. That boy's known one thing in this world for nine months. Your heartbeat. Put him on your chest and watch. He could pick it out of a hundred."

Both of Hella's hands had come up over her mouth. The nurse watched her and saw exactly what she had seen a thousand times and never once missed: a girl who cared completely, and was completely terrified, and was fifteen.

A soft beat.

"Will dad be coming in? For the birth certificate?"

Hella's mouth opened.

"No."

Hard. Flat. From the doorway, as if he had always been standing there. He had. A man in a very good coat, unhurried.

The nurse straightened, professionally pleasant. "Oh, hello. And your name is..."

"Her father."

Two words, and a door closing inside them.

"...Wonderful. I'll leave you two to catch up."

She gathered her chart, and as she passed him, his hand closed around her arm. Not violent. Worse: precise.

"When can she be discharged to come back home," he said, slow and quiet, each word placed like cutlery.

The nurse looked down at the hand. Took one second to register exactly how hard he was holding her, and recalibrated the man entirely.

"...Minimum one day. She's been having blackouts."

A long moment, he was on the edge of saying something else. He let it go, and let her go with it, with a low sound half swallowed under his breath.

She walked out, and in the corridor she turned for one last glance through the closing door: the man standing at the foot of the bed, back to the world, towering over the girl and the cot, saying nothing.

Her face filed the suspicion somewhere it would keep for a lifetime.

The door clicked. Black.

7. Stonebridge House

A gate of black iron swung open, automated and silent, the letters cut into the stone pillar beside it needing no cleaning and getting it anyway: MITCHELL ESTATE. A Rolls-Royce the colour of still water glided up a drive long enough to have its own weather. Belvedire. Lawns to the horizon. The house arrived in stages, wing by wing.

And so Hella Mitchell returns to the family estate. Frightened. Fifteen. But a mother, none the less. Her mind, for the moment... blank. Empty. The body drives; the girl is a passenger.

Inside the car she sat at the window, hospital band still on her wrist, and beside her, strapped and sleeping in his car seat, was the baby. Her eyes stayed fixed on the middle distance. Not on him. Not allowed on him.

Her school, you ask? Her school has been furnished with the finest fiction money can buy: glandular fever, poor lamb, complicated by exhaustion, convalescing abroad at a Swiss clinic her father recommends to everyone and has visited never. Letterhead. A doctor's signature. Term fees paid a year forward, which in the private system is the truest form of poetry.

The car crunched to a stop before the front steps.

The girls of her year, doing their own arithmetic, have voted: modelling in Milan, says the majority. A breakdown, says an ambitious minority. One girl, and only one, knows the truth and has said nothing at all, which, as any butler will tell you, is the rarest service of them all.

The chauffeur opened Hella's door. A second pair of hands opened the far one, and a butler lifted out the car seat with perfect, impersonal care and came to stand beside her. Hella, on the gravel, glanced down once. The baby slept on, fists up by his ears like a tiny boxer.

High above them, at a first-floor window, her father looked down at the arrangement on his drive: the girl, the butler, the seat, set out on the gravel like pieces on a board.

They climbed the steps into the house.

There is a saying in houses like this one, older than the stone: the truth, like water, always finds its level. But a sufficiently determined will is a kind of dam. And in all its polished history, the Mitchell estate has never once suffered a flood.

The light at the window did him no favours, or exactly the favours he deserved: half the face in shadow, unamused, patient.

Black.

The nursery had been a guest room a month ago. In its corner now sat a soft-play square: fluffy toys, a rattle, dangling shapes on an arch, and in the middle of it all, months old and sitting up on his own wobbling authority, the baby. He reached for the dangling things and caught nothing and was delighted anyway. He smiled at his own hands.

Across the room, voices arrived the way sound comes back after a faint.

"...el... ella..."

"Hella?"

"Huh."

Hella snapped out of it. She and Audrey sat side by side on the end of the bed, and Hella had been watching the baby the way you watch weather on the horizon.

Audrey noticed the distance. Squeezed her hand.

"Don't worry. He will be fine."

She lifted what she was holding: a brochure. Thick stock. Beautiful. A crest. Green lawns, bright rooms, laughing children, a font that costs money. Across the top: STONEBRIDGE HOUSE: A FAMILY FOR EVERY CHILD.

"I have read this from front to back, and the fine print, three times," Audrey said, smiling, turning it in her hands, proud of it, relieved by it, sold by it. "It has the best of the best facilities. To make sure he grows up strong, and well taken care of. Look, they have a music room. A MUSIC room, Hella."

Hella looked at her. At the hope on her face, real hope, borrowed hope. Then down at her own lap.

Then across, at him.

The baby had captured the rattle at last and was inspecting it like a jeweller: turning it, frowning at it, tasting it. Wondering. Exploring. Curious about a world that had already decided what to do with him.

Hella stared. Her expression did not change at all.

Her eyes filled. Built. And ran: one line down one cheek, then, from the other eye, a second.

She did not blink. She did not make a sound. She just watched him, the tears falling without her, as if even her crying had been taken into private management.

Audrey, looking at the brochure, did not see.

Black.

8. The Driveway

From below, from inside the car seat, the sky was a mother's face.

Hella stood over him, looking down, and her face was lifeless. Emotionless. Not sad. Not cold. Neutral, which is the most frightening thing a face can be. She just stared down.

Then, without her face changing at all, her hand came down holding a small folded paper, cream, official, folded twice over, and tucked it deep into the padding of the seat, down where fingers would have to know to look. The hand rested half a second on the blanket. Withdrew.

Her face had still not moved.

Her father arrived beside her, coat immaculate. He did not look down at the seat.

"Call me the moment you arrive," he told the chauffeur. "The moment."

"Yes, sir."

The world moved. The seat was lifted; the sky swung.

On the drive, the Rolls had been replaced by a discreet black saloon, the kind of car that is not from a company and not from a family. The chauffeur clipped the car seat into the back and closed the door with a thump much too loud for what it was.

The car pulled away. Gravel, then tarmac, then smaller, and smaller, down the endless drive.

Hella had not moved. She stood on the steps with her arms at her sides, watching it shrink.

He stood beside her a moment longer. Then he turned, without a word, and walked toward the doors of the mansion.

She stayed. Still as the statues on the gate, staring at a car that was now a dot, and then was nothing, and staring anyway, with the great house behind her and her father's footsteps fading into it.

That is how the scene ends.

A phone rang once.

"Yes."

"Just dropped him off, sir. All signed."

Her father stood alone in his study, at the window he liked.

"Good."

He hung up. Filed the phone into his pocket. Adjusted nothing, because nothing was out of place, and turned back to his desk.

The hallway had given up long ago. Foster home fluorescents, a noticeboard with one flyer from two years back, a smell you could see. The foster carer stood over the car seat skimming a thin document folder: cardigan, lanyard, a face rationed to the essentials.

The typed folder told her nothing she cared about. The baby watched her from the seat.

Then she clocked it: a cream corner poking up from deep in the seat padding. Hand-folded. Not part of the file. She worked it free and opened it: a certificate. Handwriting. A girl's handwriting.

For half a second only, the paper: the first name, DONTE, and her thumb lying flat across the line where a surname would be.

"...Donte," she said, flat, to herself.

She glanced at the baby. Back at the paper.

"Okay."

She folded it back along its creases, filed it inside the folder, and the folder went down the side of the car seat, and the whole thing got picked up like luggage. The corridor swallowed them.

For the record, since no one else will keep one: the brochure was real. The house on its cover was not. Stonebridge House was typeset, photographed and printed by three of Mr Mitchell's most talented employees in an afternoon, and exists nowhere on this earth except in Audrey's good heart... and a mother's last hope. The truth will find its level. But it is in no hurry. It can wait years.

It usually does.

9. The Home

EAST DANIM.

A grey building the city forgot on purpose. Windows with wire in the glass. A yard of cracked concrete with one basketball hoop, no net, no ball. And years, now, passing through it like weather through a ruin.

Consider, if you will, a simple question. Not a pleasant one. But we are past the pleasant part of the evening. How long does it take... to break a man?

Donte at four: sitting on the end of the smallest bed in a dormitory of mismatched beds, while older kids swarmed a delivery of donated toys. By the time he reached the box it was empty. He looked inside anyway. Took out the packing paper. Folded it carefully. Kept it.

The romantics will tell you a man cannot be broken, only bent. The romantics, you will notice, tend to write from comfortable rooms.

Donte at six: at the long dinner table, where his plate arrived last and smallest, and a bigger kid named Terrence reached across and took his bread roll without even looking at him. The carer saw it. Said nothing. Donte ate what was left in silence, eyes down.

A more practical school holds that every man is a bridge: load him gradually, and he learns to carry. Load him suddenly... and you learn what he was made of.

Donte at seven: holding out his exercise book to show another kid a drawing. The kid looked at it, looked at him, and turned away to laugh with someone else. Donte withdrew the book slowly, looked at the drawing himself, and closed it.

But bridges, you see, have engineers. Someone measures the load. Someone cares when the cables sing. The boy we are watching has no engineer. The load is measured by children, and children, left unsupervised with power...

Donte at eight: walking the perimeter of the yard alone, one hand trailing the fence, when a window broke somewhere inside, and every head in the yard turned to him. A carer stormed out already shouting his name. The boy who had actually thrown it stood smirking ten feet away. Donte did not argue. He went where he was pointed. The black sheep. The address where blame lives.

...children measure it in laughter.

Donte at eleven: lying awake in the night dormitory, staring at the ceiling, while a bucket of water balanced on the door he would open at six a.m., and beds shook with stifled giggles. He knew. He always knew. He would open the door anyway, because the alternative was worse.

And the boy carries it. Season upon season. Load upon load. Which brings us, regrettably, to the day the measuring ended... and the testing began.

10. The Freezer

Late winter, the light already dying. Behind the kitchen block lay the dumping ground for dead appliances: a washing machine on its face, and a chest freezer, coffin-shaped, lid intact.

Donte, eleven, had been sent out alone to bring in the bins. The ambush had geometry: Terrence, fifteen now and built like a door, and four others, peeling off walls, cutting angles, closing.

And above the yard, in the kitchen window, stood the foster carer with a mug in her hand, watching the geometry assemble. She looked at Donte. At the five.

She took a sip. And drew the blind.

"Oi. Sheep."

Donte did not run. There was nowhere it would work. He put the bin down and stood, hands at his sides, and even now, even at eleven, there was that stillness.

"Why's he standing like that? Look at this guy."

"We made you a bed, bro," Terrence said, patting the freezer lid. "Try it. It's memory foam."

Laughter. Donte looked at the freezer. Back at Terrence. And for the first time in all those years of montage, he spent a word.

"No."

They swarmed him. It took all five, and it was not clean; he made them earn every centimetre, an elbow found someone's mouth, a raked shin, but he was eleven and they were many. They wrestled him up, and in.

The lid slammed.

Black. Total. His breathing, huge in the box. Fists on the inside of the lid. BOOM. BOOM. Muffled laughter warping through the metal like sound through water.

"Nah he's fine, man, it's got holes... it's got holes innit?"

"...Has it got holes?"

Something heavy scraped onto the lid. Then something heavier. They were stacking weight. Sitting on it. The banging got faster.

Inside there was nothing to see and everything to hear: breathing going ragged, the banging weakening, and underneath it, rising, a sound that had never been heard in that yard before. A hum. A pressure. Like a kettle starting three streets away.

Here, then, is the answer to our question. You do not break a man by hurting him. Pain, the boy knows. Pain is Tuesday.

Outside, the laughter died off as the banging stopped. A smile faded. The kids traded a look.

"...Terrence."

You break a man by teaching him, beyond all argument, in the dark, with the weight of the world sat comfortably upon the lid... that no one is coming.

Silence from the freezer.

Then the hum arrived through their feet. The freezer's dead compressor screamed into life for one impossible second, the metal began to tick like a pan heating, and a thin orange line drew itself around the rectangle of the lid like a fuse.

"Get off. GET OFF..."

They scattered. The paint on the lid blistered, blackened, peeled back in curls.

And the freezer erupted.

It went in two beats. First: a burst of ordinary orange fire, a column of it, the lid blowing off its hinges and cartwheeling across the yard on a fountain of sparks. Then, inside the orange, the fire concentrated: it darkened at its core into black flame, black as the inside of the box had been, and the black fire was hotter, the air warping around it, the concrete glowing beneath, the freezer's walls sagging like candle wax. Then it breathed back out to ordinary orange, as if the black had never been there.

A fragment of the bursting freezer spun across the yard and caught one of the kids across the face. Terrence. He went down clutching his cheek, blood running instantly between his fingers, screaming.

The pressure wave had thrown the rest of them skidding across the concrete, jackets scorched, eyebrows gone, scrambling backwards.

And in the wreck of the freezer, burst open, broken apart, its walls part-melted and steaming, was Donte.

Not standing. Not powerful. He was on the floor of it, curled small, and he was naked: the fire had taken his clothes off him in rags of ash and taken nothing else, not one mark on his skin, which was somehow worse to look at. The flames poured off him in thinning ropes and went back in, sucked into him like breath, and what they left behind was an eleven-year-old, shivering violently, letting out high, thin, squeaking screams, one after another, a child's screams, the sound of a boy whose body has just done something his mind cannot hold.

He cried. Curled in the melted box, naked in the cold they had locked him into, he just cried.

Windows lit up. Adults came shouting and running, and what they found was this: one boy bleeding badly from the face, four more scorched and wailing, and a naked, unmarked child crying in the wreckage of an exploded freezer.

Every finger in the yard pointed the same way.

"HE DID IT!" Terrence screamed it through the blood in his fingers. "HE'S A FREAK! HE DID IT!"

A blanket was thrown over Donte. Rough. The way you cover a thing, not warm a child.

Nobody asked him anything.

A door with three bolts opened on a crack of light, and the foster carer stood in it, a shape with the corridor behind her. She did not come down the steps. She shoved a plate of food across the concrete floor with the side of her foot, the way you feed something you have been told not to touch.

"You stay down here till we know what you are."

Not who. What.

The door shut. The bolts went across, one, two, three, and each one landed like a full stop.

Black again. His second box in a week.

There was no screaming this time and no banging on the door. He had learned by then that neither of them worked.

Above him the house carried on without him. Footsteps crossing a floor. A television. Somebody laughing at something. Water moving through a pipe near his head on its way somewhere else. Twice a day the bolts scraped and a plate came in and the bolts went back, and nobody spoke to him, and nobody asked him anything, which by then he expected, because nobody had asked him anything in the yard either.

He ate some of it. He slept on the concrete with his back against the wall so that the door was always in front of him.

And on the second night, in the black, something small and steady lit.

A flame, on the end of his finger, burning like a birthday candle and throwing just enough orange to find his face behind it. He turned his hand over and watched it hold. It did not roar out of him. It did not take his clothes. It sat there because he was calm, and it was the first time in his life he understood that the two things were connected.

He lifted the finger and carried the flame around the room. Concrete. A dead boiler. A shelf of paint tins nobody had opened in years. His own breath going up in the cold.

Then the door.

He held the light close to it and did arithmetic. The hinge side, three heavy pins, no. The boards, thick, no. The lock plate, a rectangle of brass sunk into old dry wood.

He put the flame out and sat back down with his back to the wall, because he was eleven, and he wanted to be sure, and there was no hurry any more now that he knew.

Later, in the dead of night, the lock plate began to glow. Faint at first, then orange, then bright enough to light the whole stairwell, until the wood around it charred and bubbled and let go with a sound like a knuckle cracking, and the door swung open on a boy-shaped hole in the house's authority.

He moved down a corridor of sleeping doors with everything he owned in one carrier bag, which did not need carrying carefully. He passed the room where the others slept. He did not stop, and he did not look in.

At the front door he stopped. Turned. Looked back down the hallway at the whole building, once.

Nothing in the look asked to stay.

He could have opened it. The latch was right there and it opened from the inside, and he knew it, and he stood looking at it for a moment.

Then he burned through the front lock as well. Not because he had to.

Because it was his door now.

And then he was gone, out into the night, eleven years old, made of fire, carrying a plastic bag.

11. LIT

The rain that night could not commit. Donte walked until walking stopped being a plan: shop shutters, empty pavements, a night bus sailing past like an aquarium of warm light, full of faces that did not look down.

Under a railway arch he found a faint glow: pallet fires in barrels, tarps, trolleys, tents. A squatter camp, fifteen or twenty souls arranged with the practised looseness of people who know they cannot stay anywhere long. This spot was for tonight; the police would sweep it by Friday. Everyone under the arch knew the timetable except him.

He folded himself into the darkest corner, against the brick, knees to chest, the carrier bag under his arm like a teddy, shaking with cold. He lit the finger and held it against his chest, and it showed him his own hands and did not warm them, and after a while he put it out. And here was the cruelty the night had saved up: the boy of fire was freezing, because what he could reach was a candle. The rest of it came when the world was ending. Tonight the world was merely awful.

Across the camp, by a barrel, an older man watched him. Fifties or a hundred, hard to say. Beard, army surplus coat, fingerless gloves, and a rucksack with a folded stack of clothing on top, still with tags. Shoplifted stock: his float, his livelihood, tomorrow's food.

He watched the kid shake for a long minute. Muttered something to himself. Argued with himself. Lost.

He crossed the camp and crouched at arm's length, unhurried, the way you approach a stray.

"Ay. Look at me. You runnin' from something, or to something?"

Donte just looked at him. Silence, as ever. The beggar read it fluently.

"Yeah. Same answer at your age."

He pulled the top item off his stack: a hoodie, black, brand new, tag swinging. He turned it over once in his hands, a man counting the cost of a thing. Then he bit the tag off and held it out.

Donte did not move.

"It's not a trick, son. Tricks cost more than this."

Donte took it. It swallowed him: sleeves past his hands, hem at his knees. Warmth arrived like a rumour. And across the chest, in white letters that found the streetlight, one word:

LIT.

"There he is," the beggar said, settling back on his heels. He nodded at the word, deadpan. "Suits you. Don't let nobody tell you different."

The smallest thing happened in Donte's face. Not a smile; his face did not know that road yet. But inside the too-long sleeves, the fists unclenched.

The beggar went back to his barrel. Donte, wrapped in someone's stolen kindness, watched the fire until his eyes lost.

Note the transaction closely, because the ledger of this boy's life is short, and this is its largest entry. One garment. Stolen for profit. Given for nothing... Men have built entire religions on smaller arithmetic.

Morning came grey under the arch, and Donte's eyes opened on nothing.

The camp was gone. All of it: tents, trolleys, barrels still faintly warm, the beggar. Twenty souls evaporated on the timetable everyone had known except him. He stood alone in an empty arch the size of a church, in a hoodie built for a grown man.

He looked left. Right. Nothing. No one.

He pulled the hood up. It fitted over his whole world.

He walked.

12. Alone

Days first. Then weeks. Then months. The city kept the count for him: 3 DAYS. 2 WEEKS. A MONTH. 4 MONTHS.

He learned Danim the hard way, always in the hoodie, and the hoodie slowly fitting him better as he grew into it. He ate from a bakery's bin. He sheltered under a bridge and warmed his hands at his own small flame, cupped and hidden, both shoulders checked first, because the code was already instinct in him: no one can see. He ran from a security guard with bread inside his jacket and slid under a fence in one single move that four kids in North Danim would one day be shown for free.

One later night he came back to the mouth of the arch, hopeful, and found a different camp there. Harder faces. A man rose to his feet at the sight of him with nothing kind in it, and Donte melted backwards into the dark. The one door he knew, closed.

One night there was a phone box. He stood soaked in front of it, looking at the dial pad. He picked up the receiver and held it a long time.

There was no number. There had never been a number.

He put it back with both hands, gently, like closing a small coffin.

And so the arithmetic runs on. Everyone the boy is given, the ledger takes back. A mother: entered, and struck out, before he could read. A rescuer with a stolen coat: one night only. The city is teaching him its only lesson, patiently, at scale... that a hand held out is merely a hand not yet withdrawn.

In East Danim's industrial belt he squeezed through a gap in corrugated fencing and stood in the doorway of an abandoned warehouse: cathedral-sized, pigeon-haunted, its holed roof throwing down pillars of grey light. He walked its floor. Tested the silence. Nobody. Nothing.

His.

He built his corner in quick, careful stages: pallets into a windbreak, a found tarp, a milk-crate table, the carrier bag's tiny population arranged on it with care. The last thing out of the bag was a square of packing paper, folded, seven years old. Kept.

That night he lay on his back in his corner, hood up, watching the stars through the roof-hole, industrial orange at the edges of the sky.

And across the warehouse, in the deep dark between two pillars of moonlight, something stood.

Small. Boy-sized. Perfectly, inhumanly still. A silhouette with its head tilted at a precise angle, watching him.

Donte's eyes found it. He did not startle. He did not rise. The two shapes regarded each other across the dark for a long, silent moment.

Donte turned over and went to sleep.

The silhouette watched. It did not move. Somewhere far off, a train.

That is all this story says about that.

13. Present Day

PRESENT DAY. NORTH DANIM.

Morning light, and you know this street before you can say why. This block. These parked cars.

Episode One. The other side of the window.

Donte, thirteen now, the hoodie fitting him properly at last, LIT across his chest, walked this foreign, comfortable district with a loaf of bargain bread under one arm, his eyes doing their permanent work: exits, angles, faces.

Four kids peeled off a wall ahead of him. You have seen them before, once, in muffle, through glass. This time the words come with them.

"Oi. You're not from round here."

"What's LIT then? You LIT, yeah?"

They circled. One of them flicked the loaf out from under his arm, and it landed in the gutter. Donte watched it land. Bread was breakfast and dinner.

"You deaf?" A shove at his shoulder.

Above and behind them a curtain shifted in a first-floor window. A shape at the glass. Donte's eyes flicked up for one quarter of a second, logged it, dismissed it. A kid, indoors. Irrelevant.

Only you, reading this, know that Donte just looked at Kevin.

The big one shoved him hard, and Donte gave one step backwards, and the step was a lie. It loaded him. And the four boys did not know what you now know: that they were the freezer lid. That everyone was, forever. That this was the tragedy the whole story had been for.

He moved.

The same seconds that Episode One watched from a bedroom window now ran close and at full volume: the wrist caught, the pivot, the throw that put the first boy into the pavement. The palm strike that lifted the second off the earth. The haymaker ducked with slow contempt, the sweep that folded the third. The elbow into the ribs of the smart one.

Four down. The fifth stood frozen, fists half raised.

Donte stared at him. Dead still. Hands at his sides. Inside one sleeve, unseen by anyone on that street, a single line of flame ran from wrist to knuckle and went out, like a held breath released.

The fifth kid walked. Fast.

Donte stood among the groaning like a boy alone in a field, checking each of them with his eyes: staying down. He picked his bread out of the gutter, brushed it off against the hoodie, and tucked it back under his arm.

Somewhere behind him a front door banged, and a boy's voice, distant:

"...Where did that boy go?"

But Donte was already three gardens gone, over a wall, along a ginnel, out the far end. Unhurried. Invisible. A magic trick the city had taught him.

14. The Bus Stop

At the far end of the block, Donte walked a quiet pavement in low golden morning sun, the same honey light as a flashback nobody on that street had ever seen.

And then, distant, ahead of him, a woman's voice at war with a phone.

"Ahh, you men are all the SAME! Only stick around to get what you want!"

His stride did not change. She was storming along the opposite pavement toward the bus stop: leather jacket, leggings with STYLES down the thigh, hoops like handcuffs, phone clamped to her ear, gesturing at the entire sky.

Hella Mitchell. Twenty-eight. Fourteen years, one story, and nine months from the girl on the roof.

They were going to pass each other. Everything you have read was building this pavement.

Everything slowed, just slightly. The score fell away to a single held note, and under it, so low it might have been imagination, a baby's cry, once, far away, like something remembered by the street itself.

They passed. Two metres apart, opposite pavements. Her voice at full volume. His silence at full volume.

"As SOON as you get what you came for, you're a ghost! Every single one of you! GHOSTS!"

His head did not turn. Her head did not turn. From behind, the two of them diverged: the woman storming toward the bus stop, and the boy in the LIT hoodie walking the other way, getting smaller.

And there it is. Two heartbeats on one pavement. One of them once learned the other by heart, in the dark, over nine months... and neither so much as slows.

Wide now, and high, and rising: the whole street in morning gold, Hella reaching the bus stop at the top of the frame, Donte a small dark figure leaving the bottom of it.

The truth always finds its level. This evening changed nothing about that. It only showed what sort of truth this one is.

Donte turned the corner. Gone.

It is in no hurry. It can wait years.

On the empty corner where he vanished:

It usually does.

End of Episode Two.
