FOURTEEN YEARS EARLIER

Black screen.

The refined voice arrives already amused, before it has said a word.

"Every empire keeps two sets of books."

Slow aerial.

South Danim in late-afternoon gold. Council blocks stacked like bad teeth. Washing lines between balconies. A chicken shop sign with three letters dead. Kids on bikes circling a corner like slow birds.

"The first records what happened," Archer says. "The second records what we have agreed to say happened."

The camera drifts down toward a corner shop.

Three teenage boys outside it. Laughter. One of them is mid-story, hands drawing something enormous in the air.

"Tonight's programme concerns the second kind. Fourteen years before the events you have already witnessed." A pause, purely for his own enjoyment. "Do try to keep up."

Caption: FOURTEEN YEARS EARLIER. SOUTH DANIM.

THE GIRL IN THE UNIFORM

The three boys resolve into focus. Two of them are mates and nothing more: two random South Danim boys, one loud and leaning on the shop window, one laid-back with his arms folded and half a smile. Local boys. Nobody the story ever needs again.

The third is seventeen. Tall for it. School shirt open over a vest, tie stuffed in a pocket, a scar running his cheek that he has long since stopped explaining. He is mid-laugh, and the laugh is easy, and there is nothing in his face yet that anybody would be afraid of.

And then he stops laughing.

Across the road, walking alone against the flow of the pavement: a girl. School uniform, but not a local school. Blazer too good for this postcode. Skirt rolled at the waist the way that gets you sent to the head of year. She walks like the street is a catwalk that owes her money.

Hold on the boy watching. The camera does not crawl over her. It watches him: the smile going soft and stupid, the story he was telling dying in his hands.

"Oi oi." The loud one pushes off the shop window, delighted. "Devon's buffering."

"Say nothing," Devon says, without turning round.

"Bro, look at the blazer." He is pointing now, openly, with no shame at all. "That's Belvedire. Girls like that don't give out numbers, they give out restraining orders."

"Let him find out." The laid-back one says it softly, arms still folded, and somehow that settles the whole argument.

Devon hands him his bag without looking, straightens nothing, fixes nothing. He crosses the road exactly as a bus hisses past behind him, using its cover like a stage curtain.

"Walk nicely, yeah!" the loud one calls after him, cupping his mouth. "Left, right, left..."

Devon lands on the pavement a stride ahead of her, turns, and walks backwards in front of her. She doesn't slow down. He has to keep moving or get walked through.

"You're lost," he says, easy, like he is doing her a favour.

"You're in my way." She says it to the space above his shoulder, not to him.

"Can't be both true. If you're lost, there is no way." He spreads his hands, taking in himself, the street, the whole afternoon. "I'm just... here. Scenery."

She looks at him properly for the first time. Fifteen. The look is an audit: shoes, hands, mouth, eyes... scar. Her eyes cross the scar the way you cross a road you have crossed all your life. No flinch. No lingering. Nothing.

Something in Devon's walk changes. He was braced for the flinch. It never came.

"Scenery moves out of the way," she says. "Or it gets developed."

"Developed," he repeats, like he is turning the word over to see what it is made of.

"Knocked down. Built over. Turned into flats."

"Rah." He laughs, one short surprised note. "You talk like a landlord."

"You talk like scaffolding." She doesn't even break stride to land it. "Loud, temporary."

Devon barks a laugh, genuine, delighted, and finally falls in step beside her instead of in front. She allows it the way royalty allows weather.

He lets a few paces go by before he offers it, and when it comes it costs him nothing at all.

"Devon."

"Didn't ask." Instant. She doesn't look over.

"You were about to," he says, with a grin sitting just underneath.

"I really wasn't." Flatter this time, the door shut before he reaches it.

"You were gonna ask something." He is enjoying himself now, hands in his pockets, matching her step for step.

"I was gonna ask..." She tips her head back over her shoulder and jerks a thumb down the pavement behind them. "...if the two behind us are your carers."

Cut wide: fifty metres back, the two mates following at a shameless stroll, and one of them chuckling audibly at being clocked.

"Them?" Devon doesn't look back, doesn't miss a beat. "Never seen them before in my life."

"DEV! ASK IF SHE'S GOT FRIENDS!"

The shout carries the full fifty metres. Devon closes his eyes and keeps walking, a man absorbing damage. Beside him, the girl's mouth betrays her: the corner lifts, a real one, quickly arrested.

"...Brothers," he says, eyes still shut. "Adopted. Against my will."

"Mm." She faces front again. "They seem like the smart ones."

They walk. A rhythm has started that neither of them is admitting to. She stops at the corner where the high road meets the bus lane. Her stop. He clocks it and pretends he hasn't.

"So what's Belvedire doing walking through my ends in school shoes?" he asks.

"Your ends?" She does surprise like a woman trying on a coat she has no intention of buying. "You own all this?"

"Every brick you can see." He says it deadpan, gesturing along the parade.

"The chicken shop as well?"

"That's the crown jewel." He tuts at her, mock-disappointed. "Keep up."

She turns to face him. First time she has given him the whole of her attention. It lands on him like weather.

"I get off two stops early. I walk through." She shrugs one shoulder, and there is something almost defensive in it. "It winds my dad up and I like the noise. Everything where I live is carpets. Carpets and doors that don't slam. You can hear yourself think and it's boring, it's SO boring."

"And here?" he asks, quieter.

"Here it's loud. Nobody's watching me." She looks off down the high road as she says it. "It's the only hour of my day that's mine."

Devon nods slowly. He does not do the thing. He doesn't sell the ends, doesn't perform the danger. He just tells her the truth, and his voice drops right down to do it.

"It's less fun when you can't leave it."

That lands. Her chin comes round. She studies him again: the scar, the eyes, the sudden stillness underneath all that mouth.

Her bus rounds the far corner. She sees it. He sees her see it.

"There's a thing Friday." It comes out fast, casual, far too casual, and he examines the pavement while he says it. "Nothing deep. Music. My lot. You'd hate it."

"I'd hate it?" One eyebrow, already up.

"Guaranteed. Loud, no carpets, doors slamming everywhere."

The bus pulls in with a hiss. She steps backwards onto it without breaking eye contact, and gives it to him at last: the guard down, the eyes relaxed, the voice dropped low enough that it is meant for him and nobody else on that street.

"Sounds like the only hour of my day that's mine..." A beat, and the smallest smile. "I like your face, scenery. Friday."

The doors close on his expression.

Hold on Devon through the glass as the bus pulls away: a seventeen-year-old boy with a scar he has been fighting his whole life, being told, by the most impossible girl he has ever met, that the face is what she liked.

The two mates arrive either side of him, all three watching the bus go.

"You didn't get a number," the loud one says.

"Don't need one." Devon doesn't look away from the bus.

"He didn't get a number, you know." Said to the other one now, louder, for the record.

"He got a day," the laid-back one says, and leaves it there.

The bus shrinks to nothing. Devon is still smiling at it.

FRIDAY

A front door closes on a party's noise, muffling it to a heartbeat through walls.

Then the picture flicks, like a channel changing, and the room is dark and the sound is everything.

What follows is heard and suggested, never shown. A frantic collage, cut to the muffled bassline still coming up through the floor:

"Some doors, once closed," Archer says, almost gently,

Over a bare shoulder, out of focus, a hand pressed flat against peeling wallpaper.

"do not open again in the same way."

A shadow thrown huge and doubled across a wall, two silhouettes made one, moving.

"Youth mistakes intensity for permanence."

The corner of a single bed, its legs walking themselves a centimetre at a time across bare floorboards. A trainer falls off the end of it.

"It is a common, and usually expensive, error."

A light fitting swaying. Next door, a framed picture knocks against the wall in time. From somewhere, breathless, half a laugh, hers, then his, then neither.

Beat.

The camera starts to rise. Through the ceiling. Through the roof. Up over the rooftops of South Danim at night, the city glittering all the way out to the black band of the river, the party bass shrinking to a pulse, and then, tiny beneath the sky, two voices reach one final note together and go quiet.

Hold on the city. A fox trots across an empty road.

THE LOCKER

Morning. A different world: a school, all glass and honey-brick, the kind of school with a rowing team. Corridor traffic. Blazers everywhere.

The girl in the Belvedire blazer, at her locker, putting books away, somewhere else entirely. She closes it. SLAM.

Standing exactly where the door was: a girl. Fifteen, box braids, prefect badge worn upside down, and already mid-sentence, as though the conversation has been running since birth and she has simply rejoined it.

"...so THEN he says he can't do Saturday because of football, football, Hella, a friendly, not even a real match, and I said okay cool enjoy your friendly, and he said what's that supposed to mean, and I said nothing, WHICH MEANS EVERYTHING, obviously, everyone knows that, and then he liked Priya's photo at eleven forty at NIGHT, the audacity, the sheer..."

She catches herself. Squints.

Hella is smiling. Not at her. Not at anything. At some point in the middle distance about a metre past the other girl's shoulder. A private, fully-glazed, out-of-office smile.

"Tskk." The kiss of teeth arrives first, and the outrage rides in right behind it. "Are you even listening to me?!"

"Oh." Hella surfaces about halfway. "Yeah, yeah, my bad, Mele. I'm just tryna get to class."

She gives Mele a glance, a glimpse really, sliding past eye contact on its way somewhere else, and walks. Mele stays exactly where she is, staring after her.

And then Mele notices the walk.

Hold on Mele's face as the data assembles itself. The eyes widen by degrees, like a dial being turned.

"Oh..." Her hand comes up to her mouth. "My..."

She dashes. Overtakes half the corridor, cuts Hella off at the turn, and lands both hands flat on her shoulders.

"You cheeky shit," she says, holding her still. "Look at me."

Hella slowly lifts her eyes. The smirk is still sitting there. Her whole face is in la la land, happy in a way that has no defences up at all.

Mele's gasp pulls heads three lockers down.

"You've been BANGED." It is a whisper delivered with the full lung capacity of a scream.

She checks left. Checks right. Then grabs Hella by the wrist and tows her down the corridor, out through a fire door, gone.

THE ROOF

The flat roof above the science block. A milk crate, a vent to lean on, a view of the pitches. A joint travels between them. This is clearly not the first time this roof has hosted them.

"Seven times?? SEVEN???" Mele says.

"Mm hmm."

Hella takes her pull. Holds it like a professional. Exhales slow.

"I can still feel my legs shaking and twitching, you know."

Close on her legs stretched out on the roof felt: the faintest tremor, a muscle spasming small under the skin. She watches them like they belong to someone else. Proud of them.

"You know he can go to jail, right?" Mele grabs the joint off her.

"Bitch, I'm sixteen in ten months. I'm straight."

"That's NEXT YEAR, you plum."

"Don't be acting like you ain't had sex."

"I'm sixteen."

"So... I know what you were doing at MY age..." Hella turns her head, deadpan, delivers it like a newsreader:

"...Heather Brooke."

Beat.

Mele is mid-pull. The cough detonates. Smoke everywhere, eyes streaming, half laughing, half dying, waving a hand.

"I'm DEADDD... how do you even know about the queen B..." she manages, wheezing.

The camera drifts up off the roof, the two of them shrinking, Mele's voice fading under the wind and the bell ringing somewhere below.

"...nah, seriously, who showed you that, you're actually moving like..."

Fade to black.

FIVE WEEKS

Black. Then sound first: retching. Hard, hollow, echoing off tile.

A bathroom fit for a hotel. Marble, brass, a mirror wider than most beds. A girl crouched over the toilet, back turned, one hand white-knuckled on the seat. It goes on longer than is comfortable. It is meant to.

It stops. She stays folded for a moment, breathing. Then slowly, in stages, she gets herself up: knees, hand on the wall, standing. She runs the tap and faces the mirror.

It is Hella. Rough. Grey around the mouth, eyes glassed, a fleck of sick at the corner of her lip that she wipes with the back of her wrist.

On screen: 5 WEEKS LATER.

She gets ready. And as she steps out of the bathroom, the episode quietly plays its card: the corridor is not a corridor, it is a gallery. High-end, modern, glass balustrade, art with its own lighting, a cleaner moving a hoover somewhere far away like a figure in a landscape painting. New money, sharpened daily.

This is the first time anyone learns where she lives. The uniform, the blazer, Belvedire: it assembles.

Her bedroom: beautiful, enormous, a teenage girl's room art-directed by an interior designer and then fought back into life by the teenager. Clothes over a chair the housekeeper keeps losing to, photo strips in the mirror frame, one wall of trainers.

Getting-ready montage, quick and quiet: uniform, brush, the practised face going on over the grey one. Each mirror check a little longer than it needs to be. A hand resting, once, flat on her stomach, and taken away like it burnt.

The kitchen. A kitchen the size of Devon's whole flat. At the island, swinging her legs on a stool: her little sister, Tammy, six, cereal, cartoon-watching, talking the way six-year-olds talk, constantly, about everything.

But Tammy is heard the way Hella hears her: distant, underwater, fuzzed at the edges, a radio between stations. Normal for a second, then it smears.

"...and Miss Okafor said if the caterpillars hatch on the weekend then NOBODY gets to see it and that's not fair because I fed them, Hella, I fed them the MOST..."

Hella stands at the counter with her back to her, cereal untouched, staring down at a spoon like she has forgotten what it is for.

What the fuck is wrong with me?

"Hellooooo..." Tammy leans right out over the island, waving both arms, surfacing up through the fuzz.

Black.

THE ROOF, AGAIN

Sound before picture.

"You're pregs."

The roof. Same crate, same vent. Mele is lying back against the slope of the vent housing, sunglasses on, joint lit, one arm stretched out sideways to offer it up without looking. She holds the pose. Waits.

"WHAT?!"

Mele doesn't move. Doesn't even turn her head. Just waits, hand out, the joint smoking gently between two fingers.

Hella looks at it. Looks at it properly, for a second too long. Then shakes her head. Small. Twice.

Mele clocks the refusal, and it confirms every single thing. She shrugs, takes it back, pulls.

"The fuck you mean 'what'..." The smoke comes out through the words. "You are pre-g-nant. Didn't you use a condom?"

"Yes. We had six."

A beat.

"Ha!" Mele's head tips back, smirking at the sky, smoke escaping her grin with a small cough riding out behind it.

"Seven times."

Silence. A plane draws a slow white line across the blue. Hella pulls her knees up to her chest and hugs them.

"So..." She doesn't look over. "What should I do?"

"Abort it."

It comes back instantly, with no cruelty in it at all. To Mele's mind the speed is the kindness.

"It's easy. No one has to know. Take like two secs."

A long moment. Hella curls up smaller, arms locked round her legs, chin down onto her knees. The wind moves her hair across her face and she doesn't clear it. She is fifteen and, all at once, she looks it.

Mele watches her from the corner of her eye, still flat on her back, sunglasses reflecting the clouds.

"You're not thinking of keeping it... are you."

She says it as a statement, because asking would give Hella somewhere to go. Hella doesn't move. Doesn't flinch. Stares at nothing.

Mele sits up. Slowly. Takes the sunglasses off. This is Mele serious, and Mele serious is a rare exhibit.

"Bitch." She waits until she has her. "Don't tell me you're keeping that thing."

Hella stays curled. Thinking. The silence stretches out until it becomes the answer.

"You..." Mele exhales it. "Are... FUCKED."

She lies back down. Puts the sunglasses back on. Takes the longest pull of her life, and speaks it straight up at the sky.

"This is why I swallow mines."

The line hangs there, filthy and loyal and afraid, all three at once, as it fades to black on the two of them, small on the roof, the school bell ringing underneath.

THE KITCHEN

BANG. A pot hits a wall, clatters onto a stove top, spins, settles.

A kitchen we have seen before, the island, the water dispenser, but the geometry is all wrong now, because the sound in the next room is enormous.

"You are fucking FIFTEEN!" The voice comes through the wall stripped raw. "FIFTEEN years old! This is the person you want to be! HUH?! A fucking MOTHER at FIFTEEN fucking years old!"

In the kitchen: Hella on a chair against the wall, feet up on the rung, shrunk to nothing. There is the smallest curve to her now, five months of it, under the school jumper she is still wearing like a costume of a former life.

The maid, Audrey. Forties, kind eyes, a face that has worked in this house long enough to know all its weathers. She comes down quickly to Hella's level, crouching, and takes both of Hella's hands in both of hers.

"Everything is going to be alright," she says, close, holding her eyes.

But Hella can see it on her face: Audrey is exactly as frightened as she is. The comfort is a costume too. They hold hands anyway. It is what there is.

BOOM. The door. Her father enters the kitchen.

Mid-forties, shirtsleeves, a watch worth more than the street Devon lives on. The rage has gone quiet on the way through the door, which is worse.

Audrey rises. Puts herself, without one gram of drama, between him and the chair. Shaking, and doing it anyway.

"You." His voice has dropped almost to nothing, which is how it gets when it matters. "Get the fuck out."

Audrey looks at him. Then back at Hella, and holds it a moment too long, making a promise she has no power whatsoever to keep. Then back at the man, whose face has not moved a millimetre.

She goes. Silent. The door closes behind her with a click that sounds like a verdict.

He slams the bolt across. Walks, unhurried now, to the sink. Takes a glass from the drying rack. Crosses to the water dispenser. Presses. The glass fills. The room is so quiet that the water can be heard climbing the glass, the note rising as it nears the top.

"FUCK!"

He flings it. The glass detonates against the counter edge and the wall, water and fragments everywhere. Hella jolts, hands flying up over her head.

Then, calm again, that obscene instant calm, he pulls out a stool at the kitchen island and sits. Laces his fingers. Rests them against his lips, elbows on the marble. And stares at her.

Silence. He stares. She shakes. The tap drips.

His gaze descends, deliberately, from her face to her stomach.

On screen: 5 MONTHS.

The gaze comes back up to her eyes. Music has been building under all of it, a low string pressure, tightening, tightening, up and up until it has to break.

SNAP. Black. Silence.

THE WARD

In the black: a baby crying. Close. New. That first furious astonished sound.

Light bleeds in, blurry, overexposed, swimming. Hella's point of view: shapes in scrubs, a ceiling light like a halo, everything echoing down a long tube.

"It's a beautiful baby boy..." The voice reaches her warm and underwater, a long way off.

The halo smears. Black again.

Fade up, clean and quiet.

A private room, machines idling, evening light. Hella asleep in the bed, small in the pillows. She stirs. Opens her eyes. Ceiling. Drip stand. Where...

She snaps upright.

"My baby!" Her hands are already going to the bedrail. "Where's my baby!"

"He's fine, Hella."

The voice comes from the corner, unhurried. The nurse, fifties, sleeves pushed to her elbows, carrying the calm of ten thousand nights exactly like this one. She nods to Hella's left.

"He's having a nap. Working hard at it, too."

Hella looks. Beside the bed: a clear-sided hospital cot. Inside, swaddled to the chin, impossibly small, a baby. The baby. A shock goes across her eyes, a physical thing, and then her whole face softens, muscle by muscle, into something she has never worn before.

She lowers herself back down slowly, eyes never once leaving the cot.

"You had us worried." The nurse moves round to the drip stand as she says it, casual, not making a thing of it. "You've been blacking out. Anyone home when you faint like that?"

"...He's so small," Hella says. She hasn't heard the question.

"Six pounds nine." The nurse checks a line. "That's a decent size, that."

"No, I mean... he's SMALL. Like." Hella's hands come up, trying to shape it. "What's he supposed to do like that?"

The nurse laughs softly, tidying the blanket edge, pure routine.

"Nothing. That's the arrangement. He does nothing, you do everything, and somehow he's still in charge."

Hella almost smiles. Then it collapses out from under her.

"I don't know how to do... any of it." Her voice has gone very small. "I don't know anything."

"Nobody does." The nurse says it without a scrap of pity, which is why it works. "First-time mums arrive knowing precisely nothing, same as first-time babies. You learn each other."

She checks the drip line, speaking easily, not lecturing, just laying it down like fresh sheets.

"Here's the whole trick, so you can stop being scared of the wrong things. He doesn't need you clever. He doesn't need you rich. He needs you THERE. Fed, warm, held, that's the entire curriculum for the first bit. And when he cries at three in the morning and you're crying with him, that's not failing. That's the two of you having the same conversation."

Hella listens like it is scripture. Her eyes shine.

"And I'll tell you something for free. That boy's known one thing in this world for nine months. Your heartbeat." She nods at the cot. "Put him on your chest and watch. He could pick it out of a hundred."

Hella looks at the cot. Both hands have come up over her mouth. The nurse watches her, and sees exactly what she has seen a thousand times and never once missed: a girl who cares completely, and is completely terrified, and is fifteen.

A soft beat.

"Will dad be coming in? For the birth certificate?"

Hella's mouth opens.

"No."

Hard. Flat. From the doorway, as if he had always been standing there. He has. A man in a very good coat, unhurried.

The nurse straightens, professionally pleasant.

"Oh, hello. And your name is..."

"Her father."

Firm. Final. A door closing inside two words.

"...Wonderful. I'll leave you two to catch up."

She gathers her chart. As she passes him, his hand closes around her arm. Not violent. Worse: precise.

"When can she be discharged to come back home." He places each word down separately, slow and quiet, and none of them is a question.

The nurse looks down at the hand. Takes one second to register how hard he is holding her. Recalibrates the man entirely.

"...Minimum one day. She's been having blackouts."

A long moment. He is about to say something else. He lets it go, and lets her go with it, a low sound under his breath, half a growl swallowed.

The nurse walks out. In the corridor she turns for one last glance through the closing door: the father, back turned, standing at the foot of the bed, towering over the girl and the cot, saying nothing.

Her face: suspicion filed for a lifetime.

The door clicks. Black.

THE RETURN

A gate of black iron swings open, automated, silent. Cut into the stone pillar beside it, in letters nobody has had to clean in a hundred years: MITCHELL ESTATE.

A Rolls-Royce, the latest, paintwork like still water, glides up a drive long enough to have its own weather. Belvedire. Lawns to the horizon. The house arrives in stages, wing by wing.

"And so Hella Mitchell returns to the family estate. Frightened. Fifteen. But a mother, none the less." Archer lets that sit. "Her mind, for the moment... blank. Empty. The body drives; the girl is a passenger."

Inside the car: Hella at the window, hospital band still on her wrist. Beside her, strapped and sleeping in his car seat, the baby. Her eyes fixed on the middle distance. Not on him. Not allowed on him.

"Her school, you ask? Her school has been furnished with the finest fiction money can buy: glandular fever, poor lamb, complicated by exhaustion, convalescing abroad at a Swiss clinic her father recommends to everyone and has visited never. Letterhead. A doctor's signature. Term fees paid a year forward, which in the private system is the truest form of poetry."

The car crunches to a stop before the front steps.

"The girls of her year, doing their own arithmetic, have voted: modelling in Milan, says the majority. A breakdown, says an ambitious minority. One girl, and only one, knows the truth and has said nothing at all, which as any butler will tell you is the rarest service of them all."

The chauffeur opens Hella's door. A second staff member opens the far door. A butler lifts out the car seat with the baby, handling it with perfect, impersonal care, and comes to stand beside Hella.

Hella, on the gravel, glances down. The baby sleeps on in the seat, fists up by his ears like a tiny boxer.

High above: a first-floor window. Her father looking down at the three of them on the drive.

Overhead shot, his point of view: the girl, the butler, the seat, arranged on the gravel like pieces being set on a board.

They take a moment. Then start up the steps into the house.

"There is a saying in houses like this one, older than the stone: the truth, like water, always finds its level."

Cut to the father at the glass. The light does him no favours, or exactly the favours he deserves: half his face in shadow, unamused, patient.

"But a sufficiently determined will is a kind of dam. And in all its polished history... the Mitchell estate has never once suffered a flood."

Hold on his shadowed face.

Black.

THE BROCHURE

A nursery that was a guest room a month ago. In the corner, a soft-play square: fluffy toys, a rattle, dangling shapes on an arch. The baby, months old now, sits up wobbling in the middle of it, reaching for the dangling things, catching nothing, delighted anyway. He smiles at his own hands.

The camera pulls slowly back from him. Voices reach across the room, muffled at first, arriving in focus the way sound comes back after a faint.

"...el... ella..." A pause, and the voice comes into focus. "Hella?"

"Huh."

Hella snaps out of it. She and Audrey are sitting side by side on the end of the bed. Hella has been watching the baby the way you watch weather coming in over the horizon.

Audrey notices the distance in her and squeezes her hand.

"Don't worry," she says. "He will be fine."

She lifts what she has been holding: a brochure. Thick stock. Beautiful. A crest. Green lawns, bright rooms, laughing children, a font that costs money. Across the top, STONEBRIDGE HOUSE: A FAMILY FOR EVERY CHILD.

"I have read this from front to back, and the fine print, three times." She turns it over in her hands as she says it, proud of it, relieved by it, thoroughly sold by it. "It has the best of the best facilities. To make sure he grows up strong, and well taken care of." She taps a page and holds it out for Hella to see. "Look, they have a music room. A MUSIC room, Hella."

Hella looks at her. At the hope on her face, real hope, borrowed hope. Then down at her own lap.

Then across, at him. The baby has captured the rattle at last and is inspecting it like a jeweller: turning it, frowning at it, tasting it. Wondering. Exploring. Curious about a world that has already decided what to do with him.

Hella stares. Her expression does not change at all.

Her eyes fill. Build. And run: one line down one cheek. Then, from the other eye, a second.

She doesn't blink. Doesn't make a sound. Just watches him, tears falling without her, as if even her crying has been taken into private management.

Audrey, looking at the brochure, doesn't see.

Fade to black.

THE DRIVEWAY

From below, from inside the car seat. Hella standing over us, looking down. The baby's point of view. Her face fills the sky.

It is lifeless. Emotionless. Not sad. Not cold. Neutral, which is the most frightening thing a face can be. She just stares down at us.

Then, without her face changing at all, her hand comes down into frame holding a small folded paper, cream, official, folded twice over, and tucks it deep into the padding beside us, down where fingers would have to know to look. The hand rests half a second on the blanket. Withdraws.

Her face has still not moved.

Her father arrives beside her in the frame, coat immaculate. He does not look down at the seat. Not once.

"Call me the moment you arrive." He says it past us, to someone out of frame. "The moment."

"Yes, sir," the chauffeur says, from somewhere near the car.

The world moves: the seat is lifted, the sky swings, and the shot cuts out of the point of view to a wide.

The drive. The Rolls has been replaced by a discreet black saloon, the kind of car that isn't from a company and isn't from a family. The chauffeur clips the car seat into the back. Closes the door with a thump that is much too loud for what it is.

The car pulls away, gravel, then tarmac, then smaller, and smaller, down the endless drive.

Hella has not moved. Standing on the steps, arms at her sides, watching it shrink.

He stands beside her a moment longer. Then turns, without a word, and walks towards the doors of the mansion.

Hold. Hella in the foreground, still as the statues on the gate. The car a dot. In the background, out of focus, her father walking away into his house.

She keeps staring long after there is nothing to stare at.

That is how the scene ends.

THE CALL

A phone rings once. Once is all it gets.

"Yes."

"Just dropped him off, sir." The chauffeur's voice comes through thin and dutiful. "All signed."

Her father is alone in his study, standing at the same window he was standing at before.

"Good."

He hangs up on the word. Files the phone into his pocket. Adjusts nothing, because nothing about him is out of place. Turns back to his desk.

A hallway that has given up. Foster home fluorescents, a noticeboard with one flyer from two years ago, a smell you can see. The foster carer, indeterminate age, cardigan, lanyard, a face rationed to the essentials, stands over the car seat skimming a document folder.

Silence, pages turning. The typed folder is thin and tells her nothing she cares about. The baby watches her from the seat.

Then she clocks it: a cream corner poking up from deep in the seat padding. Hand-folded. Not part of the file. She works it free and opens it: a certificate. Handwriting. A girl's handwriting.

Close on the paper, half a second only: the first name, DONTE, and her thumb lying flat across the line where a surname would be.

"...Donte," she says, to herself, flat.

A beat. She glances at the baby. Back at the paper.

"Okay."

She folds it back along its creases, files it inside the folder, and the folder goes down the side of the car seat. The whole thing gets picked up like luggage. The corridor swallows them.

Black.

"For the record, since no one else will keep one: the brochure was real. The house on its cover was not." Archer's voice arrives out of the dark, and for once there is no amusement anywhere in it. "Stonebridge House was typeset, photographed and printed by three of Mr Mitchell's most talented employees in an afternoon, and exists nowhere on this earth except in Audrey's good heart... and a mother's last hope. The truth will find its level. But it is in no hurry. It can wait years. It usually does."

THE HOME

Caption: EAST DANIM.

And now the episode changes instruments. What follows is a montage spanning years, Donte growing from toddler to eleven, intercut and underscored by Archer, whose narration for this whole section is delivered like a lecture on the philosophy of breaking. The images answer him, or he answers the images. Drill instrumental low and slow underneath, more heartbeat than song.

A grey building that the city forgot on purpose. Windows with wire in the glass. A yard of cracked concrete with one basketball hoop, no net, no ball.

"Consider, if you will, a simple question. Not a pleasant one. But then we are past the pleasant part of the evening." A beat. "How long does it take... to break a man?"

Inside, a dormitory of mismatched beds. Donte, four, sitting on the end of the smallest one while older kids swarm a delivery of donated toys. By the time he gets there, the box is empty. He looks in it anyway. Takes out the packing paper. Folds it carefully. Keeps it.

"The romantics will tell you a man cannot be broken, only bent. The romantics, you will notice, tend to write from comfortable rooms."

Donte, six, at a long dinner table. A plate is slid to him last: the smallest portion. A bigger kid, Terrence, ten, reaches over and takes his bread roll without even looking at him, mid-conversation. The carer sees it. Says nothing. Donte eats what is left in silence, eyes down.

"A more practical school holds that every man is a bridge: load him gradually, and he learns to carry. Load him suddenly... and you learn what he was made of."

A classroom corner. Donte, seven, holding out his exercise book to show a drawing to another kid. The kid looks at it, looks at him, and turns away to laugh with someone else. Donte withdraws the book slowly. Looks at the drawing himself. Closes it.

"But bridges, you see, have engineers. Someone measures the load. Someone cares when the cables sing. The boy we are watching has no engineer. The load is measured by children, and children, left unsupervised with power..."

The yard. Donte, eight, walking the perimeter alone, trailing one hand along the fence. Behind him, a window breaks somewhere inside, and every head in the yard turns to him. A carer storms out, already shouting his name. Donte doesn't argue. The boy who did it is smirking, ten feet away. Donte just goes where he is pointed. The black sheep. The address where blame lives.

"...children measure it in laughter."

Night dormitory. Donte's bed, and a bucket of water balanced on the door he will open at six a.m. Kids pretending to sleep, shaking with giggles under blankets. Donte, eleven now, lies awake staring at the ceiling. He knows. He always knows. He will open the door anyway, because the alternative is worse.

"And the boy carries it. Season upon season. Load upon load. Which brings us, regrettably, to the day the measuring ended... and the testing began."

THE FREEZER

The yard. Late winter afternoon, the light already dying. Behind the kitchen block: a dumping ground for dead appliances. A washing machine on its face. And a chest freezer, coffin-shaped, lid intact.

Donte, eleven, has been sent out to bring in the bins. Alone. Ambush geometry: Terrence, now fifteen and built like a door, and four others, peeling off walls, cutting angles, closing.

And above the yard, in the kitchen window: the foster carer, mug in hand, watching the geometry assemble. She looks at Donte. At the five. She takes a sip, and draws the blind.

"Oi." Terrence doesn't hurry. He never has to. "Sheep."

Donte doesn't run. There is nowhere it would work. He puts the bin down. Stands. Hands at his sides. Even now, even at eleven: that stillness.

"Why's he standing like that?" One of the others says it with a laugh in it, nudging the boy beside him. "Look at this guy."

"We made you a bed, bro." Terrence pats the freezer lid twice, flat-palmed, and the others start laughing before he has even finished. "Try it. It's memory foam."

Donte looks at the freezer. Then back at Terrence. And for the first time in the entire montage, he says a word.

"No."

They swarm him. It takes all five, and it is not clean. He makes them earn every centimetre, an elbow catches somebody's mouth and somebody else's shin gets raked down, but he is eleven and they are many. They wrestle him up and in.

The lid slams.

Black. Total. The sound design does the horror: Donte's breathing, huge in the box. Fists on the inside of the lid. BOOM. BOOM. Muffled laughter from outside, warped and distant like it is coming through water.

"Nah he's fine, man, it's got holes..." Terrence's voice comes through the lid, and somewhere in the middle of the sentence it stops being sure of itself. "It's got holes innit?"

"...Has it got holes?" one of the others asks. Nobody answers him.

Something heavy scrapes onto the lid. Then something heavier. They are stacking weight on it now. Sitting on it. The banging underneath gets faster.

Inside: nothing to see, and everything to hear. The breathing going ragged. The banging weakening. And beneath it, rising, a sound nobody up there has heard before: a hum. A pressure. Like a kettle starting three streets away.

"Here, then, is the answer to our question." Archer is quiet now, all the irony gone out of him. "You do not break a man by hurting him. Pain, the boy knows. Pain is Tuesday."

Outside, the laughter dies off as the banging stops. One boy's smile goes first. The others catch it off him, one by one, and look at each other.

"...Terrence," one of them says, and it comes out small.

"You break a man by teaching him, beyond all argument, in the dark, with the weight of the world sat comfortably upon the lid... that no one is coming."

Silence from the freezer.

Then the hum arrives. The kids feel it through their feet before they hear it. The freezer's dead compressor screams into life for one impossible second, and the metal begins to tick, the sound of a pan heating, and the lid seams start to glow, a thin orange line drawing itself around the rectangle like a fuse.

"Get off. GET OFF..."

They scatter off the lid. The paint on it blisters, blackens, peels back in curls.

And the freezer erupts.

It goes in two beats. First: a burst of ordinary orange fire, a column of it, the lid blowing off its hinges and cartwheeling across the yard on a fountain of sparks. Then, inside the orange, the fire concentrates: it darkens at the core into black flame, black as the inside of the box was, and the black fire is hotter, the air warping around it, the concrete underneath glowing, the freezer's walls sagging like candle wax. Then it breathes back out to ordinary orange, as if the black was never there.

A fragment of the bursting freezer spins across the yard and catches one of the kids across the face. Terrence. He goes down clutching his cheek, blood running instantly between his fingers, screaming.

The pressure wave has thrown the rest of them skidding across the concrete, jackets scorched, eyebrows gone, scrambling backwards.

And in the wreck of the freezer, burst open, broken apart, its walls part-melted and steaming: Donte.

Not standing. Not powerful. He is on the floor of it, curled small, and the fire took his clothes off him in rags of ash and took nothing else, not a mark on his skin, which is somehow worse to look at. The flames pour off him in thinning ropes and go back in, sucked into him like breath, and what they leave behind is an eleven-year-old, shivering violently, letting out high, thin, squeaking screams, one after another, a child's screams, the sound of a boy whose body has just done something his mind cannot hold.

He cries. Curled in the melted box, in the cold they locked him into, he just cries.

Windows light up. Adults shouting, running. What they find: one boy bleeding badly from the face, four more scorched and wailing, and an unmarked child crying in the wreckage of an exploded freezer.

Every finger in the yard points the same way.

"HE DID IT!" Terrence is screaming it through the blood in his fingers. "HE'S A FREAK! HE DID IT!"

A blanket is thrown over Donte. Rough. The way you cover a thing, not warm a child. Nobody asks him anything.

Snap to black.

THE BASEMENT

A door with three bolts. It opens on a crack of light, and the foster carer is standing in it, a shape with the corridor behind her. She doesn't come down the steps. She shoves a plate of food across the concrete floor with the side of her foot, the way you would feed something you had been told not to touch.

"You stay down here," she says, "till we know what you are."

Not who. What.

The door shuts. The bolts go across, one, two, three, and each one lands like a full stop.

Black again. His second box in a week.

No screaming. No banging. The boy has learned that neither works.

Above him the house carries on. Footsteps crossing a floor. A television. Somebody laughing at something. Water moving in a pipe near his head, going somewhere else. Twice a day the bolts scrape and a plate comes in and the bolts go back. Nobody speaks to him. Nobody asks him anything, which by now he expects, because nobody asked him anything in the yard either.

He eats some of it. He sleeps on the concrete with his back to the wall so the door is always in front of him.

And on the second night, in the black, something small and steady lights.

A flame. On the end of his finger, burning like a birthday candle, throwing just enough orange to find his face behind it. He turns his hand over and watches it hold. It doesn't roar out of him. It doesn't take his clothes. It sits there because he is calm, and it is the first time he has ever understood that the two things are connected.

He lifts the finger and takes the flame around the room. Concrete. A dead boiler. A shelf of paint tins nobody has opened in years. His own breath, going up in the cold.

Then the door.

He holds the light close to it and does arithmetic. The hinge side, three heavy pins, no. The boards, thick, no. The lock plate, a rectangle of brass sunk into old dry wood.

He puts the flame out and sits back down with his back to the wall, because he is eleven, and he wants to be sure, and there is no hurry now that he knows.

Time cut: night.

The lock plate begins to glow. Faint at first, then orange, then bright enough to light the whole stairwell, and the wood around it chars and bubbles and lets go with a sound like a knuckle cracking. The door swings open on a boy-shaped hole in the house's authority.

A corridor of sleeping doors. Donte moves along it with everything he owns, which fits inside one carrier bag and does not need carrying carefully. He passes the room where the others sleep. He does not stop, and he does not look in.

At the front door he stops. Turns. Looks back down the hallway at the whole building, once.

Nothing in the look asks to stay.

He could open it. The latch is right there and it opens from the inside, and he knows it, and he stands looking at it for a moment.

Then he burns through the front lock as well.

Not because he has to. Because it is his door now.

And he is gone, out into the night: eleven years old, made of fire, carrying a plastic bag.

THE SQUATTERS

Night streets. Rain that can't commit. Donte walks until walking stops being a plan. Shop shutters. A night bus sails past, an aquarium of warm light, faces that don't look down.

An arch under the railway, glowing faintly: pallet fires in barrels, tarps, trolleys, tents. A squatter camp, fifteen, twenty souls, arranged with the practised looseness of people who know they cannot stay anywhere long. This spot is for tonight. The police sweep it by Friday. Everyone here knows the timetable except Donte.

He folds himself into the darkest corner, against the brick, knees to chest, carrier bag under his arm like a teddy. He is shaking with cold.

He lights the finger and holds it against his chest. It is a candle. It shows him his own hands and it does not warm them. After a while he puts it out.

And here is the cruelty the episode has saved up: the boy of fire is freezing, because what he can reach is a candle, and the rest of it only comes when the world is ending, and tonight the world is merely awful.

Across the camp, by a barrel: an older man watching him. The beggar. Fifties or a hundred, hard to say. Beard, army surplus coat, fingerless gloves, a rucksack of things with a folded stack of clothing on top, still with tags. Shoplifted stock: his float, his livelihood, tomorrow's food.

He watches the kid shake for a long minute. Mutters something to himself. Argues with himself. Loses.

He crosses the camp and crouches down at arm's length, unhurried, the way you approach a stray you don't want to bolt.

"Ay." He waits until the boy's eyes come up. "Look at me. You runnin' from something, or to something?"

Donte just looks at him. Silence, as ever. But the beggar reads it fluently.

"Yeah," he says, nodding slowly. "Same answer at your age."

He pulls the top item off his stack: a hoodie, black, brand new, tag still swinging off it. He turns it over in his hands once, a man counting the cost of a thing out loud to himself. Then he bites the tag off and holds it out.

Donte doesn't move.

"It's not a trick, son." He keeps his arm where it is. "Tricks cost more than this."

Donte takes it. It swallows him: sleeves past his hands, hem down at his knees. Warmth arrives like a rumour. And across the chest, in white letters the streetlight picks out:

LIT

"There he is." The beggar settles back on his heels, looks at the word, and nods at it, deadpan. "Suits you. Don't let nobody tell you different."

The smallest thing happens in Donte's face. Not a smile, his face doesn't know that road yet, but the fists unclench inside the too-long sleeves.

The beggar goes back to his barrel. Donte, wrapped in someone's stolen kindness, watches the fire until his eyes lose.

"Note the transaction closely, because the ledger of this boy's life is short, and this is its largest entry. One garment. Stolen for profit. Given for nothing..." Archer pauses on it. "Men have built entire religions on smaller arithmetic."

Morning. Grey light under the arch. Donte's eyes open.

The camp is gone. All of it: tents, trolleys, barrels still faintly warm, the beggar. Twenty souls evaporated on the timetable everyone knew except him. He stands, alone in an empty arch the size of a church, in a hoodie built for a grown man.

He looks left. Right. Nothing. No one.

He pulls the hood up. It fits over his whole world.

He walks.

ALONE

The survival montage. Days, then weeks, then months, marked honestly on screen: 3 DAYS. 2 WEEKS. A MONTH. 4 MONTHS.

Donte learning the city the hard way, always in the hoodie, the hoodie slowly fitting him better as he grows into it.

Eating from a bakery's bin, sheltered from the rain under a bridge, warming his hands at his own small flame, cupped and hidden, checked over both shoulders first, the code already instinctive in him: no one can see.

Running from a security guard with bread inside his jacket, sliding under a fence in one move that four kids in North Danim will one day get shown for free.

Standing at the mouth of the arch on a later night, hopeful, and finding a different camp there, harder faces, a man rising to his feet at the sight of him with nothing kind in it, and Donte melting backwards into the dark. The one door he knew, closed.

A phone box. Donte, soaked, looking at it. At the dial pad. He picks up the receiver. Holds it a long time. There is no number. There has never been a number. He puts it back with both hands, gently, like closing a small coffin.

"And so the arithmetic runs on. Everyone the boy is given, the ledger takes back. A mother: entered, and struck out, before he could read. A rescuer with a stolen coat: one night only. The city is teaching him its only lesson, patiently, at scale... that a hand held out is merely a hand not yet withdrawn."

East Danim. The industrial belt. Donte squeezes through a gap in corrugated fencing and stands in the doorway of an abandoned warehouse: cathedral-sized, pigeon-haunted, holed roof throwing down pillars of grey light.

He walks its floor. Tests the silence. Nobody. Nothing. His.

He builds his corner over quick cuts: pallets into a windbreak, a found tarp, a milk-crate table, the carrier bag's tiny population arranged on it with care. The last item out: the folded packing paper from the toy box, seven years old, kept.

Night in the warehouse. Donte lies on his back in his corner, hood up, watching the roof-hole. Stars over East Danim, industrial orange at the edges.

And across the warehouse, in the deep dark between two pillars of moonlight, something stands.

Small. Boy-sized. Perfectly, inhumanly still. A silhouette with its head tilted at a precise angle, watching him.

Donte's eyes find it. He doesn't startle. Doesn't rise. The two shapes regard each other across the dark for a long, silent moment.

Donte turns over and goes to sleep.

The silhouette watches. It does not move. Somewhere far off, a train.

(That is all this episode says about that.)

PRESENT DAY

Caption: PRESENT DAY. NORTH DANIM.

Morning light, and it is recognisable before anyone can say why: this street. This block. These parked cars.

Episode 1. The other side of the window.

Donte, thirteen, the hoodie fitting him properly now, LIT across his chest, walks this foreign, comfortable district with a loaf of bargain bread under one arm. His eyes do their permanent work: exits, angles, faces.

Four kids peel off a wall ahead of him. We know them. We watched them from Kevin's window, once, in muffle. Now we get the words.

"Oi." The biggest one steps into his path first, the others fanning out behind. "You're not from round here."

"What's LIT then?" another one says, plucking at the chest of the hoodie without touching him. "You LIT, yeah?"

They circle. A third one flicks the loaf out from under his arm and it lands in the gutter. Donte watches it land. That bread was breakfast and dinner.

"You deaf?" The big one shoves his shoulder.

Above and behind them, unnoticed, a curtain shifts in a first-floor window. A shape at the glass. Donte's eyes flick up at it for one quarter of a second, log it, dismiss it: a kid, indoors, irrelevant.

The big one shoves him hard. Donte gives one step, and the step is a lie, it loads him. They are the freezer lid now. Everyone is, forever.

He moves. The same seconds Episode 1 showed from the window, now full-volume and close: the wrist caught, the pivot, the throw into the pavement. The palm to the chest that lifts the second boy off the earth. The haymaker ducked in slow contempt, the sweep. The elbow into the ribs of the smart one.

Four down. The fifth, frozen, fists half up.

Donte stares at him. Dead still. Hands at his sides. Inside one sleeve, unseen by anyone on that street, a single line of flame runs from wrist to knuckle and goes out, like a held breath released.

The fifth kid walks. Fast.

Donte stands among the groaning like a boy alone in a field. Checks each of them with his eyes: staying down. He picks his bread out of the gutter, brushes it off against the hoodie, tucks it back under his arm.

A door bangs somewhere behind him. A boy's voice, distant.

"...Where did that boy go?"

But Donte is already three gardens gone, over a wall, along a ginnel, and out the far end, unhurried, invisible, a magic trick the city taught him.

THE BUS STOP

The far end of the block. Donte walks the quiet pavement, morning sun low and gold, the same honey light as a flashback nobody in this street has ever seen.

And then, distant, ahead of him, a woman's voice, at war with a phone.

"Ahh, you men are all the SAME! Only stick around to get what you want!"

Donte's stride doesn't change. Late twenties, leather jacket, leggings with STYLES down the thigh, hoops like handcuffs, storming along the opposite pavement toward the bus stop, phone clamped to her ear, gesturing at the whole sky.

Hella Mitchell. Twenty-eight. Fourteen years, one episode, and nine months from the girl on the roof.

They are going to pass each other. The episode has been building this pavement for forty minutes.

Slow everything, just slightly. The score drops to almost nothing: a single held note, and under it, so low it might be imagination, a baby's cry, once, far away, like something remembered by the street itself.

They pass. Two metres apart, opposite pavements. Her voice at full volume, his silence at full volume.

"As SOON as you get what you came for, you're a ghost! Every single one of you! GHOSTS!"

Donte's head does not turn. Her head does not turn.

The camera holds the two-shot from behind as they diverge: the woman storming toward the bus stop where, in another episode, a boy called Kevin is waiting to meet her, and the boy in the LIT hoodie walking the other way, getting smaller.

"And there it is. Two heartbeats on one pavement. One of them once learned the other by heart, in the dark, over nine months... and neither so much as slows."

Wide and high now, rising: the whole street in morning gold. Hella reaching the bus stop at the top of frame. Donte a small dark figure leaving the bottom of it.

"You will recall my saying the truth always finds its level. I stand by it. But do remember, dear viewer, what we established this evening about the truth..."

Donte turns the corner. Gone.

"...It is in no hurry. It can wait years."

Beat. On the empty corner where he vanished:

"It usually does."

Snap to black.
