Episode Three: How Hard Can It Be

The Book Edition

Novelised from the final script. The script remains canonical on any conflict.

Episode Three belongs to Sharon. Everything she is looking back on is in her own voice. The night she is looking back from is not, because nobody narrates the thing they are still standing in.

1. The Drive

A key in a lock. Three tries. The third one takes.

The door opens onto an unlit flat and stays open a second too long, because the woman in the doorway has stopped.

Sharon. Still in yesterday's coat. There is brick dust on one shoulder and a long grey smear down her forearm that she has not noticed yet.

She shuts the door with her heel and crosses the room without turning on a light, and takes something out of her inside pocket. A disk drive, matte and ugly, about the size of a paperback.

She looks at it.

Then she tosses it onto the bed the way you throw keys into a bowl, and it lands heavier than it should, and the mattress takes a second longer than it ought to about it.

She looks at that too.

"...Yeah," she says, to nobody.

She does not touch it again for the rest of the night.

2. Get Me Something By Six

Earlier, in daylight, there had been a borough station. Strip lighting, a photocopier eating itself somewhere out of sight, and a room of detectives who had all found something else to look at.

A door stood open. Behind it a man in shirtsleeves was on his feet, and had been on his feet for a while.

"...I have got the borough commander, I have got the press office, and I have got a fucking hole in a building the size of a bus," he was saying. "Do not tell me what we do not know. Tell me who is running it."

A pause.

"Sir, with respect, that is a PIP 3." Nelson said it from the doorway, cautious for once. "That is a DCI job, minimum..."

"Then find me a DCI who wants it," the man said, and he did not turn round to say it.

Silence in the outer office. Nobody moved. It was the specific silence of a room full of people not volunteering.

Sharon was at her desk with a coffee she had not opened. She was not part of this. She was filling in a form.

"...Young."

He said it into the room rather than to anybody in it.

She looked up.

Every head in the room turned to her, and then away.

"Sharon. You are lead on this. Get me something by six."

He was already walking when he said it. He did not look at her while he said it and he did not look at her after. A door shut.

Sharon had not said a word. The pen was still in her hand.

Two desks away, Nelson said it quietly to the man beside him, and not quite quietly enough.

"...Three years," Nelson said, and he did not bother making it sound like a joke.

Somebody laughed through their nose.

Sharon looked at the form in front of her. She put the pen down. She picked it back up.

She carried on filling it in.

3. It Wasn't Always Like This

Night again. The flat.

Water, too hot from the sound of it. Steam builds against the glass and comes off the top of the cubicle in a slow roll, and the small room disappears into it a piece at a time.

Sharon stands under it with her head down and her hands flat against the tiles, letting it hit the back of her neck.

She is not washing.

She closes her eyes.

The steam finds the mirror and takes the room out of it, and then it takes her out of it, until there is a shape in the glass where a woman used to be.

It wasn't always like this.

A long beat.

...I wasn't always like this.

My name is Sharon Young.

Six years ago I walked into a police station. A locker, a stab vest going on over a white shirt, hands doing the straps without looking.

Before that I worked my arse off to get out of the bullshit and earn a law degree. There is a photograph of that day. Four people squeezed into frame outside a hall: a young woman in a gown, her mother crying and pretending not to, an old man in the only suit he owns, and an older woman between them holding onto the girl's arm with both hands. The shutter goes, and the picture holds one beat longer than it needs to.

Made my mum proud. Made my grandparents proud.

I never knew my father. None of us did. Nothing ever landed on that. It went past, and the next thing was always already arriving.

And none of it mattered.

Not after that night.

4. A Pair of Shoes That Weren't Mine

I keep starting in the same place.

A flat I lived in when I was nineteen, and a pair of shoes in the hall that weren't mine.

I came up the stairs two at a time with a carrier bag in one hand and my keys already out. Nineteen. Cheaper coat, better mood, a face that had not yet learned to stay still. There was a bottle of wine in the bag and it was Friday and I had done the shop on the way home.

I let myself in.

His coat was on the floor, which was normal. A woman's coat was on the floor on top of his, which was not.

And a pair of shoes. White, both of them kicked off at angles, one on its side, the inside heel scuffed grey the way it always was.

I had watched those shoes come off in that hallway maybe two hundred times.

The rest of it arrived from the bedroom, and it arrived as sound before it arrived as anything else. Neither of them was being quiet. There was no reason for either of them to be quiet. There was nobody in the world who was supposed to be able to hear it.

I put the carrier bag down on the floor. Carefully. The bottle did not clink.

I did not call out.

The bedroom door was open. I walked down my own hall and stopped in it.

My room. My bed.

My best friend was bent over the foot of it, face down and turned away, both hands gripping my duvet, eyes shut, so she was the last one in the room to know.

He was behind her, standing, one hand flat between her shoulder blades holding her there.

The duvet was half off the bed and pooled on the carpet. His jeans were on the floor inside out with one leg still holding the shape of his leg. There was a foil wrapper by the skirting board and no condom anywhere in the room. There was a wet patch on the beige carpet at the foot of the bed, dark, about the size of a saucer, and a glass on its side beside it, and the red gone down into the pile and never coming out of it.

The whole room smelled of them.

That was my room. I painted it.

I was not shocked. That is the part people get wrong, and I have only ever told it twice. I was taking it in properly, item by item, the way you read a bill. My sheets. My pillow. Her hair on it. The wrapper. The wine in the carpet.

My jaw moved once.

Then he saw me.

He came off her fast and stood up straight in the middle of my bedroom with nothing on, still hard, going soft, one hand held out towards me the way you would put a hand out to a horse. There was one full second where he was not frightening and not even shameful. He was a naked man in a small room with nowhere to put himself, and the second went on slightly too long.

"...Shar. Shar. Shar, listen..." He talked fast and low and reasonable, the way you talk to a dog that has got out.

She came up off the pillow. My pillow. Her mascara had gone. She went for the duvet and the duvet was on the floor, so her hand closed on nothing, and then she got a fistful of the bottom sheet and held it up against herself with both hands.

I looked at her for about as long as you would look at a bus timetable.

Then I turned and walked back down the hall, and from down there came the sound of a wardrobe.

"Sharon," she said, from the bed.

I came back into the hall with an armful of clothes. I was not crying and I was not hurrying. I was packing, and I was doing it properly, the way I do everything.

He was following me by then. He had got his jeans up off the floor and they were still inside out and he could not get his foot through, and he kept fighting the leg of them while he talked, hopping, and he would not stop talking.

"It is not, right, it is not what... look at me. Look at me. For fuck's sake, Shar, it is not even..." He said it to the back of my head and he kept saying it.

I went back into the room and around the bed, past both of them, and pulled a jumper out from under a pile of her things, and shook it out, and folded it.

"Please," she said. "Please just say something."

I did not.

On my way past the foot of the bed I looked down at the wet patch on the carpet. Two seconds. Then I stepped over it.

I took my own things. I took nothing of his. At the door there was a jacket on the hook that he had bought me, and I looked at it for one second and left it there.

"SHARON." It came out of him from the bedroom door, and it was the first honest sound he had made all night, because it was anger.

I picked the carrier bag back up off the hall floor on my way out.

I closed the door behind me. Quietly. It clicked.

And on the walkway, in the cold, I stood for a moment with the bag in one arm and my clothes in the other, and my face did not change at all.

Then I started walking.

People think that was the bit that broke me.

It wasn't. I'd already gone. That was just the first person to notice and not care.

I got a flat on my own that my mum and my grandad paid half of, and I never cried about him once.

I went out instead. Every weekend, for about four years. And if you'd asked me at the time I'd have told you I was having the time of my life.

5. The Party Years

Music, from underwater. A club toilet.

I was on the floor of a cubicle. Not unconscious. Somewhere adjacent to it. My cheek was on the tile and there was a pair of heels standing by my face and a voice above me saying my name in the bored way you say a name you have said before.

"Shar. Shar. Sharon. Get up. Shar," the voice said, flat with it, the way you say a name you have said a lot.

A hand under my arm.

And I got up.

And I fixed my hair in the mirror with wet hands, and I looked at myself, and I smiled at myself, and I went back out.

I wasn't the girl who couldn't handle it. I was the girl who got back up. There's a difference, and I was proud of it, which tells you everything.

A smoking area. Cold. Everyone in short sleeves pretending otherwise.

A lad I half knew held something out on his palm.

"Go on," he said, grinning, already looking past me for who else wanted some. "Fresh batch of Jenny."

I looked at it for about a second and a half.

I took it.

Everyone was on it that year. It was in every smoking area in Danim and nobody could tell you where it came from or why it was called that.

Later, the same night, I was against a wall with my eyes open, waiting for something.

And it arrived.

My pupils went. The music came up like somebody had pulled a blanket off the speakers, and the ugly strip-lit smoking area turned into somewhere else entirely.

I laughed. Once. At nothing.

And then it hit.

Inside, I was in the middle of the floor and I was not looking for anybody. Everything was on my skin. A pair of hands found my waist and I did not turn round to see whose they were.

My flat. The front door not properly shut. Lights off.

And this is not the cold part and it is not the sad part, and I am not going to skip it. It was the best night of my adult life.

Me on top of him, my back arched, my head right back, both his hands on me, and I was loud. Properly loud. Nothing performed in any of it.

I came hard enough that my arm went out for the headboard and took half the shelf off the wall with it, and neither of us stopped.

Somewhere underneath, the woman downstairs started banging on her ceiling with something.

I heard it. I laughed. I kept going.

I'm not going to sit here and lie to you. Best sex of my life. I felt every second of it.

Twenty quid.

In the morning he was gone, and the shelf was still on the floor where it landed with a picture face down next to it, and I looked at it from the bed.

I took it a few more times that year, when it was about. I never went looking for it. That's the bit I told myself made it fine.

I never asked what was in it. Not that night. Not the week after. Not for six years.

Three of them, and I can still put them in order, and nobody said anything in any of them.

One. An alley off a main road. Wheelie bins, a fire door, the bass coming through the wall from inside. Me face to the brick with both palms flat above my head, short dress up round my waist, underwear pulled down and left halfway down my thighs, heels not quite steady on the wet. Somebody behind me. I was looking at the wall. A taxi went past the mouth of the alley and neither of us stopped.

Two. A bathroom in somebody's house. The music coming up through the floor, all bass and no top end. Somebody knocking. Somebody had been knocking a while. Me sat up on the sink with my legs open round him and my heels still on, both arms wrapped round his head, holding him into my neck. The knocking again. I turned my head towards the door and did not stop.

Three. A girls' toilets in a club, seen from above. Down one side, a row of women at the mirrors, washing their hands, leaning in, doing their lips. The other side, one cubicle with the door shut. Inside it me, stood with my back flat against the partition and one leg up on the toilet seat, dress round my hips, and another girl knelt in front of me with her face between my legs and both hands on the back of my thighs. My head back against the wall and my eyes shut. At the mirror one of the women stopped. She had heard something. She found the cubicle in the reflection, and then she turned and looked at it properly, and she could not work out what she was looking at.

Boy, girl, it didn't matter. It was never about wanting anyone. It was about the four hours where I wasn't in the room.

Then a morning, in the good flat, the one I could not afford. My mum was standing in the middle of the front room with a carrier bag of shopping she had brought round, looking at the state of the place. A woman I did not know was on the sofa putting her shoes on.

I came out of the bathroom, saw her, and stopped.

My mother looked at me.

And said nothing about any of it.

"...I got you them yoghurts you like," she said, to the middle of the room, in the voice you use when you have decided not to have the argument.

She put the bag on the side. She squeezed my arm on the way past.

And she left.

I stood in the middle of my own front room and looked at a bag of yoghurts.

I wanted her to shout at me.

She brought me yoghurts.

6. Twelve Week Scan

The water is still running behind the bathroom door.

The flat as it is tonight: the coat over the back of a chair, the drive on the bed where she threw it. And on a shelf, in among the post and a dead plant and a charger with no phone on the end of it, a photograph in a frame that has never once been dusted.

Four women in a bar. All of them laughing. One of them holding a phone up.

Twelve week scan.

That's the last night the four of us were ever in a room together.

A table in a bar. Four of us. One holding a phone up with a photograph on it and the other three screaming.

"...twelve weeks, we didn't want to say anything until..." She could not get to the end of the sentence and she did not need to.

Delight. Hands over mouths. Somebody crying.

I was delighted too. I am very good at it.

I was also the only one on that table with a drink in front of me.

Later, the same bar, emptier. The same dress a year on. Me at the bar on my own with my back to the room and my drink in both hands, not looking at anything, checking the door every so often.

Nobody came.

The barman collected glasses around me.

They all grew up. One got pregnant, two got jobs with lanyards, and the group chat went quiet in about six weeks.

And I kept going out. On my own. In the same dress. Waiting for literally anyone to walk over.

A man arrived beside me. He was nothing. He was anyone.

"Alright?" he said, already half turned towards the bar, like it cost nothing either way.

I turned my head and looked at him for less than a second.

Then my bed, dark, me on top of him, riding him, both hands flat on his chest, looking over his shoulder at the wall.

They always did. That was never the problem.

And then the money went, because it does.

So I got a job.

7. Aisle Four

A supermarket. Fluorescent. The specific silence of a Tuesday afternoon.

"Cleaner to aisle four, please. Cleaner to aisle four."

Me, twenty-one, in a polo shirt with somebody else's name badge on it, wheeling a yellow mop bucket that did not steer.

Aisle four was a warzone. Four jars down, sauce and glass across two metres of floor, and a toddler in the middle of it with a fifth jar in both hands, deciding.

The mother was on her phone.

I got down on my knees in it. I picked the glass out first, with my fingers, one piece at a time, into a cloth.

The mother lowered the phone.

"Excuse me," she said, not moving. "Are you actually going to clean that, or..."

I looked up at her from the floor.

"Sorry," I said. "Won't be a minute."

And I went back to it.

The child dropped the fifth jar. It went everywhere. Some of it went on me, and the mother laughed the way people do when it is not their mess.

I did not look up again.

Six pound eighty an hour. My rent was more than that job was.

A back office, and my manager, a man in his forties with a lanyard and a clipboard, not looking at me.

"I need you to do the four til close Thursday and Friday," he said, without looking up, and it was not a question.

"...Yeah," I said. "No, that's fine."

And that is where I learned it. Not later. There.

I lasted seven months. Then I got behind a bar, which I thought was a step up, because it was nights and there was a staff discount.

A pub, busy, loud. Me, twenty-two, carrying two pints high through a crowd.

A hand went up my skirt.

I did not stop walking. I did not spill either pint. My face did one thing for a quarter of a second and then put itself away.

I set the drinks down on the right table and turned back through the crowd.

Behind the bar, the manager had watched the whole thing from six feet away.

He turned to the till.

Making a scene costs you the shift. Everyone learns that in about a fortnight.

There is a narrow stretch behind a bar, between the glass washer and the fridges, where two people cannot get past each other without touching.

I was bent over the low fridge, getting bottles out.

He came through behind me and put his whole hand on my arse, and left it there, and squeezed on the way past.

He did not break stride. He did not break sentence either. He was halfway through telling the other barman about a delivery and he finished it.

I straightened up with four bottles in my hands.

I put them on the counter.

I carried on.

Trevor. Fifty-eight. Wedding ring. He did that to every girl who worked that bar and not one of us ever said a word, because he did the rota.

Then it went quickly. A measure poured for a customer and a mouthful taken from the bottle. A vodka in a Coke glass under the counter. A hand shaking on a pump.

And then the floor of the pub, full, and him saying it to me in the middle of it, and not lowering his voice for anybody.

"You've been drinking on my till," he said. "Do you think I'm thick? Get your shit and get out."

Every head at the bar turned.

I took the apron off over my head. Folded it. Put it on the counter, squared to the edge.

And I walked out through all of them.

8. A Bloke in a Corsa

The water is still going. She has not moved.

And I won't sit here and tell you all of that was miserable, because it wasn't. That's the trouble with it.

I was twenty-three when it turned. And it wasn't a person, and it wasn't my brother, and it wasn't anything you'd put in a film.

It was a bloke in a Corsa who didn't know how a give way works.

Daylight. A car at a junction with L plates on it, and me in it, screaming.

"...NO, because it is MINE, mate, it is my junction, you came from a give way, THERE IS A FUCKING GIVE WAY THERE..."

The other driver was out of his car by then, arms out, doing the what-are-you-going-to-do-about-it walk. My driving instructor had both hands flat on the dashboard and the expression of a man reviewing his career.

"Sharon. Sharon." He had both hands up and was trying to get his voice under mine.

"HE CAME FROM A GIVE WAY," I said, straight through him, to the whole street.

That night I was still in my coat, on a laptop that took a long time to do anything, and I was reading. The room around me was a mess and I had not noticed it in an hour.

The Highway Code, section by section. I scrolled.

I found it.

I read it twice.

I sat back.

"...I was right," I said, to the ceiling, to nobody.

I stared at that ceiling for a second with an expression I would not want photographed.

Then I leaned forward and clicked the next section. And the next one.

That is genuinely how it happened. Not a calling. I wanted to win an argument with a man whose name I never found out, and there was a book that said I had.

I was still reading when it got light.

So I joined a university.

A lecture theatre, and me in the third row with sunglasses pushed up on my head and a bin bag complexion, and one page of notes with about nine words on it. Around me, people typing.

"...so if anyone would like to try and reconcile those two authorities for me. Anyone at all," the lecturer said, turning round from the board and pushing his glasses back up the bridge of his nose with one finger, waiting.

To study law.

Nothing.

I did not put my hand up. I just started talking, flat and bored, still looking down at the desk.

"You can't," I said. "One of them is about the duty and one of them is about the remedy. They're not in conflict, they're not even about the same thing, it's just that everyone cites them together because they were in the same textbook."

A pause. He looked at me for slightly too long.

"...Yes," he said, slowly, like a man revising his opinion of somebody in real time. "That is right."

The girl next to me turned and stared. I put my head back down on my arms.

I never got clean. I passed drunk.

There is a phone in a kitchen somewhere on loudspeaker on a table, my mother's voice too loud and delighted, an old man laughing in the background, an older woman saying put her on, put her on.

I could out-argue anybody in that building on four hours' sleep. So nobody ever made me build the other thing. The discipline. The bit underneath.

When it went, there was nothing under it.

Four years of it. I was twenty-seven when I finished.

9. The Cap

Outside a hall. Sunshine. A crowd of gowns.

The four of us again: my mum, my grandad, my nan, and me in the middle in the gown with the certificate.

Somebody counted us in.

I threw the cap.

It went up. Blue sky. It turned over once.

And a phone rang while it was still in the air.

I was still smiling when I reached into the gown for it with my other hand still up, laughing at something my nan had just said.

"Hello?"

The smile did not fall off my face. It stopped being connected to anything, which is worse.

"...Sorry, say that again." I said it lightly, still half in the noise of the crowd, one finger going into my other ear.

Behind me my mother had stopped smiling, because she was watching her daughter's back.

"No." Flat. Immediate. Not a refusal of the news. A refusal of the sentence.

I turned away from my family.

"No, no, it can't... no, because he was..." And I was arguing with it by then, building a case out of nothing, because that is what I do.

My hand went over my mouth and stayed there.

Somewhere behind me the cap came down and hit the grass, and nobody picked it up.

They told me.

That is the sentence I have used for seven years. They told me. I have never once, in seven years, asked myself who they were.

Winter, and a small turnout. Twelve people, maybe.

My mother was being held up on both sides. A boy of six in a black coat that was a size too big was holding my grandad's hand and looking at the hole with his mouth slightly open, because nobody had explained it to him in a way that worked.

I stood slightly apart.

Dry-eyed.

And I tried. I want that on the record, because I did try, for a second, and nothing came.

Two people from the family clocked that I was not crying, and looked at each other.

They noticed. Of course they noticed.

A glass-fronted office, a fortnight later. A partner in a good suit, being kind.

"Take the six weeks, Sharon," he said gently, both hands flat on the desk. "Take longer. It'll be here."

I was at my desk the following morning at ten past seven, first one in, coat still on.

The same desk, later, with nobody at it.

The same desk, later still, with somebody else's things on it.

I never used the degree again.

My nan went eighteen months after him.

That was a different funeral. Spring, a church, a proper turnout, people in hats, somebody laughing in the second row at a story about her.

I was at the back.

And this time it came out of me and I could not stop it, and I was furious about that, and I was holding onto the pew in front with both hands.

My nan. Ninety-one. In her own bed, in her sleep, in a house she owned, with the telly still on.

My mother reached over and put a hand on my back, and I let her, which I had not at the other one.

And I sat there in bits and I thought: oh.

So that's what it's supposed to feel like.

That's the one they let me have.

I went out that night. Same dress.

10. You're Making It Weird

Loud, and late, and I was at the bar on my own. Twenty-five. I was not dressed for it. I had come out because the alternative was the flat.

A man arrived at my shoulder. He was fine. He was nothing.

"Can I get you one?" he said, and he had clearly said it before, that night, to somebody else.

I looked at him for slightly less time than it takes to decide anything.

"Yeah."

Then the street, cold, the two of us walking, not touching, not talking. He was telling a story. I was not listening to it and he had not noticed.

My building.

I had the key in the lock.

And I stopped.

Something arrived in me, from a long way down, for the first time in years.

I turned round.

"...I don't think I want you to come in," I said, and it came out surprised, like I was hearing it at the same time he was.

Quiet. Not an argument. A fact I had just found out about myself.

His smile dropped for half a second.

And came back different.

"Ohh. Come on." Warm. Reasonable. A little bit hurt on my behalf. "I've come all the way over here. It's freezing. I'm not going to do anything."

I said nothing.

"Ten minutes. I'll have a glass of water and I'll go." A little laugh in it. And then, lighter, easier, the one that works. "You're making it weird."

And that is the one that did it. Not the charm. The last four words.

I turned the key.

11. The Ceiling

The door shut.

I am not going to take you into that room with us, because I did not stay in it either. I went where I always went, which was up.

My ceiling. Artexed, badly, by somebody in about 1988. A crack running from the light fitting towards the window that I had looked at a thousand times. A dead fly in the bowl of the shade, a little dark comma that had been up there for months.

The room moved. The light moved with it.

I was looking at the fly.

There was no music in my flat and there is none here either. There was the bed. The headboard finding the wall on a beat you could count, and I was counting it. His breath going in and out somewhere above my collarbone. One of my own arms folded up underneath me and going dead at the elbow, and I left it there.

My breath came out of me in small pushes, because it was being pushed. That was the only part of me moving on its own.

I let him in. I kissed him. I lifted my hips so it'd come off easier. I opened my legs and I waited.

The crack. The fly.

And then I stopped.

My eyes had been open and flat on that fly for a long time. They twitched.

A sound got out of me. Small. I did not authorise it.

It happened again.

My eyes opened wider.

Again.

Wider.

And my knees were going further apart and I had not told them to. My hips came up once, towards him, and I caught myself doing it, and it happened again anyway.

I was still looking at the ceiling. I was not looking at it the same way. I was holding onto it.

And there it is. The bit I've never said out loud.

He felt the change in me, all of it at once, how wet I had suddenly got, and he took it as his.

And that is what finished him.

He buried himself and let out one long satisfied noise somewhere above my ear.

And on my face, and only on my face:

No. No no no no no.

Not because he had finished.

Because I wanted him to keep going.

And the flat face came back. Exactly the same face I had before, and not the same at all, because before there was nothing underneath it and now there was.

I didn't want him. And when he stopped, I was angry with him for stopping.

Six years. That's still the one I can't file.

He did not get off me.

His whole weight came down, all of it, dead, and he was panting, and my ribs could not get all the way open underneath him.

I did not move him.

My arms came up and I put them around his back, both of them, and I held him, the way you hold somebody you are pleased to see.

And I did not stop looking at the ceiling.

He stayed inside me until he had gone soft. It took a while. Long enough for me to work out that he was not waiting by accident.

Then he pulled out of me slowly, taking his time about it, like a man being considerate.

I made no sound at all.

I did not move afterwards. I stayed in the shape he left me in, one arm still dead underneath me, looking up.

He was dressing. I saw as much of it as I wanted to, which was the edge of the room and out of focus, a shape doing a belt.

He was in no hurry. He had a look round while he did it, the way you check a hotel before you hand the key back.

"You alright?" he said, to the room, doing his belt.

Nothing.

"You're quiet, you," he said, amused by it.

Nothing.

"...Was alright though, weren't it."

It was not a question. None of them were. He was already looking for his other shoe.

"Nah, cos you were proper into it at the end there," he said, and he was smiling when he said it.

And there it was on his face. He was pleased with himself. He thought the quiet was him.

I saw all of it. I gave him nothing.

He asked me four things on the way out and not one of them had a question in it.

Footsteps. My kitchen tap running for two seconds and going off again, because he had helped himself to a glass of water.

The front door. It did not even slam. It closed the way a door closes when somebody has had a normal evening.

Silence in the flat.

I lay there long enough that anybody watching would have wanted me to get up.

Then I moved, and not to get up.

I tightened everything I had and held it, hard, because I could feel him about to come out of me and there was one set of sheets in that flat and I was lying on them.

I got my hand down between my legs and held it there.

And I got off the bed like that, bent over, one hand between my legs and the other flat on the mattress, and I crossed my own bedroom and went into the bathroom.

I did not put the light on.

At the sink I took my hand away and turned it over.

My palm and my fingers were covered in him.

I looked at it.

My face still had nothing on it.

12. The Cabinet

I washed my hands first. Both of them, at the sink, in the dark, for longer than washing hands takes.

Then I reached past the curtain and put the shower on, and sat down on the closed lid of the toilet, still dressed, and waited for the water to get hot enough.

Too hot. Much too hot. My skin came up red and blotched across the chest and shoulders and I stood straight into it and did not flinch.

I was not washing.

Then I started washing, and I did it hard, with the flannel, in one place, for a long time.

And down at the drain, water going round it and going down it, and going down with it, a thin white thread of him coming off me.

I watched it go.

I keep waiting for the bit where I feel something about it.

It never came. Not that night. Not the week after. Nothing. That frightened me more than he did.

The mirror was steamed over. I wiped an oval in it with the side of my fist and there I was.

I opened it.

Inside: a strip of birth control, a box of paracetamol, a box of something to sleep. That was the entire contents of that cabinet. There was nothing in there for a person who was planning anything.

I popped one out of the strip and took it with water from the tap, and it was not a moment, and it took four seconds, and I had done it a thousand times.

I shut the cabinet.

The mirror came back and I was in it, towel round me, hair flat, the red already going out of my skin.

I looked at myself for a while.

I got up, and I had a shower, and I took a pill, and I went to work.

She has been in there a long time now. The water has started to go cold at the edges and she has not turned it up.

Her hand is flat on the tile. Her head is down.

She is not crying.

Right.

I got up at seven the next morning, same as I did every morning.

Daylight through the curtains.

I stripped the bed. I did it properly. Corners, pillowcases, the lot, into the machine.

I showered again.

I put on the clothes for the job I was not going to keep.

I picked up my phone. Contacts. My thumb went down the list.

MUM.

I looked at it.

I put the phone in my pocket.

And I went to work.

I never told anyone.

On the wall by the door, in a cheap clip frame my mother bought, was a law degree with my name on it.

I could argue anything. With anyone.

I could not tell you why I let him in. Maybe I just wanted to feel something. Anything.

Then, weeks later, on one night.

13. How Hard Can It Be

There was no music in my flat that night and there was none in what came after it either. There was room tone, and the telly, and the extractor fan still labouring away in the bathroom.

I was on the floor with my back against the sofa, a towel round me and another one in my hands, drying my hair. The telly was on because the telly was on.

My face was the flat one. Not sad. Not anything. I was watching it the way you watch a bus go past.

"...found no misconduct on the part of any officer involved, although the family have described the outcome as, and I quote, an insult to his memory..." the newsreader was saying.

I kept drying my hair.

I swapped hands.

"...figures out this morning put stop and search in the borough up thirty-one per cent, with the force again declining to publish a breakdown by..."

I reached sideways without looking, missed, got the moisturiser on the second go, and started doing my arms.

Nothing on my face. Not agreement, not anger, nothing. It was furniture.

The programme changed. It became one of the ones shot off a dashboard, blue light washing the inside of a car.

"...he's coming back towards us, he's coming back towards..." an officer said over a radio.

"He's getting away! HE'S GETTING AWAY!"

I rolled my eyes.

It was the first thing my face had done in about ninety seconds.

I went back to my legs with the towel.

"...pursued for around four miles before officers made the decision to stand down on safety grounds. The occupants have not been traced. A spokesperson said the force's priority remains public safety..."

And my hands slowed down in the towel.

I looked at the screen properly for the first time all night.

"...You don't know how to do your job."

I said it to a television, quietly, with total contempt.

And then I said the other thing.

"Maybe if you did, people like Jaden wouldn't die."

And I sat with that.

Then I got up to turn it off.

And I caught myself in the glass. Not a mirror. The glass of the clip frame on the wall. My own face, sitting on top of my own name, on top of a degree I had not opened a book for in months.

I stopped.

I looked at it for a long time.

"...How hard can it be?"

I dropped the towel on the bed on my way past and went into the bathroom with nothing on.

It was still steamy in there from earlier. The mirror was fogged at the edges and clear in the middle where I had wiped it hours before.

I reached for my toothbrush. It was on the window ledge, next to the toothpaste.

And I caught myself in the mirror, and my hand stopped halfway.

I looked at myself.

A long time. The fan. Somebody else's telly through the wall.

"...How hard can it be."

Not a question that time.

Then my right hand came up. Index finger out. Thumb up.

Slowly. All the way, until it was pointed at my own face.

I held it there.

I put it down.

I did it again. Quicker.

Down.

Again, and that time it was fast, and it was nearly good.

Down.

I stood there and looked at myself.

Then I reached past my own reflection and took the toothbrush in one hand and the toothpaste in the other, and I looked down at the two of them, and at the sink.

And I dropped the toothpaste.

It went in the basin.

Both hands snapped up round the toothbrush, straight out at the mirror, arms locked, one eye shut, the whole thing.

"Freeze."

Nothing moved.

A naked woman on her own in a small steamy bathroom at night, aiming a toothbrush at herself in a mirror, holding it, and not laughing.

14. Uniform

It went quickly, and it took years, because both of those are true.

A form on a kitchen table, filled in with a biro that stopped working halfway. A gym hall, a row of us in identical black, being shouted at. A locker with SHARON YOUNG on a strip of tape.

Night, rain, a shoplifter face down on a wet pavement and my knee in his back and my voice completely level. A domestic, and a woman in a doorway saying nothing while I wrote. Paperwork. A lot of paperwork. Fluorescent light. Four in the morning. A canteen. More paperwork.

I was good at it almost straight away.

Not because I'm a nice person. Because I could out-argue anyone in that building, and because there was nothing left anybody could say to me that would land.

Then a corridor with better carpet, and a door with a small brass plate on it.

SUPERINTENDENT T. LUCAS.

I was in uniform. Twenty-eight. I knocked.

"Come." One word, through the door, from a man who has never had to say it twice.

Inside: books nobody has read, a window with a view of a car park, and a man in his fifties behind a desk. Big. Properly overweight. A good suit that had been let out and a shirt working hard at the buttons. He did not look like a monster, because he was not one. He was something much more ordinary than that.

There was a personnel file open on the desk in front of him. It stayed open for the whole time I was in that room and I never once looked down at it. I was looking at him, and then at the door.

"Sit down, Sharon." He did not get up. "Do you want a coffee? It's terrible."

"I'm alright, sir."

He turned a page.

"Your annual. And your training file. And two things from the borough that I asked for myself, which I do not do." He looked up. "You are the best natural investigator to come through this building in about fifteen years."

I did not know what to do with that. Nobody had said anything like it to me since I was nineteen.

"You see between things," he said, and he said it like a man reading out a measurement. "It's not something we can teach and it is not something most of them will ever have. You hold detail. You had that Kemp statement in your head three weeks after you took it, and you were right about it, and a DS with nine years on you was wrong."

"...Thank you, sir."

And I meant it. That is the part I would take back if I could take one part back.

He closed the file. Not all the way. Just enough.

"So. You want CID."

"Yes, sir."

"Four years. Two in uniform, two on the programme, and that is if nothing goes wrong and nobody takes a dislike to you."

"I know, sir."

He nodded slowly, like a man being asked to explain the weather.

"Let me tell you something about this force, and I am not being unkind, I am being accurate, because I think you have earned accurate." He sat back. "No woman climbs the ranks here. Not on merit. Not on results. I have been here twenty-six years and I have watched it not happen to better officers than you."

Silence.

He did not leer. He did not lean forward. He did not threaten me. He looked mildly regretful, the way you look when you deliver a policy you did not write.

"So the question is only ever how much you want it," he said, pleasantly, the way you would say it about a mortgage.

And he let it sit there.

He did not ask me for anything. He had not, technically, said a single word he could not have repeated in a room full of people.

I looked at the door.

I looked at the desk. Not at the file on it. At the desk.

And I thought about it. I want that in, because I did think about it, and I was not overwhelmed and I was not panicking. I was pricing it, the way I price everything.

And then it was decided.

I got up.

And I did not go to the door.

I came round the side of the desk and I stood over him. Twenty-eight, uniform pressed, back straight, and my face was the flattest thing in that building. Underneath me, filling a chair that was not big enough for him, a fat man in his fifties with a good haircut and a pen still in his hand, smiling up at me, entirely at ease, because nothing about his own body had ever embarrassed him.

And then I went down.

The man in the chair did not move. A belt buckle came undone, unhurried, because nobody was in a rush.

The pleasant smile was still there.

And then it changed. It did not become a leer. It became something quieter and worse: the face of a man who has just been proved right about the world.

15. The Tap

A station toilet. Strip light, one of them flickering. Running water, the extractor, and a corridor somewhere behind the door.

I was at the sink with the tap on, looking at myself the way you look at yourself when there is nobody else in the building.

I cupped water and rinsed my mouth. Spat. Did it again.

He tasted bad.

I did it a third time and held it longer.

I wiped the corner of my mouth with the side of my thumb and checked the thumb.

My lipstick was gone off one side of my mouth and still there on the other.

I lifted the collar of my own shirt and smelled it.

And what is that smell.

I looked down at myself.

I brushed at the knees of my uniform trousers. Twice.

There was nothing on them.

I straightened up. I swallowed and it went down wrong and I pulled a face at myself.

Then I stopped.

I put two fingers into my mouth, right to the back, and hooked at something.

I could not get it.

I tried again and gagged, quietly, and steadied myself on the edge of the sink with my other hand.

Third go.

And I got it, and brought it out on the end of my finger.

One hair. Not mine.

I looked at it for a long time.

Then I put my hand under the tap and washed it off and watched it go round and go down.

A cubicle door opened behind me.

She had been in there the whole time.

A woman in her forties. Plain clothes, lanyard, the face of somebody who had been on shift for eleven hours. She came to the next sink and put her hands under the water.

She did not look at me.

She looked at my reflection.

One flick of the eyes. Down and up. The knees. The mouth. The hair at the front, flattened on one side.

Then back to her own hands, and she washed them properly, and she said absolutely nothing at all.

I turned my tap off.

I dried my hands. I squared my shoulders in the glass, once, the way you do before a room.

And I went.

The door swung shut behind her.

The woman was still at the sink with the water running over her hands.

She was not washing them any more.

She was watching the door in the mirror.

Upstairs, on a desk, a hand closed a file.

A warrant card in a plastic wallet.

DETECTIVE CONSTABLE S. YOUNG.

I walked through the office with it in my hand and my chin up.

Two officers watched me go past. One of them said something to the other. I did not hear it.

The other one laughed.

It worked.

That's the bit nobody warns you about. It worked.

16. The Donut

Cold water now, properly cold, and she is standing straight in it.

Three years in. Plain clothes by then, and a caseload, and a shoulder number people had started to remember.

And this is the one I still can't file.

Night. A parade of shops, most of them shuttered.

I came out of a place with a paper bag and a coffee, in plain clothes by then, and I took a bite and then stopped chewing and looked at the thing in my hand with genuine self-disgust.

"...Oh, you're joking."

A detective. Eating a donut. At night. In a car park.

I shook my head at myself.

And then I stopped.

Because down the side of the building, in the gap between the shops, there were two people in black having an argument they did not want anybody to hear.

I put the donut down on the roof of the car.

I moved along the wall.

Two figures. Hoods, dark clothes, the tops of their faces covered. One of them had the other by the front of his coat.

"...I'm not asking you again, you get me?" He had him by the front of the coat and he was close enough to be quiet about it.

"Bruv..."

"I will nank you, bruv. In front of your mum, in front of your fucking dog, I do not care."

I drew.

I came round the corner in a proper stance, both hands on it, and it was textbook, and my voice was clear and level and exactly right.

"Armed police! Show me your hands! Do not move!"

The two of them turned and looked at me.

And then one of them started laughing. Genuinely. Delightedly. He had to put a hand on the wall.

"...Girl said freeze, yano!"

"She never said freeze."

"She said don't move, same ting." He wiped his eye. "Or else what, darlin'? You gonna arrest us? Fuck off, man."

I did not lower the weapon.

I had done everything right. Everything. The stance, the words, the distance.

And it had bought me nothing at all, and it had taken about four seconds to find that out.

Then the laughing stopped.

Not because of me. Because both of them were looking past my shoulder.

The change on their faces was total.

I did not turn round.

"Move."

One syllable, from behind me, low.

And my body did it before my mind agreed to. I stepped aside. I have no memory of deciding to.

He walked past me.

I did not get his face.

He did not look at me.

"Run along." Still not looking at me. "You don't belong here."

And because I am who I am, I brought the weapon back up.

"Sir, put your hands..." My voice had gone somewhere I could not get it back from.

I did not finish it.

Not because I was interrupted. Because the gun was no longer in my hands.

He had it. He was holding it the way you hold something you have been asked to look after.

And then his hand closed.

The sound was wrong. Metal is not supposed to make that sound.

He opened his hand and let the pieces go and they hit the ground like change.

My hand went to my radio.

It was not there.

He was holding it. He had been holding it since before I reached for it.

He crushed that too, in the same movement, without looking at it, and dropped it.

He had not touched me once.

"Go home," he said, and there was nothing in it. Not a threat. Not even much interest.

17. There Isn't a Word For It

Running. My own breath. Shoes on wet pavement.

I got my phone out at a corner and I was dialling before I had stopped.

"This is Detective Constable Sharon Young, shoulder number four-one-nine-two, I need urgent assistance at the rear of the parade on..."

"...there's a, there's something..."

And I heard the wobble in my own voice on the word.

I heard it.

"...I mean someone. There's someone."

The line was asking me a question.

I looked at the phone.

I hung up.

And I stood in the street with my hand over my mouth.

Then I went back.

The alley was empty. No ninjas. No man. No sound but a fan unit somewhere.

I walked in slowly, and I was nearly hoping it would not be there.

It was there.

The pieces of my firearm on the wet ground, and the pieces of my radio next to them, in a spread about a metre across.

I crouched.

I picked a piece of it up and turned it over in my fingers.

The metal was folded. Not broken. Folded, like paper.

"...How?"

Nobody answered me.

They put me in an interview room and used it as an office. A colleague across the table with a pen he was barely moving.

On the table between us, sealed in a clear exhibit bag, was what was left of my firearm. I had bagged it, sealed it, signed the label and booked it in, all of it correctly, because I do everything correctly.

He did not touch it once.

"So you're telling me a bloke appeared out of nowhere..."

"I'm telling you what happened."

"...took your firearm off you, and crushed it. With his hand."

"Yes."

"And your radio."

"Yes."

He looked up.

"And then what? He just, what, disappeared into thin fucking air?"

And I opened my mouth to answer.

And heard exactly how it was going to sound before it came out.

I stood up. The chair went over behind me.

"Forget it."

And I was out of the door.

The colleague looked at the fallen chair. He picked his pen back up, wrote one short line, and closed the book.

An exhibit label, filled in in her handwriting. SY/1.

A ballistics report, weeks later. Two lines of it.

DAMAGE CONSISTENT WITH MECHANICAL COMPRESSION. MOST PROBABLE CAUSE VEHICULAR.

A property store. Shelf after shelf of bags. One of them says SY/1.

Nobody ever called me about it again.

Outside, in the car park, with the rain starting, I stood with both hands on the roof of my car and my head down.

I was shaking. Not from fear.

I looked up.

"There isn't a word for it," I said, out loud, in a car park, in the rain, to nobody at all.

"That's the whole problem. There's no word for it, so there's no box for it, so there's no form for it."

"So it didn't happen."

I got in the car.

I sat there with the keys in my hand and did not put them in.

"...So I'll find one."

And I started the engine.

18. Twenty Past Two

The shower shuts off. Silence, and the drip of it, and the extractor fan labouring.

Sharon steps out into the steam, gets a towel, and stands there for a second with her eyes shut.

She comes out into the front room in a t-shirt and her underwear, hair wet, and stops.

The drive is exactly where she threw it on the bed.

Ten past two in the morning.

Something is cooking that she is not watching. She is eating out of the pan with a fork, standing up.

The telly is on and it is not television. It is the CCTV off the stolen drive, running at half speed, and she has been through it enough times to know the frame numbers.

What are you.

On the screen: the wrecked corridor. The impossible blur. The wall coming apart.

She rewinds it. Watches it again. Rewinds it again.

Right. The wall. That's a charge. Plastic, PE4, something like that, on a timer, and the blur is the frame rate.

She nods at her own telly, satisfied, for about a second and a half.

Then she rewinds it again.

...There's no flash.

She points the fork at the screen.

And how did he get up there. Fifth floor. The lifts were off, the stairwell is covered, and he is not on it.

She squints at it, chewing.

So he came in the window. He came in the window from... from where. From what.

She stops chewing.

She leans in.

She does not finish the sentence.

And in shot behind her, unremarked, nobody looking at it:

BIO GENETIX.

EVERYTHING YOU ARE. ONLY BETTER.

She freezes the frame.

A hand, mid-movement, on the edge of a window frame. Pixelated to almost nothing.

She leans forward.

She gets closer.

And then she puts the pan down and gets down onto the floor, on her hands and knees, and crawls across her own living room carpet until her face is about eight inches from the screen.

She tilts her head.

On the wrist, in about nine pixels: a mark. Small. Raised. Old.

She does not know what she is looking at.

She reaches up without looking, finds a pen, and writes something on the back of her own hand.

And the phone goes.

It is on the arm of the sofa, face down, buzzing itself round in a half circle.

She does not want to move. She is eight inches from the answer to something.

It keeps going.

She reaches back for it without taking her eyes off the screen.

She looks at the screen of the phone.

MUM.

Twenty past two in the morning.

And that is when she takes her eyes off the television.

She sits back on her heels.

"...Mum?" she says, still on her heels on the carpet.

And on the other end it arrives before it can be understood: her mother, trying to keep her voice reasonable and failing at it inside the first four words.

"Sharon. Sharon, I'm sorry, I know what time it is..."

"What's happened."

"It's Kevin."

Sharon is already standing up.

"He come in and he's not right. He's not right, Sharon." It is coming out of her in one go now. "He's not saying nothing and he won't let me look at him and he's just sat in the dark on the floor of his room and he's..."

A breath on the line.

"...I didn't know who else to ring," her mother says, and that is the sentence that does it.

And Sharon stands in the middle of her flat, at twenty past two in the morning, with the frozen frame of a man she cannot explain still glowing on the wall behind her.

"...I'm on my way."

She is already reaching for her keys.

And then the room leaves her. It turns away from her and goes to the wall, to the frozen frame on the screen, and it starts to move in on it. Slowly. It does not stop.

A wrecked office floor with the dust still hanging where the picture stopped it. A hole where a wall was. And sat up on the window frame with one foot on the sill and the whole white sky of Danim behind him, a man in a dark cloak, already half out of the building.

He is not looking down at the street.

He is looking back into the room.

You cannot see his face. You have never once been able to see his face.

Behind, off in the flat somewhere, a drawer goes. A coat comes off a hook. Keys. Feet. And the front door pulled shut hard enough to shake the frame she is walking away from.

And music, for the first time in a long time. It comes up under the push and it builds.

The frame gets bigger and softer and dirtier as it comes on, until it is not a picture of a man any more, it is grain.

And on the wrist of the hand holding the window frame, nine pixels of something old, filling the screen.

END OF EPISODE 3
