"How Hard Can It Be"

DRAFT IN PROGRESS

Episode 3 is narrated by Sharon. First person, her voice, looking back from now. SHARON (V.O.) is that retrospective narration and is never heard in the room. SHARON (THOUGHT) is what she is thinking in the moment of the scene. SHARON is spoken aloud.

Built from the outline in this folder. Canon references: Sharon is a Detective Constable about three years in; DS Nelson is one rank above her; Superintendent Teddy Lucas; DI Marcia Boateng. No American ranks. Nobody is named in narration before somebody says it aloud.

COLD OPEN: THE DRIVE

Black.

A key in a lock. Three tries. The third one takes.

A door opens onto an unlit flat and stays open a second too long, because the woman in the doorway has stopped.

Sharon. Still in yesterday's coat. There is brick dust on one shoulder and a long grey smear down her forearm that she has not noticed yet.

She shuts the door with her heel.

She crosses the room without turning on a light and takes something out of her inside pocket: a disk drive, matte and ugly, the size of a paperback.

She looks at it.

Then she tosses it onto the bed the way you throw keys into a bowl, and it lands heavier than it should, and the mattress takes a second longer than it ought to about it.

She looks at that too.

SHARON:
"...Yeah."

She does not touch it again for the rest of the night.

THE OFFICE

Daylight. A borough station. Strip lighting, a photocopier eating itself somewhere off screen, a room of detectives who have all found something else to look at.

A door is open. Behind it, a man in shirtsleeves is on his feet, and he has been on his feet for a while.

CHIEF SUPERINTENDENT (O.S.):
"...I have got the borough commander, I have got the press office, and I have got a fucking hole in a building the size of a bus. Do not tell me what we do not know. Tell me who is running it."

A pause.

DS NELSON:
"Sir, with respect, that is a PIP 3. That is a DCI job, minimum..."

CHIEF SUPERINTENDENT (O.S.):
"Then find me a DCI who wants it."

Silence in the outer office. Nobody moves. It is the specific silence of a room full of people not volunteering.

Sharon is at her desk with a coffee she has not opened. She is not part of this. She is filling in a form.

CHIEF SUPERINTENDENT (O.S.):
"...Young."

She looks up.

Every head in the room turns to her, then away.

CHIEF SUPERINTENDENT:
"Sharon. You are lead on this. Get me something by six."

He is already walking. He is not looking at her while he says it and he does not look at her after.

A door shuts.

Sharon has not said a word. The pen is still in her hand.

Nelson, from two desks away, quietly, to the man beside him, not quite quietly enough:

DS NELSON:
"...Three years."

Somebody laughs through their nose.

Sharon looks at the form in front of her. She puts the pen down. She picks it back up.

She carries on filling it in.

THE SHOWER

Night again. The flat.

Water. Too hot, from the sound of it.

Steam builds against the glass and comes off the top of the cubicle in a slow roll, and the small room disappears into it a piece at a time.

Sharon stands under it with her head down and her hands flat against the tiles and lets it hit the back of her neck.

She is not washing.

She closes her eyes.

The steam finds the mirror and takes the room out of it, and then it takes her out of it, until there is a shape in the glass where a woman used to be.

SHARON (V.O.):
"It wasn't always like this."

A long beat.

SHARON (V.O.):
"...I wasn't always like this."

THE SPINE

The following plays over images. Her voice is flat, level and cold. It is not a confession. It is a summary, and she has given it to herself many times.

SHARON (V.O.):
"My name is Sharon Young."

A woman in a dorm room at a desk at two in the morning, hair scraped back, one lamp on, books open in a semicircle around her like a wall she is building.

SHARON (V.O.):
"Six years ago I walked into a police station."

A locker. A stab vest going on over a white shirt. Hands doing the straps without looking.

SHARON (V.O.):
"Before that I worked my arse off to get out of the bullshit and earn a law degree."

A hand holding a rolled certificate. The hand is shaking very slightly and the woman it belongs to is grinning like an idiot.

SHARON (V.O.):
"Made my mum proud. Made my grandparents proud."

A photograph being taken. Four people squeezed into frame outside a hall: a young woman in a gown, her mother crying and pretending not to, an old man in the only suit he owns, and an older woman between them holding onto the girl's arm with both hands.

The shutter goes. The image holds one beat longer than it needs to.

SHARON (V.O.):
"I never knew my father. None of us did."

It goes past. Nothing lands on it. The next image is already arriving.

SHARON (V.O.):
"And none of it mattered."

A phone, face down on a kitchen counter, buzzing.

SHARON (V.O.):
"Not after that night."

Black.

THE FLAT. NOW.

Steam. Her forehead against the tile, eyes shut, the water on the back of her neck. She has not moved since we left her.

SHARON (V.O.):
"I keep starting in the same place."

The steam has taken the room out of the mirror.

SHARON (V.O.):
"A flat I lived in when I was nineteen, and a pair of shoes in the hall that weren't mine."

NINETEEN

Caption or not, Bupe's call. If a caption is used it is the only one in the episode.

A walkway four floors up. A young woman comes up the stairs two at a time with a carrier bag in one hand and her keys already out. Nineteen. Cheaper coat, better mood, a face that has not yet learned to stay still. There is a bottle of wine in the bag and it is Friday and she has done the shop on the way home.

She lets herself in.

The hall. His coat is on the floor, which is normal. A woman's coat is on the floor on top of his, which is not.

And a pair of shoes.

Close on them. White, both of them kicked off at angles, one on its side, the inside heel scuffed grey the way it always is.

Sharon has watched those shoes come off in this hallway maybe two hundred times.

We stay on her face, and we let the rest of it arrive. It arrives from the bedroom and it arrives as sound before it arrives as anything else. Neither of them is being quiet. There is no reason for either of them to be quiet. There is nobody in the world who is supposed to be able to hear it.

She puts the carrier bag down on the floor. Carefully. The bottle does not clink.

She does not call out.

The bedroom door is open. She walks down her own hall and stops in it.

Her room. Her bed.

Her best friend is bent over the foot of it, face down and turned away, both hands gripping Sharon's duvet, and her eyes are shut, so she is the last one in the room to know.

He is behind her, standing, one hand flat between her shoulder blades holding her there.

The duvet is half off the bed and pooled on the carpet. His jeans are on the floor inside out with one leg still holding the shape of his leg. There is a foil wrapper by the skirting board and no condom anywhere in the shot. There is a wet patch on the beige carpet at the foot of the bed, dark, about the size of a saucer, and a glass on its side beside it, and the red gone into the pile and never coming out of it.

The whole room smells of them.

This is her room. She painted it.

We stay on her face.

She is not shocked. That is the thing to play and it has to be played all the way. She is taking it in properly, item by item, the way you read a bill: her sheets. Her pillow. Her friend's hair on it. The wrapper. The wine in the carpet.

Her jaw moves once.

He sees her.

He comes off the girl fast and stands up straight in the middle of Sharon's bedroom with nothing on, still hard, going soft, one hand held out towards Sharon the way you would put a hand out to a horse. There is one full second where he is not frightening and not even shameful. He is just a naked man in a small room with nowhere to put himself, and the camera should let it be exactly that stupid, and hold it slightly too long.

BOYFRIEND:
"...Shar. Shar. Shar, listen..."

The girl comes up off the pillow. Sharon's pillow. Her mascara has gone. She goes for the duvet and the duvet is on the floor, so her hand closes on nothing, and then she gets a fistful of the bottom sheet and holds it up against herself with both hands.

Sharon looks at her for about as long as you would look at a bus timetable.

Then she turns and walks back down the hall, out of frame.

Sound of a wardrobe.

BEST FRIEND (O.S.):
"Sharon..."

Sharon comes back into frame in the hall with an armful of clothes. She is not crying and she is not hurrying. She is packing, and she is doing it properly, the way she does everything.

The boyfriend is following her now. He has got his jeans off the floor and they are still inside out and he cannot get his foot through, and he keeps fighting the leg of them while he talks, hopping, and he will not stop talking.

BOYFRIEND:
"It is not, right, it is not what... look at me. Look at me. For fuck's sake, Shar, it is not even..."

She goes back into the room and around the bed, past both of them, and pulls a jumper out from under a pile of the other woman's things, and shakes it out, and folds it.

BEST FRIEND:
"Please. Please just say something."

She does not.

On her way past the foot of the bed she looks down at the wet patch on the carpet. Two seconds. Then she steps over it.

She takes her own things. She takes nothing of his. At the door there is a jacket on the hook that he bought her and she looks at it for one second and leaves it there.

BOYFRIEND (O.S.):
"SHARON."

She picks the carrier bag back up off the hall floor on her way out.

She closes the door behind her. Quietly. It clicks.

And on the walkway, in the cold, she stands for a moment with the bag in one arm and her clothes in the other, and her face does not change at all, and that is the point.

SHARON (V.O.):
"People think that was the bit that broke me."

She starts walking.

SHARON (V.O.):
"It wasn't. I'd already gone. That was just the first person to notice and not care."

Beat.

SHARON (V.O.):
"I got a flat on my own that my mum and my grandad paid half of, and I never cried about him once."

Beat.

SHARON (V.O.):
"I went out instead. Every weekend, for about four years. And if you'd asked me at the time I'd have told you I was having the time of my life."

THE PARTY YEARS

Music, from underwater. A club toilet.

Sharon on the floor of a cubicle. Not unconscious. Somewhere adjacent to it. Her cheek is on the tile and there is a pair of heels standing by her face and a voice above her saying her name in the bored way you say a name you have said before.

FRIEND (O.S.):
"Shar. Shar. Sharon. Get up. Shar."

A hand under her arm.

And she gets up.

And she fixes her hair in the mirror with wet hands, and she looks at herself, and she smiles at herself, and she goes back out.

SHARON (V.O.):
"I wasn't the girl who couldn't handle it. I was the girl who got back up. There's a difference, and I was proud of it, which tells you everything."

A smoking area. Cold. Everyone in short sleeves pretending otherwise.

A lad she half knows holds something out on his palm.

LAD:
"Go on. Fresh batch of Jenny."

She looks at it for about a second and a half.

She takes it.

SHARON (V.O.):
"Everyone was on it that year. It was in every smoking area in Danim and nobody could tell you where it came from or why it was called that."

Later. Same night. She is against a wall with her eyes open, waiting for something.

And it arrives.

Close on her face. Her pupils go. The music comes up like somebody has pulled a blanket off the speakers, and the ugly strip-lit smoking area turns into somewhere else entirely.

She laughs. Once. At nothing.

SHARON (V.O.):
"And then it hit."

Inside. She is in the middle of the floor and she is not looking for anybody. Everything is on her skin. A pair of hands finds her waist and she does not turn round to see whose they are.

Cut.

Her flat. The front door not properly shut. Lights off.

And this one is not cold and it is not sad and we do not cut away from it. It is the best night of her adult life and it has to look like it.

Her on top of him. Her back arched, her head right back, both his hands on her, and she is loud. Properly loud. Nothing performed in any of it.

She comes hard enough that her arm goes out for the headboard and takes half the shelf off the wall with it, and neither of them stops.

Somewhere underneath, the woman downstairs starts banging on her ceiling with something.

Sharon hears it. Laughs. Keeps going.

SHARON (V.O.):
"I'm not going to sit here and lie to you. Best sex of my life. I felt every second of it."

Beat.

SHARON (V.O.):
"Twenty quid."

Morning. Him gone. The shelf still on the floor where it landed and a picture face down next to it.

She looks at it from the bed.

SHARON (V.O.):
"I took it a few more times that year, when it was about. I never went looking for it. That's the bit I told myself made it fine."

Beat.

SHARON (V.O.):
"I never asked what was in it. Not that night. Not the week after. Not for six years."

Three shots. No music. Nobody says anything in any of them.

One. An alley off a main road. Wheelie bins, a fire door, the bass coming through the wall from inside. Sharon face to the brick with both palms flat above her head, short dress up round her waist, underwear pulled down and left halfway down her thighs, heels not quite steady on the wet. Somebody behind her. She is looking at the wall. A taxi goes past the mouth of the alley and neither of them stops.

Two. A bathroom in somebody's house. The music is coming up through the floor, all bass and no top end. Somebody is knocking. Somebody has been knocking a while. Sharon is sat up on the sink with her legs open round him and her heels still on, both arms wrapped round his head, holding him into her neck. The knocking again. She turns her head towards the door and does not stop.

Three. Birds eye. A girls' toilets in a club. Down one side, a row of women at the mirrors, washing their hands, leaning in, doing their lips. The other side, one cubicle with the door shut. Inside it Sharon is stood with her back flat against the partition and one leg up on the toilet seat, dress round her hips, and another girl is knelt in front of her with her face between her legs and both hands on the back of Sharon's thighs. Sharon's head is back against the wall and her eyes are shut. At the mirror one of the women stops. She has heard something. She finds the cubicle in the reflection, and then she turns and looks at it properly, and she cannot work out what she is looking at.

SHARON (V.O.):
"Boy, girl, it didn't matter. It was never about wanting anyone. It was about the four hours where I wasn't in the room."

Morning. Her flat, the good one, the one she could not afford. Her mother is in it, standing in the middle of the front room with a carrier bag of shopping she has brought round, looking at the state of the place.

A woman on the sofa Sharon does not know is putting her shoes on.

Sharon comes out of the bathroom, sees her mum, and stops.

Her mother looks at her.

And says nothing about any of it.

IVY:
"...I got you them yoghurts you like."

She puts the bag on the side. She squeezes Sharon's arm on the way past.

And she leaves.

Sharon stands in the middle of her own front room and looks at a bag of yoghurts.

SHARON (V.O.):
"I wanted her to shout at me."

Beat.

SHARON (V.O.):
"She brought me yoghurts."

THE FLAT. NOW.

The water still running behind the bathroom door. The camera leaves her in it and goes out into the front room on its own.

The flat as it is tonight. The coat over the back of a chair. The drive on the bed where she threw it.

And on a shelf, in among the post and a dead plant and a charger with no phone on the end of it, a photograph in a frame that has never once been dusted.

Four women in a bar. All of them laughing. One of them is holding a phone up.

SHARON (V.O.):
"Twelve week scan."

Push in on it until the photograph is the whole frame.

SHARON (V.O.):
"That's the last night the four of us were ever in a room together."

THE NIGHTS EMPTY OUT

A table in a bar. Four women. One of them is holding a phone up with a photograph on it and the other three are screaming.

FRIEND:
"...twelve weeks, we didn't want to say anything until..."

Delight. Hands over mouths. Somebody crying.

Sharon is delighted too. She is very good at it.

Wide: she is the only one on the table with a drink in front of her.

Later. Same bar. Emptier.

Same dress, a year on. She is on her own at the bar with her back to the room and her drink in both hands, and she is not looking at anything, and every so often she checks the door.

Nobody comes.

The barman collects glasses around her.

SHARON (V.O.):
"They all grew up. One got pregnant, two got jobs with lanyards, and the group chat went quiet in about six weeks."

She is still there when the lights come up.

SHARON (V.O.):
"And I kept going out. On my own. In the same dress. Waiting for literally anyone to walk over."

A man arrives beside her. He is nothing. He is anyone.

MAN:
"Alright?"

She turns her head and looks at him for less than a second.

CUT.

Her bed. Dark. She is on top of him, riding him, both hands flat on his chest, and she is looking over his shoulder at the wall.

CUT.

She puts the glass down and gets her coat.

SHARON (V.O.):
"They always did. That was never the problem."

Beat.

SHARON (V.O.):
"And then the money went, because it does."

Beat.

SHARON (V.O.):
"So I got a job."

AISLE FOUR

Supermarket. Fluorescent. The specific silence of a Tuesday afternoon.

TANNOY:
"Cleaner to aisle four, please. Cleaner to aisle four."

Sharon, twenty-one, in a polo shirt with somebody else's name badge on it, wheeling a yellow mop bucket that does not steer.

Aisle four is a warzone. Four jars down, sauce and glass across two metres of floor, and a toddler in the middle of it with a fifth jar in both hands, deciding.

The mother is on her phone.

Sharon gets down on her knees in it.

She picks glass out first, with her fingers, one piece at a time, into a cloth.

The mother lowers the phone.

CUSTOMER:
"Excuse me. Are you actually going to clean that, or..."

Sharon looks up at her from the floor.

Beat.

SHARON:
"Sorry. Won't be a minute."

She goes back to it.

The child drops the fifth jar.

It goes everywhere. Some of it goes on Sharon.

The mother laughs, the way people do when it is not their mess.

Sharon does not look up again.

SHARON (V.O.):
"Six pound eighty an hour. My rent was more than that job was."

A back office. Her manager, a man in his forties with a lanyard and a clipboard, is not looking at her.

MANAGER:
"I need you to do the four til close Thursday and Friday."

A beat.

SHARON:
"...Yeah. No, that's fine."

SHARON (V.O.):
"And that is where I learned it. Not later. There."

Beat.

SHARON (V.O.):
"I lasted seven months. Then I got behind a bar, which I thought was a step up, because it was nights and there was a staff discount."

THE BAR

A pub, busy, loud. Sharon, twenty-two, carrying two pints high through a crowd.

A hand goes up her skirt.

She does not stop walking. She does not spill either pint. Her face does one thing for a quarter of a second and then puts itself away.

She sets the drinks down on the right table and turns back through the crowd.

Behind the bar, the manager has watched the whole thing from six feet away.

He turns to the till.

SHARON (V.O.):
"Making a scene costs you the shift. Everyone learns that in about a fortnight."

The narrow stretch behind the bar between the glass washer and the fridges, where two people cannot get past each other without touching.

Sharon is bent over the low fridge, getting bottles out.

The manager comes through behind her and puts his whole hand on her arse, and leaves it there, and squeezes on the way past.

He does not break stride. He does not break sentence either. He is halfway through telling the other barman about a delivery and he finishes it.

Sharon straightens up with four bottles in her hands.

She puts them on the counter.

She carries on.

SHARON (V.O.):
"Trevor. Fifty-eight. Wedding ring. He did that to every girl who worked that bar and not one of us ever said a word, because he did the rota."

A quick series, each one a beat shorter than the last: a measure poured for a customer and a mouthful taken from the bottle. A vodka in a Coke glass under the counter. A hand shaking on a pump.

Then: the floor of the pub, full, and the manager saying it to her in the middle of it, and not lowering his voice for anybody.

MANAGER:
"You've been drinking on my till. Do you think I'm thick? Get your shit and get out."

Every head at the bar turns.

Sharon takes the apron off over her head. Folds it. Puts it on the counter, squared to the edge.

And she walks out through all of them.

The door swings.

THE FLAT. NOW.

The water is still going. She has not moved.

SHARON (V.O.):
"And I won't sit here and tell you all of that was miserable, because it wasn't. That's the trouble with it."

Beat.

SHARON (V.O.):
"I was twenty-three when it turned. And it wasn't a person, and it wasn't my brother, and it wasn't anything you'd put in a film."

Beat.

SHARON (V.O.):
"It was a bloke in a Corsa who didn't know how a give way works."

THE JUNCTION

Daylight. A car at a junction with L plates on it.

Sharon, twenty-three, is screaming.

SHARON:
"...NO, because it is MINE, mate, it is my junction, you came from a give way, THERE IS A FUCKING GIVE WAY THERE..."

The other driver is out of his car now, arms out, doing the what-are-you-going-to-do-about-it walk.

The driving instructor in the passenger seat has both hands flat on the dashboard and the expression of a man reviewing his career.

INSTRUCTOR:
"Sharon. Sharon."

SHARON:
"HE CAME FROM A GIVE WAY."

Cut.

Her flat. Night. She is still in her coat.

She is on a laptop that takes a long time to do anything, and she is reading.

Wide: the room around her is a mess, and she has not noticed it in an hour.

Close: the screen. Highway Code, section by section. She scrolls.

She finds it.

She reads it twice.

She sits back.

SHARON:
"...I was right."

She stares at the ceiling for a second with an expression that is almost frightening in how pleased it is.

Then she leans forward and clicks the next section.

And the next one.

Time passes in the light on her face.

SHARON (V.O.):
"That is genuinely how it happened. Not a calling. I wanted to win an argument with a man whose name I never found out, and there was a book that said I had."

She is still reading when it gets light.

HUNGOVER

A lecture theatre. Sharon in the third row with sunglasses pushed up on her head and a bin bag complexion. Around her, people are typing.

SHARON (V.O.):
"So I joined a university."

She has one page of notes with about nine words on it.

LECTURER:
"...so if anyone would like to try and reconcile those two authorities for me. Anyone at all." He turns round from the board and pushes his glasses back up the bridge of his nose with one finger, waiting.

SHARON (V.O.):
"...To study law."

Nothing.

Sharon does not put her hand up. She just starts talking, still looking at the desk.

SHARON:
"You can't. One of them is about the duty and one of them is about the remedy. They're not in conflict, they're not even about the same thing, it's just that everyone cites them together because they were in the same textbook."

A pause.

The lecturer looks at her for slightly too long.

LECTURER (O.S.):
"...Yes. That is right."

The girl next to her turns and stares.

Sharon puts her head back down on her arms.

SHARON (V.O.):
"I never got clean. I passed drunk."

A phone in a kitchen somewhere, on loudspeaker on a table, her mother's voice too loud and delighted, an old man laughing in the background, an older woman saying "put her on, put her on".

SHARON (V.O.):
"I could out-argue anybody in that building on four hours' sleep. So nobody ever made me build the other thing. The discipline. The bit underneath."

Beat.

SHARON (V.O.):
"When it went, there was nothing under it."

Beat.

SHARON (V.O.):
"Four years of it. I was twenty-seven when I finished."

THE CAP

Outside a hall. Sunshine. A crowd of gowns.

The four of them again: mum, grandad, nan, and Sharon in the middle in the gown with the certificate.

Somebody counts them in.

She throws the cap.

It goes up.

We stay on it. Blue sky. It turns over once.

A phone rings.

The cap is still in frame when it does.

Cut to her face, and the smile is still there, and she is reaching into her gown for the phone with the other hand still in the air, and she is laughing at something her nan has just said.

She answers it.

SHARON:
"Hello?"

And we do not hear the other end.

We stay on her.

The smile does not fall off her face. It stops being connected to anything, which is worse.

SHARON:
"...Sorry, say that again."

A beat.

Her mother, behind her, has stopped smiling because she is watching her daughter's back.

SHARON:
"No."

She turns away from her family.

SHARON:
"No, no, it can't... no, because he was..."

Her hand goes over her mouth and stays there.

Somewhere behind her the cap comes down and hits the grass and nobody picks it up.

Long hold.

SHARON (V.O.):
"They told me."

Beat.

SHARON (V.O.):
"That is the sentence I have used for seven years. They told me. I have never once, in seven years, asked myself who they were."

THE GRAVE

Winter. A small turnout. Twelve people, maybe.

Her mother is being held up on both sides.

A boy of six in a black coat that is a size too big is holding an old man's hand and looking at the hole with his mouth slightly open, because nobody has explained it in a way that worked.

Sharon stands slightly apart.

Dry-eyed.

And we see her try. We see her actually try, for a second, and nothing comes.

And we see two people from the family clock that she is not crying, and look at each other.

SHARON (V.O.):
"They noticed. Of course they noticed."

A glass-fronted office. A partner in a good suit, being kind.

PARTNER:
"Take the six weeks, Sharon. Take longer. It'll be here."

Cut: Sharon at her desk the following morning at ten past seven, first one in, coat still on.

Cut: the same desk, later, with nobody at it.

Cut: the same desk, later still, with somebody else's things on it.

SHARON (V.O.):
"I never used the degree again."

Beat.

SHARON (V.O.):
"My nan went eighteen months after him."

THE NAN

A different funeral. Spring. A church, a proper turnout, people in hats, somebody laughing in the second row at a story about her.

Sharon at the back.

And this time it is coming out of her and she cannot stop it, and she is furious about that, and she is holding onto the pew in front with both hands.

SHARON (V.O.):
"My nan. Ninety-one. In her own bed, in her sleep, in a house she owned, with the telly still on."

Her mother reaches over and puts a hand on her back and Sharon lets her, which she did not at the other one.

SHARON (V.O.):
"And I sat there in bits and I thought: oh."

Beat.

SHARON (V.O.):
"So that's what it's supposed to feel like."

She looks up at the front of the church.

SHARON (V.O.):
"That's the one they let me have."

Beat.

SHARON (V.O.):
"I went out that night. Same dress."

Hold on her.

Black.

THE BAR, ANY BAR

Interior. Loud. Late.

Sharon at the bar on her own. Twenty-five. She is not dressed for it. She has come out because the alternative was the flat.

A man arrives at her shoulder. He is fine. He is nothing.

MAN:
"Can I get you one?"

She looks at him for slightly less time than it takes to decide anything.

SHARON:
"Yeah."

Cut.

Street. Cold. The two of them walking, not touching, not talking. He is telling a story. She is not listening to it and he has not noticed.

Her building.

THE DOOR

She has the key in the lock.

And she stops.

Hold on her hand on the key.

Something arrives in her, from a long way down, for the first time in years. We should be able to see it get to her face.

She turns round.

SHARON:
"...I don't think I want you to come in."

Quiet. Not an argument. A fact she has just found out about herself.

The man's smile drops for half a second.

And comes back different.

MAN:
"Ohh. Come on."

Warm. Reasonable. A little bit hurt on her behalf.

MAN:
"I've come all the way over here. It's freezing. I'm not going to do anything."

She says nothing.

MAN:
"Ten minutes. I'll have a glass of water and I'll go. You're making it weird."

A beat.

And that is the one that does it. Not the charm. The last four words.

She turns the key.

THE CEILING

Inside.

The door shuts.

We do not stay with the two of them for any of it. We go where she goes, and where she goes is up.

Her ceiling.

Artexed, badly, by somebody in about 1988. A crack running from the light fitting towards the window that she has looked at a thousand times. A dead fly in the bowl of the shade, a little dark comma that has been up there for months.

The room moves. The light moves with it.

She is looking at the fly.

Sound is in the room and it is not softened and there is no music in this scene. The bed. The headboard finding the wall on a beat you can count, and she is counting it. His breath going in and out somewhere above her collarbone. One of her own arms is folded up underneath her and going dead at the elbow, and she leaves it there.

Her breath comes out of her in small pushes, because it is being pushed. That is the only part of her moving on its own.

SHARON (V.O.):
"I let him in. I kissed him. I lifted my hips so it'd come off easier. I opened my legs and I waited."

The crack. The fly.

And she stops.

Close on her eyes.

They have been open and flat on that fly for a long time. They twitch.

A sound gets out of her. Small. She did not authorise it.

Nothing in the voiceover. She has lost her place.

It happens again.

Her eyes open wider.

Again.

Wider.

And her knees are going further apart and she has not told them to. Her hips come up once, towards him, and she catches herself doing it, and it happens again anyway.

She is still looking at the ceiling. She is not looking at it the same way. She is holding onto it.

SHARON (V.O.):
"And there it is. The bit I've never said out loud."

He feels the change in her. All of it at once, how wet she has suddenly got, and he takes it as his.

And that is what finishes him.

He buries himself and lets out one long satisfied noise somewhere above her ear.

On her face, and only on her face:

SHARON (THOUGHT):
"No. No no no no no."

Not because he has finished.

Because she wanted him to keep going.

And the flat face comes back. Exactly the same face she had before, and not the same at all, because before there was nothing underneath it and now there is.

SHARON (V.O.):
"I didn't want him. And when he stopped, I was angry with him for stopping."

Beat.

SHARON (V.O.):
"Six years. That's still the one I can't file."

He does not get off her.

His whole weight comes down, all of it, dead, and he is panting, and her ribs cannot get all the way open underneath him.

She does not move him.

Her arms come up and she puts them around his back, both of them, and she holds him, the way you hold somebody you are pleased to see.

And she does not stop looking at the ceiling.

He stays inside her until he has gone soft. It takes a while. Long enough for her to work out that he is not waiting by accident.

Then he pulls out of her slowly, taking his time about it, like a man being considerate.

She makes no sound at all.

Hold. Longer than is comfortable. Do not cut early.

AFTERWARDS

She has not moved. She is in the shape he left her in, one arm still dead underneath her, looking up.

He is dressing. We see him only as much as she does, which is at the edge of frame and out of focus, a shape doing a belt.

He is in no hurry. He has a look round the room while he does it, the way you check a hotel before you hand the key back.

MAN:
"You alright?"

Nothing.

MAN:
"You're quiet, you."

Nothing.

MAN:
"...Was alright though, weren't it."

It is not a question. None of them are. He is already looking for his other shoe.

MAN:
"Nah, cos you were proper into it at the end there."

And there it is on his face. He is pleased with himself. He thinks the quiet is him.

She sees all of it. She gives him nothing.

SHARON (V.O.):
"He asked me four things on the way out and not one of them had a question in it."

Footsteps. Her kitchen tap running for two seconds and going off again, because he has helped himself to a glass of water.

The front door. It does not even slam. It closes the way a door closes when somebody has had a normal evening.

Silence in the flat.

She is still looking at the ceiling. Stay there long enough that the audience starts wanting her to get up.

Then she moves, and not to get up.

She tightens everything she has and holds it, hard, because she can feel him about to come out of her and there is one set of sheets in this flat and she is lying on them.

She gets her hand down between her legs and holds it there.

And she gets off the bed like that, bent over, one hand between her legs and the other flat on the mattress, and she crosses her own bedroom and goes into the bathroom.

She does not put the light on.

At the sink she takes her hand away and turns it over.

Close on it.

Her palm and her fingers are covered in his cum.

She looks at it.

Her face still has nothing on it.

THE CABINET

She washes her hands first. Both of them, at the sink, in the dark, for longer than washing hands takes.

Then she reaches past the curtain and puts the shower on and sits down on the closed lid of the toilet, still dressed, and waits for the water to get hot enough.

Cut: under the water.

Too hot. Much too hot. Her skin has come up red and blotched across the chest and shoulders and she is standing straight into it and not flinching.

She is not washing.

Then she starts washing, and she does it hard, with the flannel, in one place, for a long time.

Low shot. The drain. Water going round it, and going down it, and going down with it, a thin white thread of him coming off her.

She watches it go.

SHARON (V.O.):
"I keep waiting for the bit where I feel something about it."

Beat.

SHARON (V.O.):
"It never came. Not that night. Not the week after. Nothing. That frightened me more than he did."

The mirror. Steamed over. She wipes an oval in it with the side of her fist and there she is.

She opens it.

Inside: a strip of birth control, a box of paracetamol, a box of something to sleep. That is the entire contents of the cabinet. There is nothing in there for a person who is planning anything.

She pops one out of the strip and takes it with water from the tap, and it is not a moment, and it takes four seconds, and she has done it a thousand times, and the audience should notice that it takes four seconds.

She shuts the cabinet.

The mirror comes back and she is in it, towel round her, hair flat, the red already going out of her skin.

She looks at herself for a while.

SHARON (V.O.):
"I got up, and I had a shower, and I took a pill, and I went to work."

THE FLAT. NOW.

She has been in there a long time. The water has started to go cold at the edges and she has not turned it up.

Her hand is flat on the tile. Her head is down.

She is not crying.

SHARON (V.O.):
"Right."

Beat.

SHARON (V.O.):
"I got up at seven the next morning, same as I did every morning."

THE MORNING

Daylight through the curtains.

She strips the bed. She does it properly. Corners, pillowcases, the lot, into the machine.

She showers again.

She puts on the clothes for the job she is not going to keep.

She picks up her phone.

Contacts. Her thumb goes down the list.

MUM.

She looks at it.

She puts the phone in her pocket.

And she goes to work.

SHARON (V.O.):
"I never told anyone."

Wide: the flat behind her as she leaves.

On the wall by the door, in a cheap clip frame her mother bought, is a law degree with her name on it.

SHARON (V.O.):
"I could argue anything. With anyone."

SHARON (V.O.):
"I could not tell you why I let him in... Maybe I just wanted to... Feel... Something... Anything."

The front door closes.

SHARON (V.O.):
"Then, weeks later, on one night..."

Black.

THE TELEVISION

Weeks later. The flat. Evening.

There is no music in this scene and there is none in the next one. Room tone, the telly, and the extractor fan still labouring away in the bathroom.

Sharon on the floor with her back against the sofa, a towel round her and another one in her hands, drying her hair. The telly is on because the telly is on.

Her face is the flat one. Not sad. Not anything. She is watching it the way you watch a bus go past.

NEWSREADER (O.S.):
"...found no misconduct on the part of any officer involved, although the family have described the outcome as, and I quote, an insult to his memory..."

She keeps drying her hair.

She swaps hands.

REPORTER (O.S.):
"...figures out this morning put stop and search in the borough up thirty-one per cent, with the force again declining to publish a breakdown by..."

She reaches sideways without looking, misses, gets the moisturiser on the second go, and starts doing her arms.

Nothing on her face. Not agreement, not anger, nothing. It is furniture.

The programme changes. Now it is one of the ones shot off a dashboard, blue light washing the inside of a car.

OFFICER (O.S., radio):
"...he's coming back towards us, he's coming back towards..."

SECOND OFFICER (O.S.):
"He's getting away! HE'S GETTING AWAY!"

Sharon rolls her eyes.

It is the first thing her face has done in about ninety seconds.

She goes back to her legs with the towel.

PRESENTER (O.S.):
"...pursued for around four miles before officers made the decision to stand down on safety grounds. The occupants have not been traced. A spokesperson said the force's priority remains public safety..."

And her hands slow down in the towel.

She looks at the screen properly for the first time all night.

SHARON:
"...You don't know how to do your job."

She says it to a television, quietly, with total contempt.

Beat.

SHARON:
"Maybe if you did, people like Jaden wouldn't die."

She sits with that.

FOUR WORDS

She gets up to turn it off.

And catches herself in the glass.

Not a mirror. The glass of the clip frame on the wall. Her own face, sitting on top of her own name, on top of a degree she has not opened a book for in months.

She stops.

She looks at it for a long time.

SHARON:
"...How hard can it be?"

Hold on the reflection.

Hold.

FREEZE

She drops the towel on the bed on her way past and goes into the bathroom with nothing on.

It is still steamy in there from earlier. The mirror is fogged at the edges and clear in the middle where she wiped it hours ago.

She reaches for her toothbrush. It is on the window ledge, next to the toothpaste.

And she catches herself in the mirror, and the hand stops halfway.

She looks at herself.

A long time.

Room tone. The fan. Somebody else's telly through the wall.

SHARON:
"...How hard can it be."

Not a question this time.

Then her right hand comes up. Index finger out. Thumb up.

Slowly. All the way, until it is pointed at her own face.

She holds it there.

She puts it down.

Beat.

She does it again. Quicker.

Down.

Again, and this time it is fast, and it is nearly good.

Down.

She stands there and looks at herself.

Then she reaches past her own reflection and takes the toothbrush in one hand and the toothpaste in the other, and she looks down at the two of them, and at the sink.

And she drops the toothpaste.

It goes in the basin.

Both hands snap up round the toothbrush, straight out at the mirror, arms locked, one eye shut, the whole thing.

SHARON:
"Freeze."

Nothing moves.

Pull out. Wide. A naked woman on her own in a small steamy bathroom at night, aiming a toothbrush at herself in a mirror, holding it, and not laughing.

Hold.

Black.

UNIFORM

Quick, and it should feel like it takes years, because it does.

A form on a kitchen table, being filled in with a biro that stops working halfway.

A gym hall. A row of people in identical black, being shouted at.

A locker with SHARON YOUNG on a strip of tape.

Night. Rain. A shoplifter face down on a wet pavement and Sharon's knee in his back and her voice completely level.

A domestic. A woman in a doorway saying nothing while Sharon writes.

Paperwork. A lot of paperwork. Fluorescent light. Four in the morning. A canteen. More paperwork.

SHARON (V.O.):
"I was good at it almost straight away."

She is signing something, and the officer next to her is watching her do it.

SHARON (V.O.):
"Not because I'm a nice person. Because I could out-argue anyone in that building, and because there was nothing left anybody could say to me that would land."

THE OFFICE

A corridor. Better carpet up here.

A door.

On it, a small brass plate:

SUPERINTENDENT T. LUCAS

Sharon, in uniform, twenty-eight, knocks.

LUCAS (O.S.):
"Come."

Inside. Books nobody has read. A window with a view of a car park. A man in his fifties behind a desk, big, properly overweight, a good suit that has been let out and a shirt working hard at the buttons. He does not look like a monster, because he is not one. He is something much more ordinary than that.

On the desk in front of him, open, is a personnel file.

It stays open for the entire scene.

The camera can see it. She never does. She is looking at him, and then at the door.

LUCAS:
"Sit down, Sharon. Do you want a coffee? It's terrible."

SHARON:
"I'm alright, sir."

He turns a page.

LUCAS:
"Your annual. And your training file. And two things from the borough that I asked for myself, which I do not do."

He looks up.

LUCAS:
"You are the best natural investigator to come through this building in about fifteen years."

She does not know what to do with that.

Nobody has said anything like it to her since she was nineteen.

LUCAS:
"You see between things. It's not something we can teach and it is not something most of them will ever have. You hold detail. You had that Kemp statement in your head three weeks after you took it, and you were right about it, and a DS with nine years on you was wrong."

A beat.

SHARON:
"...Thank you, sir."

And she means it. That is the part that has to hurt.

He closes the file. Not all the way. Just enough.

LUCAS:
"So. You want CID."

SHARON:
"Yes, sir."

LUCAS:
"Four years. Two in uniform, two on the programme, and that is if nothing goes wrong and nobody takes a dislike to you."

SHARON:
"I know, sir."

He nods slowly, like a man being asked to explain the weather.

LUCAS:
"Let me tell you something about this force, and I am not being unkind, I am being accurate, because I think you have earned accurate."

He sits back.

LUCAS:
"No woman climbs the ranks here. Not on merit. Not on results. I have been here twenty-six years and I have watched it not happen to better officers than you."

Silence.

He does not leer. He does not lean forward. He does not threaten her. He looks mildly regretful, the way you look when you deliver a policy you did not write.

LUCAS:
"So the question is only ever how much you want it."

And he lets it sit there.

He does not ask her for anything.

He has not, technically, said a single word he could not repeat in a room full of people.

Hold on Sharon.

She looks at the door.

She looks at the desk. Not at the file on it. At the desk.

She thinks about it. We watch her think about it. She is not overwhelmed and she is not panicking. She is pricing it, the way she prices everything, and the audience should be able to see the arithmetic happening.

And then it is decided.

She gets up.

And she does not go to the door.

She comes round the side of the desk and she stands over him.

We are looking up at her. She is looking down.

Hold it there. This is the shot of the episode. Twenty-eight, uniform pressed, back straight, and her face is the flattest thing in the building. Underneath her, filling a chair that is not big enough for him, a fat man in his fifties with a good haircut and a pen still in his hand, and he is smiling up at her, entirely at ease, because nothing about his own body has ever embarrassed him.

She goes down, out of frame.

Stay on him.

Sound: a belt buckle coming undone. Unhurried. Nobody is in a rush.

Push in on the lower half of his face.

The pleasant smile is still there.

And then it changes. It does not become a leer. It becomes something quieter and worse: the face of a man who has just been proved right about the world.

Cut.

THE TAP

A station toilet. Strip light, one flickering. No music in this scene and none anywhere near it. Running water, the extractor, and a corridor somewhere behind the door.

Sharon at the sink with the tap on.

She is looking at herself the way you look at yourself when there is nobody else in the building.

She cups water and rinses her mouth. Spits. Does it again.

SHARON (V.O.):
"He tasted bad."

She does it a third time and holds it longer.

She wipes the corner of her mouth with the side of her thumb and checks the thumb.

Her lipstick is gone off one side of her mouth and still there on the other.

She lifts the collar of her own shirt and smells it.

SHARON (V.O.):
"And what is that smell."

She looks down at herself.

She brushes at the knees of her uniform trousers. Twice.

There is nothing on them.

She straightens up. She swallows and it goes down wrong and she pulls a face at herself.

Then she stops.

She puts two fingers into her mouth, right to the back, and hooks at something.

She cannot get it.

She tries again and gags, quietly, and steadies herself on the edge of the sink with her other hand.

Third go.

And she gets it, and brings it out on the end of her finger.

One hair. Not hers.

She looks at it for a long time.

Then she puts her hand under the tap and washes it off and watches it go round and go down.

A cubicle door opens behind her.

She has been in there the whole time.

A woman in her forties. Plain clothes, lanyard, the face of somebody who has been on shift for eleven hours. She comes to the next sink and puts her hands under the water.

She does not look at Sharon.

She looks at Sharon's reflection.

One flick of the eyes. Down and up. The knees. The mouth. The hair at the front, flattened on one side.

Then back to her own hands, and she washes them properly, and she says absolutely nothing at all.

Sharon turns her tap off.

She dries her hands. She squares her shoulders in the glass, once, the way you do before a room.

And she goes.

The door swings shut behind her.

The woman is still at the sink with the water running over her hands.

She is not washing them any more.

She is watching the door in the mirror.

Cut to: the file on Lucas's desk, being closed by a hand.

Hold on it one beat longer than the scene needs.

THE CARD

A warrant card in a plastic wallet.

DETECTIVE CONSTABLE S. YOUNG.

She is walking through the office with it in her hand and her chin up.

Two officers watch her go past.

One of them says something to the other. We do not hear it.

The other one laughs.

SHARON (V.O.):
"It worked."

Beat.

SHARON (V.O.):
"That's the bit nobody warns you about. It worked."

THE FLAT. NOW.

Cold water now, properly cold, and she is standing straight in it.

SHARON (V.O.):
"Three years in. Plain clothes by then, and a caseload, and a shoulder number people had started to remember."

Beat.

SHARON (V.O.):
"And this is the one I still can't file."

THE DONUT

Night. Three years later. A parade of shops, most of them shuttered.

Sharon comes out of a place with a paper bag and a coffee, in plain clothes now, and she takes a bite and then stops chewing and looks at the thing in her hand with an expression of genuine self-disgust.

SHARON:
"...Oh, you're joking."

She is a detective. Eating a donut. At night. In a car park.

She shakes her head at herself.

And then she stops.

Because down the side of the building, in the gap between the shops, there are two people in black having an argument they do not want anybody to hear.

She puts the donut down on the roof of the car.

THE ALLEY

She moves along the wall.

Two figures. Hoods, dark clothes, the tops of their faces covered. One of them has the other by the front of his coat.

NINJA 1:
"...I'm not asking you again, you get me?"

NINJA 2:
"Bruv..."

NINJA 1:
"I will nank you, bruv. In front of your mum, in front of your fucking dog, I do not care."

Sharon draws.

She comes round the corner in a proper stance, both hands on it, and it is textbook, and her voice is clear and level and exactly right.

SHARON:
"Armed police! Show me your hands! Do not move!"

The two of them turn and look at her.

A beat.

And then one of them starts laughing.

Genuinely. Delightedly. He has to put a hand on the wall.

NINJA 1:
"...Girl said freeze, yano!"

NINJA 2:
"She never said freeze."

NINJA 1:
"She said don't move, same ting."

He wipes his eye.

NINJA 1:
"Or else what, darlin'? You gonna arrest us? Fuck off, man."

Sharon does not lower the weapon.

She has done everything right. Everything. The stance, the words, the distance.

And it has bought her nothing at all, and it has taken about four seconds to find that out.

MOVE

The laughing stops.

Not because of her.

Because both of them are now looking past her shoulder.

The change on their faces is total.

Sharon does not turn round.

MAN (O.S.):
"Move."

One syllable, from behind her, low.

And her body does it before her mind agrees to. She steps aside. She has no memory of deciding to.

He walks past her.

We do not get his face.

He does not look at her.

FACE:
"Run along. You don't belong here."

And Sharon, because she is Sharon, brings the weapon back up.

SHARON:
"Sir, put your hands..."

She does not finish it.

Not because she is interrupted.

Because the gun is no longer in her hands.

He has it. He is holding it the way you hold something you have been asked to look after.

And then his hand closes.

The sound is wrong. Metal is not supposed to make that sound.

He opens his hand and lets the pieces go and they hit the ground like change.

Sharon's hand goes to her radio.

It is not there.

He is holding it. He has been holding it since before she reached for it.

He crushes that too, in the same movement, without looking at it, and drops it.

He has not touched her once.

FACE:
"Go home."

THE CALL SHE CANCELS

Running. Her own breath. Shoes on wet pavement.

She gets her phone out at a corner and she is dialling before she has stopped.

SHARON:
"This is Detective Constable Sharon Young, shoulder number four-one-nine-two, I need urgent assistance at the rear of the parade on..."

A beat.

SHARON:
"...there's a, there's something..."

And she hears it.

We watch her hear herself.

SHARON:
"...I mean someone. There's someone."

The line is asking her a question.

She looks at the phone.

She hangs up.

She stands in the street with her hand over her mouth.

SHE GOES BACK

The alley. Empty.

No ninjas. No man. No sound but a fan unit somewhere.

She walks in slowly, and she is nearly hoping it is not there.

It is there.

The pieces of her firearm on the wet ground, and the pieces of her radio next to them, in a spread about a metre across.

She crouches.

She picks up a piece of it and turns it over in her fingers.

The metal is folded. Not broken. Folded, like paper.

SHARON:
"...How?"

Nobody answers her.

THE STATION

An interview room being used as an office. A colleague across the table with a pen he is barely moving.

On the table between them, sealed in a clear exhibit bag, is what is left of her firearm. She has bagged it, sealed it, signed the label and booked it in, all of it correctly, because she does everything correctly.

He has not touched it once.

COLLEAGUE:
"So you're telling me a bloke appeared out of nowhere..."

SHARON:
"I'm telling you what happened."

COLLEAGUE:
"...took your firearm off you, and crushed it. With his hand."

SHARON:
"Yes."

COLLEAGUE:
"And your radio."

SHARON:
"Yes."

He looks up.

COLLEAGUE:
"And then what? He just, what, disappeared into thin fucking air?"

And Sharon opens her mouth to answer.

And hears exactly how it is going to sound before it comes out.

Beat.

She stands up. The chair goes over behind her.

SHARON:
"Forget it."

She is out of the door.

The colleague looks at the fallen chair. He picks his pen back up and writes one short line and closes the book.

Cut: an exhibit label being filled in. Her handwriting. SY/1.

Cut: a ballistics report, weeks later. Two lines of it in focus.

DAMAGE CONSISTENT WITH MECHANICAL COMPRESSION. MOST PROBABLE CAUSE VEHICULAR.

Cut: a property store. Shelf after shelf of bags. One of them says SY/1.

Nobody ever calls her about it again.

THE TRUTH

Outside. The car park. Rain starting.

Sharon stands with both hands on the roof of her car and her head down.

She is shaking. Not from fear.

She looks up.

SHARON:
"There isn't a word for it."

Beat.

SHARON:
"That's the whole problem. There's no word for it, so there's no box for it, so there's no form for it."

Beat.

SHARON:
"So it didn't happen."

She gets in the car.

She sits there with the keys in her hand and does not put them in.

SHARON:
"...So I'll find one."

She starts the engine.

Black.

OUT OF THE WATER

Present day. The flat.

The shower shuts off.

Silence, and the drip of it, and the extractor fan labouring.

Sharon steps out into the steam, gets a towel, and stands there for a second with her eyes shut.

She comes out into the front room in a t-shirt and her underwear, hair wet, and stops.

The drive is exactly where she threw it on the bed.

THE WORK

Later. Ten past two in the morning.

Something is cooking that she is not watching. She is eating out of the pan with a fork, standing up.

The telly is on and it is not television. It is the CCTV off the stolen drive, running at half speed, and she has been through it enough times to know the frame numbers.

SHARON (THOUGHT):
"What are you."

On screen: the wrecked corridor. The impossible blur. The wall coming apart.

She rewinds it. Watches it again. Rewinds it again.

SHARON (THOUGHT):
"Right. The wall. That's a charge. Plastic, PE4, something like that, on a timer, and the blur is the frame rate."

She nods at her own telly, satisfied, for about a second and a half.

Then she rewinds it again.

SHARON (THOUGHT):
"...There's no flash."

She points the fork at the screen.

SHARON (THOUGHT):
"And how did he get up there. Fifth floor. The lifts were off, the stairwell is covered, and he is not on it."

She squints at it, chewing.

SHARON (THOUGHT):
"So he came in the window. He came in the window from... from where. From what."

She stops chewing.

She leans in.

She does not finish the sentence.

And on the wall behind her, above the sofa, unremarked, there is a poster in a bus shelter frame she got from somewhere, or a magazine open on the arm, or a box on the side with a logo on it. It does not matter which. It is in shot and nobody looks at it.

BIO GENETIX.

EVERYTHING YOU ARE. ONLY BETTER.

THE WRIST

She freezes the frame.

A hand, mid-movement, on the edge of a window frame. Pixelated to almost nothing.

She leans forward.

She gets closer.

And then she puts the pan down and gets down onto the floor, on her hands and knees, and crawls across her own living room carpet until her face is about eight inches from the screen.

She tilts her head.

On the wrist, in about nine pixels: a mark.

Small. Raised. Old.

She does not know what she is looking at.

She reaches up without looking and finds a pen and writes something on the back of her own hand.

THE CALL

The phone goes.

It is on the arm of the sofa, face down, buzzing itself round in a half circle.

She does not want to move. She is eight inches from the answer to something.

It keeps going.

She reaches back for it without taking her eyes off the screen.

She looks at the screen of the phone.

MUM.

Twenty past two in the morning.

And that is when she takes her eyes off the television.

She sits back on her heels.

SHARON:
"...Mum?"

And on the other end, we hear it before we understand it: her mother, trying to keep her voice reasonable and failing at it in the first four words.

IVY (O.S.):
"Sharon. Sharon, I'm sorry, I know what time it is..."

SHARON:
"What's happened."

IVY (O.S.):
"It's Kevin."

Sharon is already standing up.

IVY (O.S.):
"He come in and he's not right. He's not right, Sharon. He's not saying nothing and he won't let me look at him and he's just sat in the dark on the floor of his room and he's..."

A breath on the line.

IVY (O.S.):
"...I didn't know who else to ring."

And Sharon stands in the middle of her flat, at twenty past two in the morning, with the frozen frame of a man she cannot explain still glowing on the wall behind her.

Hold on her.

In E1 she rang him and he had his earphones in.

SHARON:
"...I'm on my way."

She is already reaching for her keys.

And the camera leaves her.

It turns away from her and goes to the wall, to the frozen frame on the screen, and it starts to move in on it. Slowly. It does not stop.

The paused frame. A wrecked office floor with the dust still hanging where the picture stopped it. A hole where a wall was. And sat up on the window frame with one foot on the sill and the whole white sky of Danim behind him, a man in a dark cloak, already half out of the building.

He is not looking down at the street.

He is looking back into the room.

You cannot see his face. You have never once been able to see his face.

Behind the camera, off screen, the flat: a drawer going, a coat coming off a hook, keys, feet, the front door pulled shut hard enough to shake the frame she is walking away from.

And music, for the first time in a long time in this episode. It comes up under the push and it builds.

The frame gets bigger and softer and dirtier as we go into it, until it is not a picture of a man any more, it is grain.

And on the wrist of the hand holding the window frame, nine pixels of something old, filling the screen.

Hold.

Black.

END OF EPISODE 3.

Draft complete, first pass. Outstanding per the outline: D1's remaining detail level is Bupe's, the Bio Genetix product in THE WORK needs choosing (poster, magazine or box), and the Kemp statement referenced by Lucas is a placeholder name for a real past case if one is ever wanted.
